### [1] [Just Keep Prompting: Evaluating Repetitive Socratic Prompting in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14099)
*Shayda Moezzi,Bishoy Galoaa,Lorena Genua,Taskin Padir,Sarah Ostadabbas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: JKP is a multi-turn evaluation framework that stress-tests Vision-Language Models by repeatedly challenging their answers across up to 10 turns. Testing GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B on STAR benchmark data reveals that repeated prompting often destabilizes rather than aids reasoning, with strongly model-dependent stability profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world VLM deployment requires not just strong single-turn visual reasoning but stability under sustained conversational pressure — when users repeatedly challenge, question, or contradict the model. Existing benchmarks evaluate one-shot accuracy but fail to capture epistemic stability, calibration drift, and compliance behavior across extended interactions.

Method: The authors introduce Just Keep Prompting (JKP), a multi-turn evaluation framework applying up to 10 follow-up turns with three perturbation strategies: (1) Adversarial Negation — repeatedly rejecting the model's answer; (2) Pure Socratic Interrogation — repeatedly asking the model to reassess its certainty; (3) Context-Aware Socratic Summarization — reflecting the model's prior rationale back before soliciting reconsideration. Evaluation covers 720 multi-turn runs on a subset of the STAR benchmark using GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B.

Result: Aggregate accuracy changes only modestly from Turn 0 to Turn 10, masking trajectory-level instability: correct answers regress, wrong answers recover, and many runs show repeated answer flipping. Repeated prompting provides bounded upside and more often acts as a destabilizer. Effects are strongly model-dependent: Qwen3-VL-30B achieves highest final accuracy but becomes confidently wrong under direct contradiction; Gemini 2.5 Pro is comparatively stable but token-expensive; GPT-4o is the most brittle and oscillatory.

Conclusion: Multi-turn VLM evaluation captures pressure-response profiles — how models trade off visual grounding, calibration, and conversational compliance under repeated challenge — revealing that sustained prompting is not a reliable reasoning aid and that epistemic stability is a distinct, model-specific capability deserving dedicated benchmarking.

Abstract: Deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world settings requires not only strong visual reasoning but also stability under sustained conversational pressure. We introduce Just Keep Prompting (JKP), a multi-turn evaluation framework that measures VLM epistemic stability when users repeatedly challenge, question, or contradict a model's answer. JKP probes models for up to 10 follow-up turns using three strategies: Adversarial Negation (repeated rejection), Pure Socratic Interrogation (repeated calls to reassess certainty), and Context-Aware Socratic Summarization (reflecting the model's prior rationale back before asking for reconsideration). We evaluate GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B on a subset of the STAR benchmark across 720 multi-turn runs. Aggregate accuracy changes modestly from Turn 0 to Turn 10, but trajectory-level analysis reveals substantial instability: correct answers regress, wrong answers recover, and many runs exhibit repeated answer flipping. Repeated prompting has bounded upside and often acts as a destabilizer rather than a reasoning aid. The effect is strongly model-dependent: Qwen3-VL-30B achieves the highest final accuracy but becomes confidently wrong under direct contradiction; Gemini 2.5 Pro is comparatively stable but token-expensive; GPT-4o is the most brittle and oscillatory. These findings reveal that multi-turn VLM evaluation captures not just additional reasoning but pressure-response profiles: how models trade off visual grounding, calibration, and conversational compliance under repeated challenge.

</details>


### [2] [Quantum Compositional NLP for Arabic: Grammar, Morphology, and Word Sense in Circuit Topology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14100)
*Wajahath Mohammed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First application of pregroup grammar-based quantum NLP to Arabic, converting sentences into quantum circuits where grammar dictates gate wiring. Evaluated on word order, morphological tense, and verb sense disambiguation against AraVec and AraBERT baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Arabic's morphological richness, free word order, and structural complexity make it an ideal testbed for evaluating whether quantum compositional models can capture grammatical structure in ways classical embeddings cannot. No prior QNLP work has addressed such a linguistically complex language.

Method: Pregroup grammar types assign grammatical roles to words, then map these onto quantum circuits via the DisCoCat (distributional compositional categorical) framework. Subjects, verbs, and objects become quantum gates; pregroup type reductions determine gate connectivity/wiring. Three experiments compare quantum circuit encodings against AraVec (static embeddings) and AraBERT (transformer) on classification tasks.

Result: Not specified in the provided abstract excerpt — the abstract describes the experimental design but does not include quantitative outcomes or performance comparisons.

Conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract — the excerpt focuses on system description and experimental setup rather than findings or implications.

Abstract: We present the first application of pregroup grammar-based quantum compositional natural language processing (QNLP) to Arabic; a morphologically rich, free-word-order language whose structural complexity provides a uniquely demanding testbed for theories of meaning composition in quantum circuits. Our system converts Arabic sentences into quantum circuits whose topology mirrors grammatical structure: subjects, verbs, and objects become quantum gates, and the typed dependencies between them (the pregroup grammar) determine how those gates are wired together. We conduct three controlled experiments spanning word order, morphological tense, and verb sense disambiguation, comparing quantum circuit methods against classical baselines including AraVec (Arabic word embeddings) and AraBERT (a pre-trained Arabic transformer).

</details>


### [3] [LBA: Textual Hard-Label Adversarial Attack under Low Query Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14101)
*Shixin Guo,Ming Zhong,Xuhong Zhang,Dandan Zhao,Zhe Wang,Bo Zhang,Shouling Ji,Hao Peng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LBA is a sampling-based hard-label adversarial attack that constructs an approximate distribution over promising adversarial text candidates by integrating prior and posterior knowledge, outperforming greedy/local search methods in query efficiency and adversarial text quality across diverse models and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hard-label adversarial text generation methods rely on greedy local search (substituting one position at a time), which fails to explore globally optimal position combinations and incurs excessive query costs. Exhaustive search over all position combinations is computationally infeasible, motivating a sampling-based approach that can efficiently approximate the optimal search.

Method: The proposed method, LBA (Likelihood-Based Attack), constructs an approximate distribution over high-quality adversarial examples by combining prior knowledge (initial heuristics about promising substitutions) and posterior knowledge (feedback from queries). Sampling from this distribution efficiently explores the combinatorial space, and as sampling progresses, posterior knowledge iteratively refines the distribution to guide more effective subsequent sampling.

Result: Extensive experiments on six language models (small-scale to large-scale) across four datasets show LBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on all evaluation metrics. LLM-based evaluations further confirm that LBA generates adversarial texts with better semantic preservation and comprehensibility.

Conclusion: LBA offers a novel sampling-based paradigm for hard-label adversarial text generation that overcomes the limitations of greedy local search, achieving superior attack performance, query efficiency, and text quality through distribution-guided sampling with iterative posterior refinement.

Abstract: Generating high-quality adversarial texts with low query budgets remains a challenging problem in the hard-label scenario. Most existing approaches rely on greedy algorithms, where one position in the text is selected for substitution, followed by the substitutions of other positions. This local search approach may fail to discover high-quality adversarial examples and often leads to excessive query costs. Ideally, an optimal adversarial sample would consider all possible position combinations in the text, but exhaustive search is computationally impractical. To address this challenge, we propose a sampling-based method called LBA, which constructs an approximate distribution of high-quality adversarial examples by integrating both prior and posterior knowledge, and utilizes this distribution for sampling. As sampling progresses, posterior knowledge updates the approximate distribution, which in turn guides more effective sampling. Extensive experiments on six language models, ranging from small-scale to large-scale architectures across four datasets, demonstrate that LBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on all evaluation metrics. Additionally, LLM-based assessment indicates that LBA generates more semantically preserved and comprehensible adversarial texts.

</details>


### [4] [UniSAGE: Unifying Static and Dynamic Attributes with Hyper-Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14102)
*Taoran Fang,Yan Deng,Chunping Wang,Yang Wang,Lei Chen,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: UniSAGE is a unified framework that jointly models static and dynamic attributes via a global attribute graph with orthogonal parameter subspaces and a hyper-structure mechanism, outperforming existing methods by over 10% on several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for hierarchical heterogeneous data require extensive manual design, are tightly coupled to specific schemas, and process static and dynamic attributes in isolation, ignoring their implicit interactions. A unified, automated, and schema-robust solution is needed.

Method: UniSAGE constructs a global attribute graph unifying hierarchical and temporal relationships. It introduces two orthogonal parameter subspaces for static aggregation and dynamic reasoning within a shared semantic space, and employs a lightweight hyper-structure mechanism to enable task-specific static-dynamic interaction.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks and a real-world financial behavior dataset show UniSAGE consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving over 10% performance improvement on several tasks.

Conclusion: UniSAGE provides a fully automated, schema-robust, unified framework that effectively captures complex cross-attribute dependencies between static and dynamic data, validated by significant empirical gains.

Abstract: With the rapid growth of digital data, real-world applications increasingly involve hierarchical information that combines static attributes with dynamic records. Modeling such heterogeneous data in a unified and generalizable manner remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on extensive manual design, are tightly coupled to specific data schemas, and typically process static and dynamic attributes in isolation, thereby overlooking their implicit interactions. We propose UniSAGE, a unified framework for modeling data with both static and dynamic attributes. UniSAGE constructs a global attribute graph that represents hierarchical and temporal relationships in a unified structure. To ensure representational consistency, it introduces two orthogonal parameter subspaces that jointly support static aggregation and dynamic reasoning within a shared semantic space. Building on these unified representations, UniSAGE further enables task-specific interaction between static and dynamic attributes via a lightweight hyper-structure mechanism. UniSAGE is fully automated, robust to evolving data schemas, and capable of capturing complex cross-attribute dependencies. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks and a real-world financial behavior dataset demonstrate that UniSAGE consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving performance improvements of over 10% on several tasks.

</details>


### [5] [Latent Communication Between Language Model Agents: Channels, Alignment, and the Limits of Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14103)
*Markus Wenzel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LLM agents lose information when communicating via text compared to latent-space communication. Using SAE feature analysis across three communication channels, the authors find text serialization destroys 88% of SAE features, but conclude these lost features primarily encode surface form rather than task-relevant semantics, negating their initial hypothesis that latent communication offers semantic advantages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors hypothesize that LLMs may possess world models exceeding text expressibility, and that text-based inter-agent communication in multi-agent systems loses information when conveying complex concepts. They aim to test this through structured experiments comparing text vs. latent communication channels.

Method: Three communication channels are constructed: (1) text channel, (2) dense-latent channel, and (3) SAE-sparse channel. The authors use Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis to quantify concept-discriminating information, probe accuracy under compression, cross-architecture alignment (Procrustes between Llama and Mistral), round-trip feature survival analysis, and task-level evaluation on cross-lingual concept tasks with and without latent feature augmentation.

Result: The SAE-sparse channel achieves 99.4% probe accuracy at 28x compression vs. 80.4% for text. Cross-architecture Procrustes alignment yields 92% top-1 retrieval. Text round-trip destroys 88% of SAE features via identity replacement (not attenuation). Linear Procrustes alignment incurs a 3-10pp penalty; nonlinear methods improve this. On cross-lingual concept tasks, the latent channel matches but never exceeds the text channel, and text augmentation with latent features provides no benefit.

Conclusion: The initial hypothesis is rejected: lost features during text communication mostly encode surface form, not task-relevant semantics. Latent communication shows no practical advantage over text for current tasks. Deeper tasks requiring complex concepts and improved analysis frameworks are needed to identify any genuine benefit of latent channels.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are utilized in many contexts and many professions. Those MAS rely on inter-agent communication, usually implemented by clear-text message passing. We hypothesize that Large Language Models may have a world model at their disposal that exceeds expressibility in text when complex concepts need to be communicated. Our aim is to approach a proof of this hypothesis with structured experiments. In this work, we show that LLM agents communicating via text lose information, which we quantify via Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis. We construct three communication channels and measure concept-discriminating information in each. We first show that the SAE-sparse channel retains a 99.4% probe accuracy at 28-fold compression over the dense-latent channel vs 80.4% for the text channel. We then proceed to examine the same for cross-architecture communication by using sparse latent space alignment. We find for Procrustes alignment a 92% top-1 retrieval between Llama and Mistral. Using a text round-trip, we perform feature survival analysis to find that text serialization destroys 88% of SAE features, replacing them with a different feature set. We attribute the loss to identity replacement, not attenuation. By our analysis, we were able to attribute a 3-10pp performance penalty to the linear Procrustes alignment, improving with nonlinear alignment methods. In a task-level evaluation we find that the latent channel matches the text channel on cross-lingual concept tasks but never exceeds it. Text augmentation with latent features provides no benefit, leading us to negative conclusions for the initial hypothesis: lost features mostly or completely encode surface form, not task-relevant semantics. To pinpoint the practical advantage of latent communication over a text channel, deeper tasks eliciting complex concepts and an corresponding analysis framework are needed.

</details>


### [6] [UzWordnet and Generative AI for Learning Uzbek by Game Playing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14104)
*Alessandro Agostini,Saydobid Khusanov,Mirkamol Mirkamilov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: An educational game platform for learning Uzbek that combines UzWordnet, an orthographic dictionary, and generative AI, while using game dynamics to simultaneously improve the lexical resource itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the scarcity of digital learning tools for the Uzbek language by creating an integrated system that supports both language acquisition and the enrichment of lexical resources like UzWordnet.

Method: Design of a system architecture incorporating UzWordnet and a large orthographic dictionary as lexical backends, generative AI for learning support, and four purpose-built educational games. Proposes a game-based methodology where player interactions yield data that directly improves and expands UzWordnet.

Result: An implemented architecture with four educational games that serves dual purposes: facilitating Uzbek language practice for learners and generating lexical data to enhance UzWordnet as a by-product of gameplay.

Conclusion: The dual-purpose approach — combining game design with lexical resource curation — effectively serves both educational and lexicographic goals, demonstrating a symbiotic relationship between language learning technology and linguistic resource development.

Abstract: This paper presents an educational system architecture that enables learners to practice the Uzbek language through game-playing. The architecture integrates UzWordnet and the largest currently available orthographic dictionary for Uzbek as core lexical resources, together with generative AI as a fundamental component for learning support. We design four educational games to facilitate Uzbek language learning and propose a game-based methodology for improving UzWordnet as a direct by-product of game dynamics. Our approach combines game design and lexical resources to address objectives that are at the same time educational (language learning) and lexical (improvement and enrichment of a lexical resource).

</details>


### [7] [Automatically Evolving Prompt Guidelines for Task-Specific Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14105)
*Cedric Richter,Salah Ghamizi,Mike Papadakis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: User queries are often underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer missing assumptions that misalign with user intent. AGOPS automatically generates task-specific guidelines from reference examples to help users write better-specified prompts, recovering 15.5–81.7% of performance lost due to underspecification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world user queries are frequently underspecified, lacking necessary requirements, context, and constraints. This forces LLMs to infer unstated assumptions that often diverge from actual user intent, causing significant performance degradation. Existing prompt engineering guidelines are manually crafted, generic, task-agnostic, and unsystematic, limiting their practical value. There is a need for an automatic, data-driven method to generate task-specific guidelines that help users formulate well-specified prompts.

Method: AGOPS formulates prompt guideline optimization as an iterative process with three components: (1) a prompt LLM writer that generates candidate task-specific guidelines, (2) a solver LLM that applies those guidelines to answer queries, and (3) a prompt evolution mechanism that refines guidelines by maximizing downstream effectiveness on a set of example user queries paired with reference answers. The key insight is that reference answers implicitly encode missing information (behavioral constraints, contextual assumptions, evaluation criteria) needed to resolve underspecified queries. At inference time, users follow the optimized guidelines to produce well-specified prompts.

Result: Prompt underspecification causes major performance drops of up to 95.3% compared to well-specified prompts across mathematical reasoning, medical QA, and coding benchmarks. Existing prompt optimization techniques fail to recover this loss. AGOPS guidelines enable users to regain 15.5–81.7% of lost performance on average, consistently across all benchmarks tested.

Conclusion: AGOPS demonstrates that automatically generated, task-specific guidelines derived from reference examples can effectively bridge the gap between underspecified user queries and model performance. The approach outperforms existing prompt optimization methods and provides a systematic, automated alternative to manual prompt engineering guidelines.

Abstract: For Large Language Models to reliably answer user queries, users must clearly specify requirements, context, and constraints. In practice, however, user queries are often underspecified, forcing models to infer unstated assumptions that may misalign with the actual user intent. Existing prompt engineering guidelines aim to mitigate this issue, they are typically generic and task-agnostic, limiting their practical utility. Additionally, existing guidelines are formed manually and in a non-systematic way. To this end, we study prompt guideline optimization: the problem of automatically generating task-specific guidelines that help write better-specified prompts for a given task and model. Our key observation is that existing (completed) task examples (aka reference answers) often implicitly encode the missing information required to complete underspecified queries, including behavioral constraints, contextual assumptions, and evaluation criteria. We therefore propose AGOPS, an automatic approach that evolves task-specific guidelines via an optimization scheme that involves a prompt LLM writer, a solver LLM and prompt evolution, which maximize downstream effectiveness on a set of examples (user queries with reference answers). At inference time, our guidelines help users write well-specified prompts, boosting the effectiveness of LLMs. We show across mathematical reasoning, medical question answering, and coding tasks, that prompt underspecification leads to major drops (up to 95.3%) in downstream task performance (compared to well-specified prompts) and, perhaps more importantly, that this drop can hardly be recovered by existing prompt optimization techniques. Users following AGOPS guidelines can regain this loss (increasing performance between 15.5 to 81.7% on average) consistently across all benchmarks.

</details>


### [8] [Token Time Continuous Diffusion for Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14106)
*Parikshit Bansal,Sujay Sanghavi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TTCD is a new diffusion language model that operates in continuous space with per-token timesteps, enabling faster and more accurate text generation at high speedups compared to discrete-space diffusion models, particularly excelling in conditional generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion language models operating purely in discrete space suffer from inaccuracy at high speedups due to the need for parallel sampling of multiple tokens. The authors aim to overcome this limitation while also improving conditional generation and enabling differentiated token-level refinement dynamics.

Method: TTCD operates in continuous space, deterministically mapping Gaussian noise to a final token canvas without requiring additional sampling. Crucially, it introduces per-token times, where different tokens can transition from noise to their final token state at different rates. A 160M parameter model is trained on OpenWebText and subsequently self-distilled.

Result: TTCD outperforms discrete-space diffusion models at high speedups. The self-distilled 160M model achieves comparable unconditional generation quality and superior conditional generation quality versus similarly sized models trained and distilled on the same data. Gains are also demonstrated on Sudoku solving.

Conclusion: Combining continuous-space diffusion with per-token timesteps effectively addresses the accuracy-speed tradeoff in diffusion language models, offering a promising direction for fast, high-quality text generation, especially in conditional settings.

Abstract: In this paper we introduce token time continuous diffusion (TTCD), a new diffusion language model which (a) operates in continuous space, deterministically mapping Gaussian noise to a final token canvas with no further sampling, and crucially (b) incorporates a new notion of per-token times, with some tokens proceeding from noise to token at a faster rate than others. Continuous space modeling helps TTCD avoid the parallel sampling of multiple tokens, which is a key source of inaccuracy at high speedups for models that iterate purely in discrete space. The notion of per-token times helps TTCD to better model conditional generation, allows for more sure tokens to proceed at a faster rate, and allows for differentiated inter-token influences during refinement. TTCD outperforms discrete models at high speedups. We train a 160M parameter TTCD model on OpenWebText, and then self-distill it; we find that at high speedups we are comparable in unconditional generation quality, and outperform in conditional generation, several existing models of similar size trained, on the same data, and self-distilled. We achieve similar gains in Sudoku solving as well.

</details>


### [9] [DS@GT ARC at LongEval: Citation Integrity and Factual Grounding in Scientific QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14400)
*Brandon Michaels,Brendon Johnson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a submission to CLEF 2026 LongEval Task 4 that investigates the tension between standard NLG metrics and citation integrity in RAG QA systems. Using a corrective pipeline combining CRAG and CiteFix, the authors show that while frontier models achieve high relevance and fluency, they often ignore retrieved context. Their pipeline marginally improves citation faithfulness and grounding, leading to a call for evaluation metrics that reward strict answer grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe a divergence between traditional natural language evaluation metrics (which prioritize relevance and fluency) and citation integrity in RAG-based QA systems. They are motivated by the problem that frontier models may generate fluent, relevant answers without faithfully using the retrieved documents they cite, undermining trustworthiness.

Method: The authors implement a corrective pipeline with two stages: (1) Corrective RAG (CRAG) for filtering retrieved chunks pre-generation to improve document relevance, and (2) CiteFix for post-generation enforcement of strict entailment between generated claims and cited source material. They evaluate this pipeline against baseline and frontier model RAG QA systems using both standard metrics and RAGAs LLM-as-judge diagnostics.

Result: Frontier models maximized answer relevance and fluency scores, but RAGAs diagnostics revealed they correctly identify relevant documents without actually using their context in answer generation. The corrective pipeline (CRAG + CiteFix) marginally improved citation faithfulness and answer grounding compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Evaluating trustworthy RAG QA requires moving beyond surface-level relevance and fluency metrics toward metrics that reward strict answer grounding and faithful citation usage. The divergence between standard metrics and citation integrity must be addressed for building reliable RAG systems.

Abstract: This paper describes DS@GT ARC's submission to the CLEF 2026 LongEval Task 4 on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In this submission, we examine a divergence between traditional natural language evaluation metrics and citation integrity as applied to RAG QA systems. We evaluate a corrective pipeline using Corrective RAG (CRAG) and CiteFix against baseline and frontier model benchmark RAG QA scores. While frontier models maximized answer relevance and fluency scores, our RAGAs LLM-as-judge diagnostics indicate that frontier models would correctly identify relevant documents without using their context in answer generation. Conversely, by filtering chunks pre-generation and enforcing strict entailment of generated claims to the cited material post-generation, our corrective pipeline marginally improved citation faithfulness and answer grounding. We propose that evaluation of trustworthy RAG QA requires metrics that reward strict answer grounding.

</details>


### [10] [Polestar: Drift-Aware Cache Calibration and Token Commitment for Efficient Inference of Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14107)
*Mingyu Lee,Akshat Ramachandran,Souvik Kundu,Tushar Krishna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Polestar is a training-free inference framework for diffusion LLMs that uses token representation drift as a unified signal to enable efficient KV-cache reuse and reliable parallel decoding, achieving up to 10.73% accuracy gains and 3.7× throughput improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs face two key inference bottlenecks: (1) bidirectional attention prevents efficient KV-cache reuse, and (2) static confidence thresholds for parallel decoding harm generation quality. Both issues stem from a shared root cause — token representations drift (evolve) across decoding steps due to contextual integration via bidirectional attention.

Method: Polestar is a training-free framework with two components built on a unified drift signal: (1) Polestar-Cache tracks token representation drift to identify stale KV-cache positions, performing sparse refreshes only where needed to enable efficient reuse; (2) Polestar-Commit detects sharp drift events to reliably determine which tokens are commit-ready, enabling high parallelism without compromising quality.

Result: Across math and coding benchmarks on multiple dLLM families, Polestar achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier results: up to 10.73% accuracy improvement, up to 3.7× higher throughput, and 3.67 tokens per forward pass in decoding parallelism over existing baselines.

Conclusion: Token representation drift serves as a powerful unified signal for jointly optimizing KV-cache efficiency and decoding parallelism in diffusion LLMs, enabling substantial practical gains without any retraining.

Abstract: The inference efficiency of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is constrained by two challenges: bidirectional attention precludes efficient KV-cache reuse, while increasing decoding parallelism with static confidence thresholds can compromise generation quality. We observe that both challenges arise from a shared phenomenon: as tokens are decoded, their contextual integration through bidirectional attention causes token representations to drift (evolve) across decoding steps. This insight motivates Polestar, a training-free inference framework that uses token representation drift as a unified signal to jointly address both challenges. Polestar comprises two components: Polestar-Cache, which identifies stale KV-cache positions via drift and performs sparse KV-cache refreshes to enable efficient reuse, and Polestar-Commit, which detects sharp drift events to reliably identify commit-ready tokens. Across mathematics and coding benchmarks on several dLLM families, Polestar sets a new state of the art on the accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier, achieving up to 10.73% accuracy improvement, up to 3.7x higher throughput, and high decoding parallelism of 3.67 tokens per forward pass over existing baselines.

</details>


### [11] [Eta Given Delta: Defining LLM Tool Efficiency With Marginal Tool Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14108)
*Nyx Iskandar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes two new metrics — tool efficiency (rate of useful tool calls in an agent trajectory) and marginal tool utility (usefulness of individual tool calls) — to directly quantify LLM agent tool-use efficiency in post-hoc analyses, as a complement to accuracy-based evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on LLM tool use focuses on improving tool-use capabilities and evaluates efficiency indirectly via accuracy. There is a lack of direct, quantitative metrics for measuring the efficiency of tool calls in agent trajectories, which this work aims to address.

Method: The authors define two novel quantitative metrics: (1) tool efficiency, measuring the proportion of useful tool calls in an agent trajectory, and (2) marginal tool utility, determined per tool call via LLM-as-a-Judge to assess whether a tool can be removed without accuracy loss. These are applied in post-hoc trajectory analyses.

Result: The paper introduces well-defined, direct metrics for evaluating tool-use efficiency, distinct from accuracy, and demonstrates their application in post-hoc trajectory analysis. (Specific empirical results are not detailed in this abstract.)

Conclusion: The proposed metrics serve as a foundation for future LLM evaluation benchmarks and agent harness engineering, particularly for designing leaner tool suites that optimize for efficiency as a complement to accuracy.

Abstract: This paper introduces tool efficiency, a new quantitative metric to evaluate the rate of useful tool calls in an LLM agent trajectory. To ensure that tool efficiency is well-defined, we also introduce marginal tool utility, a new quantitative metric defined per tool call indicating whether a tool is useful or whether it can be safely removed from the tool suite without affecting accuracy while increasing tool efficiency; in this paper, we determine the sign of marginal tool utility for each tool call in a trajectory using LLM-as-a-Judge. While much prior work has been done to develop techniques that improve tool use by LLMs and design evaluation methods measuring efficiency indirectly using accuracy as a proxy, our work is centered on measuring efficiency directly via the quantitative metric proposed in this paper in post hoc trajectory analyses. It is our intention that this work contributes to the frontier of LLM evaluation research as a springboard for future benchmark designs and agent harness engineering (specifically with regards to creating lean tool suites) that optimize for metrics that complement but are distinct from accuracy.

</details>


### [12] [Simplicity Paradox: Debunking myths about prompting and datasets for LLM evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14109)
*Inder Preet,Shuxin Lin,Dhaval Patel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study (8 prompting techniques, 10 MCQA datasets, 27 model configurations, 430K evaluations) finds that baseline prompting consistently outperforms complex reasoning techniques, with only minimal gains (~3pp) from CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive framing, challenging the assumption that more sophisticated prompts yield better LLM performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has created an implicit and untested assumption that more sophisticated prompting techniques yield better performance. Prior studies claim benefits from complex prompting but lack comprehensive, systematic evaluation across diverse models and datasets. This paper addresses that evaluation gap.

Method: A comprehensive empirical study testing 8 prompting techniques (including baseline, various Chain-of-Thought variants, Self-Analogical, and role-framing approaches) across 10 MCQA datasets, 27 model configurations, and approximately 4,300 unique questions, totaling over 430,000 evaluations. Analysis includes Elo ratings, performance-efficiency trade-offs, and dataset difficulty assessment.

Result: Baseline prompting consistently outperforms complex reasoning techniques. Only CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive yield a statistically significant ~3pp gain. All other elaborate techniques match or underperform baseline, sometimes drastically (e.g., Self-Analogical trails by up to 31pp). Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 unexpectedly tops Elo ratings. Dataset difficulty spans a 47.5pp accuracy range, with 60% of benchmarks below 70% accuracy.

Conclusion: The LLM evaluation community may be overcomplicating prompt engineering. Simple baselines are hard to beat, and substantial performance gaps across diverse benchmarks remain, suggesting that efforts should shift from prompt optimization toward genuine model improvements.

Abstract: Probing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and building robust solutions for Multiple-Choice Question Answering (MCQA) remain central challenges in natural language understanding. Furthermore, the rapid proliferation of LLMs has created the implicit assumption that more sophisticated prompting techniques yield better performance. Several studies claim better performance with more sophisticated prompting techniques, but do not provide a comprehensive evaluation. We address this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of 8 prompting techniques across 10 multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) datasets, encompassing 27 model configurations and roughly 4,300 unique questions evaluated more than 430,000 times. Our findings reveal a striking paradox that baseline prompting consistently outperforms complex reasoning techniques on various benchmarks. Only minimal expert and inductive role framing (CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive) yields a small but statistically significant $\sim$3 percentage-point (pp) gain over baseline whereas every other elaborate technique we tested matches or under-performs it, often by large margins (up to 31~pp for Self-Analogical). We further investigate three critical phenomena: (1) the unexpected victory of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 in Elo ratings, (2) the performance-efficiency trade-offs across model variants with different thinking budgets, revealing model-dependent optimal configurations, and (3) the substantial variation in dataset difficulty, with 60% of benchmarks below 70% accuracy and a 47.5~pp spread from easiest to hardest, indicating considerable room for model improvement. These results suggest that the LLM evaluation community may be overcomplicating prompt engineering and that substantial performance gaps remain across diverse benchmarks, offering opportunities for genuine model improvements rather than prompt optimization.

</details>


### [13] [MAPS: Modeling Co-Existing Subjective Perspectives and Shared Meaning in Multi-Agent Cognitive Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14110)
*Molood Arman,Clément Bonnafous*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MAPS is a multi-agent dialogue framework that models cognitively distinct agents using domain-weighted profiles, GRU-based memory, and token-level attention, achieving semantic alignment while preserving subjectivity across three dialogue benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI dialogue systems enforce semantic uniformity, sacrificing the diversity, expressiveness, and interpretability inherent in human dialogue — where participants express beliefs, emotions, and subjective cognitive styles beyond mere information exchange.

Method: The MAPS framework models dialogue between cognitively distinct agents via three components: (1) domain-weighted profiles that encode individualized agent perspectives, (2) dynamic GRU-based memory for tracking conversational context, and (3) interpretable token-level attention mechanisms that allow agents to maintain distinct reasoning while progressively converging on shared meaning.

Result: Evaluations on EmpatheticDialogues, TopicalChat, and MultiWOZ demonstrate that MAPS achieves semantic alignment between agents without collapsing their subjective, individualized response patterns.

Conclusion: MAPS provides a viable path toward cognitively grounded, interpretable dialogue systems that successfully balance conversational expressiveness (preserving agent subjectivity) with coherence (achieving shared understanding).

Abstract: Human dialogue involves more than exchanging information; it also expresses beliefs, emotions, and subjective cognitive styles. Yet current AI dialogue systems often enforce semantic uniformity, sacrificing diversity and interpretability. We present MAPS (Multi-Agent Perspective Spaces), a novel framework that models dialogue between cognitively distinct agents through domain-weighted profiles, dynamic GRU-based memory, and interpretable token-level attention. MAPS enables agents to maintain individualized reasoning while progressively converging on shared meaning. Evaluations on EmpatheticDialogues, TopicalChat, and MultiWOZ show that MAPS supports semantic alignment without collapsing subjectivity. Our results demonstrate a path toward cognitively grounded, interpretable dialogue systems that balance expressiveness and coherence.

</details>


### [14] [Dialogue Summarization with Emotion Dynamics Using Topic- and Participant-Centric Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14769)
*Linyun Xiang,Mark Neerincx,Stephanie Tan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A dialogue summarization framework using hierarchical Chain-of-Agents that models both semantic content and emotion dynamics from multimodal inputs, evaluated with novel emotion trajectory metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing summarization research overlooks the interactive, back-and-forth nature of dialogues and fails to capture emotional dynamics, focusing instead on monologic text like news articles.

Method: A hierarchical Chain-of-Agents framework that decomposes dialogues into topic segments and participant-specific utterance segments, infers emotions automatically, generates topic- and participant-level summaries, and aggregates them into a final summary capturing both semantics and emotion trajectories.

Result: Experiments with small language models on multimodal dialogue datasets demonstrate that the framework produces summaries preserving both semantic content and emotional flow. Additional experiments with explicit emotion labels further validate the methodology's efficacy.

Conclusion: Modeling both semantic and emotion dynamics in dialogue summarization is feasible and beneficial; the proposed framework and emotion trajectory metrics open new opportunities for dialogue analysis using language models.

Abstract: Existing text summarization research has focused much on monologic information (e.g., newspaper articles, reports) without accounting for the interaction between speakers or authors. In contrast, dialogues are a rich communication channel where multiple participants conduct back and forth exchanges to construct meaning. We propose a dialogue summarization framework that explicitly models both semantic and emotion dynamics using multimodal dialogue inputs, built on an adapted hierarchical Chain-of-Agents approach. We decompose dialogues from two perspectives: (1) topic segments based on the utterances of all participants, and (2) participant-specific utterance segments. These are used to generate corresponding summaries while incorporating automatically inferred emotions. Topic- and participant-level summaries are aggregated into a dialogue summary capturing semantic content and emotion trajectories. To evaluate beyond content accuracy, we introduce emotion trajectory metrics measuring how well summaries preserve emotional flow. Experiments with small language models on multimodal dialogue datasets show that our framework produces summaries with both semantic and emotion content. Further experiments on explicit emotion label availability highlight the efficacy of our proposed methodology and the opportunities in dialogue analysis using language models.

</details>


### [15] [Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT): Training Small LLMs to Introspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14111)
*Ely Hahami,Ishaan Sinha,Lavik Jain*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether small language models can introspect on their own internal activations after activation steering. The authors identify a confound in prior binary detection paradigms and propose two robust evaluation methods. They find introspective ability generally scales with model size, and introduce Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT) which dramatically improves self-detection, even generalizing zero-shot, suggesting introspective capacity can be trained rather than merely emergent with scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on activation steering used binary Yes/No detection paradigms that are confounded in small models — steering biases them toward affirmative responses regardless of content. The authors seek a robust way to evaluate whether models can genuinely introspect on perturbations to their own residual stream, and whether this ability can be improved beyond what scale alone provides.

Method: The authors propose two confound-free evaluation paradigms: (1) sentence localization — identifying which of N sentences was perturbed (chance = 1/N), and (2) strength comparison — identifying which of two sentences received a stronger injection (chance = 50%). They evaluate six models from Llama-3.2 and Gemma-4 families (1B–8B). They then introduce Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT): supervised fine-tuning on sentence-localization examples constructed from the model's own perturbed forward passes, and test zero-shot generalization to strength comparison.

Result: Models ≥2B parameters introspect reliably above chance, with ability generally increasing with scale. Llama-1B performs at or below chance. IFT dramatically raises Llama-1B sentence-localization accuracy from 9.6% to 60.6% (6× improvement), with zero-shot generalization to strength comparison (30.2% → 52.2%). IFT also improves introspection in 3B and 8B models while inducing negligible degradation on standard capability benchmarks.

Conclusion: Introspective ability is not fixed by scale alone — it can be directly trained via IFT. This unlocks latent self-monitoring capacity with implications for AI transparency and alignment. The findings suggest that even small models can learn to reliably report on internal perturbations when appropriately fine-tuned.

Abstract: Can small language models detect and report on perturbations their own internal activations? We investigate this question through the lens of activation steering: injecting concept vectors into a model's residual stream and measuring whether the model can accurately report on the perturbation. We first show that the binary detection paradigm used in prior work -- prompting the model to answer Yes'' or No'' to whether it detects an injected thought -- is confounded in small models, as steering biases the model toward affirmative responses regardless of the question content. We therefore propose two confound-free evaluation paradigms: sentence localization (identifying which of $N$ sentences was perturbed, chance $= 1/N$) and strength comparison (identifying which of two sentences received a stronger injection, chance $= 50\%$). Evaluating across six models from two families (Llama-3.2 and Gemma-4), we find that models as small as 2B parameters introspect reliably well above chance, and that introspective ability generally increases with scale. Llama-1B, however, performs at or below chance. We then introduce \emph{Introspection Fine-Tuning} (IFT): supervised fine-tuning on sentence-localization examples constructed from the model's own perturbed forward passes. IFT raises Llama-1B sentence-localization accuracy from $9.6\%$ to $60.6\%$ (a $6\times$ improvement), with gains generalizing zero-shot to the held-out strength-comparison task ($30.2\% \to 52.2\%$). IFT also improves introspection for 3B and 8B models, while inducing negligible degradation on standard capability benchmarks. Our results suggest that introspective ability is not fixed by scale alone: it can be directly trained, and doing so unlocks latent self-monitoring capacity with implications for AI transparency and alignment. Our code is \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/IFT-introspection-2092/README.md}{here}.

</details>


### [16] [The Misclassification of Autistic Writing as AI-Generated](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14729)
*Summer Chambers,Matthew C. Kelley*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study empirically tests whether autistic writers are disproportionately flagged by AI-detection models. Using ~60,000 Reddit posts, results show significantly more likely-autistic texts were flagged as AI-generated, though textual feature overlaps were not straightforward. The authors call for ethical scrutiny of AI-detection models given potential bias against autistic writers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Anecdotal claims suggest AI-generated text detectors may exhibit bias against autistic writers, flagging their work as AI-generated more frequently. This study seeks to empirically test that claim, addressing concerns about fairness and equity in detection model deployment, particularly in academic contexts.

Method: A corpus of ~60,000 Reddit posts was split into "likely-autistic" and "general-Reddit" subcorpora. The OpenAI GPT-2 detection model was used to generate probability scores for each text. The distribution of these probabilities was compared between subcorpora, and textual features of each group were analyzed relative to known features of AI-generated text.

Result: Less than 2% of either subcorpus was flagged as AI-generated. However, significantly more texts from the likely-autistic subcorpus were flagged than from the general-Reddit subcorpus. The connection between textual features of likely-autistic writing and AI-generated text was not straightforward, suggesting bias may operate through non-obvious linguistic patterns.

Conclusion: The findings confirm a detectable bias in AI-detection models against autistic writers, warranting ethical scrutiny. The authors recommend critical reexamination of detection models and caution against their uncritical use in academic integrity settings.

Abstract: Recent findings suggest that detection models for artificial intelligence (AI) cannot accurately identify AI-generated text and may exhibit bias against certain minority groups. In the present study, anecdotal claims that autistic writers more often have their work flagged as AI-generated are examined empirically. A corpus of approximately 60,000 Reddit posts split into "likely-autistic" and "general-Reddit" subcorpora is used to compare the distribution of probabilities output by the OpenAI GPT-2 detection model. Differences in textual features between subcorpora are observed and compared to reported features of AI-generated text. Results showed that while less than two-percent of either subcorpus was flagged as AI-generated by the model, significantly more texts from the likely-autistic subcorpus were flagged. Connections between features of text with likely-autistic authors and AI-generated text were not straightforward. The widespread use of AI-detection models with a potential bias against autistic writers in their output prompts ethical scrutiny, and the authors recommend further critical examination of the models themselves as well as their use in academic contexts.

</details>


### [17] [Information-Theoretic Limits of Reliability and Scaling in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14112)
*Subhabrata Majumdar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper establishes an information-theoretic framework showing that LLM reliability has a fundamental ceiling determined by resolvable context and task ambiguity, derives a first-principles scaling law where performance is bottlenecked by data or capacity, and unifies phenomena like retrieval-augmentation and catastrophic forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of LLMs implicitly assumes perfect reliability is achievable with sufficient scale. The authors challenge this assumption by showing it lacks information-theoretic justification — every generative task has an intrinsic reliability ceiling.

Method: The framework decomposes the performance gap into a resolvable component (closeable with additional context) and a subjective component (inherent task ambiguity). It introduces a dependency kernel to quantify inter-token correlations and derives a scaling law from first principles, where LLM performance is constrained by the scarcer of training data or model capacity.

Result: The derived scaling law recovers Chinchilla scaling as a special case. The framework also structurally accounts for when scaling improves reliability and unifies practical phenomena including retrieval-augmentation benefits and the spectral mechanics of catastrophic forgetting.

Conclusion: The work formalizes resource-complexity tradeoffs governing model performance across domains, providing a unified theory of performance limits in generative language models and demonstrating that perfect reliability is fundamentally unattainable for any task.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are evaluated as though perfect reliability is achievable for any task given sufficient scale. We show this assumption is information-theoretically unjustified. Every generative task has a reliability ceiling that no model can exceed, determined by how much output uncertainty is resolvable from observable context. The gap decomposes into a resolvable component closable with additional context and a subjective component inherent to task ambiguity. Autoregressive generation further degrades this ceiling at a rate governed by the task's dependency kernel, which quantifies inter-token correlations in the output. From these two primitives, we derive a first-principles scaling law where LLM performance is bottlenecked by the scarcer resource: training data or model capacity. This law recovers the Chinchilla scaling law as a special case and provides a structural account of when scaling improves reliability. Beyond scaling, our framework unifies diverse practical phenomena, such as the benefits of retrieval-augmentation and the spectral mechanics of catastrophic forgetting. Our work formalizes the resource-complexity tradeoffs that govern model performance across domains, offering a unified theory of performance limits in generative language models.

</details>


### [18] [Digital Pantheon: Simulating and Auditing Coalition Formation with LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15095)
*Dylan Van Mulders,Matthias Bogaert,Dirk Van den Poel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A multi-agent LLM framework combining SFT, DPO, and RAG simulates partisan coalition negotiations. DPO instills party-specific personas, RAG anchors agents to manifestos, and novel metrics (MILT, CIS) trace contributions and benchmark against real agreements. Tested on the 2019 Flemish election, it yields stable rankings and shows manifesto-anchored content predicts real-world outcomes better than hallucinated content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are useful for computational political science but suffer from RLHF-induced neutrality and helpfulness biases that make them incapable of sustaining steadfast partisan behavior. There is a need for a framework that balances factual grounding with ideological alignment to credibly simulate political coalition formation.

Method: A multi-agent framework with three components: (1) Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to instill aggressive, party-specific ideological personas; (2) per-party Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that anchor each agent to its official election manifesto; (3) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for factual grounding. Agents engage in hub-and-spoke negotiations arbitrated by a formateur agent, operationalized on 2019 Flemish election data. Three novel interpretability instruments are introduced: Multi-Layered Information Lineage Topology (MILT) traces clauses to manifesto origins and classifies them into five provenance states; Coalition Influence Score (CIS) aggregates traceable contributions by party; and a real-world grounding pass benchmarks simulated provisions against the historical coalition agreement.

Result: Across three independent simulations, the framework produces a stable winner and ranking (N-VA > CD&V > Open Vld). Manifesto-anchored lineage reliably predicts real-world materialization of provisions, whereas hallucinated content does not correlate with historically adopted agreements.

Conclusion: The framework provides a transparent, scalable testbed for ex-ante exploration of party compatibility and formateur-mediated compromise. It demonstrates that combining DPO-driven partisanship with RAG-grounded manifestos yields politically coherent simulations, and that the MILT/CIS metrics enable rigorous, interpretable evaluation of emergent negotiation outcomes.

Abstract: The formation of political coalitions is a complex negotiation driven by both concrete policy objectives and deep-seated ideological convictions. While Large Language Models (LLMs) open new avenues for computational political science, the neutrality and helpfulness biases instilled by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) prevent them from sustaining steadfast partisan behaviour. We present a multi-agent framework that reconciles factual grounding with ideological alignment by combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): DPO instils aggressive party-specific personas, while a per-party RAG pipeline keeps each agent bounded to its official manifesto. We operationalize the framework on the 2019 Flemish election, deploying the partisan agents in a hub-and-spoke negotiation arbitrated by a formateur. To make the emergent negotiation interpretable, we introduce a Multi-Layered Information Lineage Topology (MILT) that traces every clause in the final agreement back to its manifesto origin and classifies it into five provenance states, a Coalition Influence Score (CIS) that aggregates these traceable contributions to identify which party shaped the agreement, and a real-world grounding pass that benchmarks each simulated provision against the historically adopted coalition agreement. Across three independent simulations the framework yields a stable winner and ranking (N-VA ahead of CD\&V and Open Vld), and manifesto-anchored lineage reliably predicts real-world materialization whereas hallucinated content does not. The result is a transparent, scalable testbed for the ex-ante exploration of party compatibility and formateur-mediated compromise.

</details>


### [19] [T5-CSBoost: Adversarial Perturbation Resistant LLM Fingerprinting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14113)
*Gayan K. Kulatilleke,Mahsa Baktashmotlagh,Siamak Layeghy,Marius Portmann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: T5-CSBoost enhances AI-generated text detection by adding a contrastive triplet loss to T5-Sentinel's decoder embeddings, achieving SOTA on multiple benchmarks with strong robustness against paraphrasing and adversarial perturbations up to 90% intensity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AIGT detectors perform well on clean text but degrade significantly under light paraphrasing, word substitutions, character edits, and distribution shifts. There is a need for a lightweight, effective defense that does not require architectural changes, adversarial training, or complex multi-task objectives.

Method: The authors propose T5-CSBoost, which extends the T5-Sentinel framework by retaining the original next-token prediction objective for source attribution and adding an auxiliary margin-based triplet loss over decoder embeddings. This contrastive style regularization encourages compact, perturbation-resistant stylistic representations without modifying the underlying T5-small backbone.

Result: T5-CSBoost achieves state-of-the-art multiclass source attribution and binary human-vs-LLM detection on OpenLLMText and HC3 benchmarks. It demonstrates enhanced robustness to word- and character-level adversarial perturbations up to 90% intensity, and achieves SOTA on the MAGE/Deepfake stress-test suite, covering unseen models, unseen domains, and extreme paraphrasing.

Conclusion: Explicitly regularizing stylistic embeddings via contrastive learning is a practical and effective strategy for building robust LLM fingerprinting systems in real-world adversarial settings.

Abstract: While many AI-generated text (AIGT) detectors achieve strong performance on clean inputs, their accuracy degrades significantly under light paraphrasing, word substitutions, character edits, and distribution shifts. We present T5 Contrastive Style Boosted Classifier (T5-CSBoost), an extension to the T5-Sentinel framework that keeps the original next-token prediction objective for source attribution while introducing an auxiliary margin-based triplet loss over decoder embeddings.
  This contrastive style regularization encourages the learning of compact, perturbation-resistant stylistic representations, offering a lightweight yet effective alternative to prior approaches that rely on architectural modifications, adversarial training, or complex multi-task objectives without altering the underlying T5-small backbone. T5-CSBoost achieves state-of-the-art multiclass source attribution and binary human-vs-LLM detection on OpenLLMText and HC3 AIGT benchmarks. More importantly, T5-CSBoost demonstrates enhanced robustness to word and character level adversarial perturbations of up to 90% intensity, achieving state-of-the-art on the challenging MAGE/Deepfake stress-test suite, including unseen models, unseen domains, and extreme paraphrasing scenarios. Our results highlight that explicitly regularizing stylistic embeddings via contrastive learning is a practical and effective strategy for building more robust LLM fingerprinting systems in real-world adversarial settings.

</details>


### [20] [CoEvoT: Co-Evolving Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Graph-LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14114)
*Haohua Niu,Xingtong Yu,Yang Liu,Junfeng Fang,Xuanting Xie,Jie Tan,Zhongjian Zhang,Hong Cheng,Yuan Fang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoEvoT proposes a co-evolving Chain-of-Thought prompting framework for graph-LLM reasoning, where intermediate textual thoughts and graph token representations mutually update each other in a closed loop, enabling step-wise structural refinement rather than reasoning over fixed graph snapshots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CoT-based graph-LLM methods generate reasoning steps while conditioning on fixed graph tokens, which prevents iterative refinement of structural cues. There is a need for dynamic, step-wise interaction between textual reasoning and graph structure representation.

Method: CoEvoT implements a closed-loop framework with two coupled operations: (1) text-to-graph token rewriting, where each intermediate thought updates graph token evidence via a lightweight condition network; (2) graph-to-text reasoning guidance, where updated tokens feed back into the next reasoning step. This creates a co-evolving process between textual thoughts and graph representations.

Result: Extensive experiments on eight datasets show that CoEvoT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Co-evolving Chain-of-Thought prompting effectively addresses distribution shift in graph learning by enabling dynamic, state-aware evidence refinement, surpassing static graph token approaches.

Abstract: Graph learning under distribution shift presents a persistent challenge, where models adapt to new graphs with limited or even no supervision. Recent graph--LLM approaches move toward label-efficient prediction by linearizing graphs into prompts and using large language models (LLMs) as predictors, and can adopt Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to exploit LLM's multi-step reasoning capability. However, existing CoT-based graph--LLM methods generate intermediate thoughts while conditioning on fixed graph tokens, limiting step-wise refinement of structural cues. In this paper, we propose CoEvoT, a simple yet effective co-evolving CoT prompting framework for graph--LLM reasoning. CoEvoT couples text-to-graph token rewriting and graph-to-text reasoning guidance in a closed loop: each intermediate textual thought is used to update the graph token evidence state via a lightweight condition network, and the updated tokens are fed back into the next-step instruction to guide subsequent LLM reasoning. This enables step-wise, state-aware evidence refinement, rather than reasoning over a fixed graph snapshot. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that CoEvoT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [21] [ReportMedSAM: Guiding Segmentation Through Radiology Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14116)
*Anghong Du,Theodoros N. Arvanitis,Colin Watts,Alejandro F. Frangi,Le Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReportMedSAM replaces brittle rule-based report parsing with a learnable concept bank aligned via BiomedCLIP, dynamically activating Mixture-of-Experts modules for free-form radiology report-driven segmentation, achieving competitive accuracy and enabling scalable, non-interfering extension to novel structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Converting free-form radiology reports into reliable segmentation masks is challenging due to linguistic variability. Existing methods depend on predefined organ phrases or brittle rule-based extraction, making them non-scalable to novel anatomical structures and sensitive to synonyms. A robust, scalable, and synonym-agnostic report-driven segmentation framework is needed.

Method: ReportMedSAM employs (1) a frozen BiomedCLIP encoder to embed clinical reports; (2) a learnable concept bank aligned via contrastive learning against large-scale clinical corpora, establishing mutually orthogonal semantic anchors to prevent organ-level semantic collapse; (3) dynamic activation of task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules based on concept-bank matching; and (4) a decoupled, parameter-isolated extension mechanism allowing new concepts and experts to be added without retraining existing components.

Result: Evaluated on AbdomenAtlas 3.0, ReportMedSAM effectively interprets free-form reports, achieves competitive segmentation accuracy, and demonstrates seamless, non-interfering extension to novel clinical tasks.

Conclusion: The learnable concept bank with MoE-based dynamic routing provides a scalable, robust alternative to rule-based parsing for report-driven medical image segmentation, validated on a large abdominal CT dataset with strong generalization to novel anatomical concepts.

Abstract: Free-form radiology reports contain rich clinical descriptions, yet converting them for reliable segmentation remains challenging due to the inherent variability of natural language. Existing pipelines often rely on predefined organ phrases or brittle rule-based inference-time extraction, which limits their scalability to novel anatomical structures and makes them sensitive to linguistic variations. To address this, we propose ReportMedSAM, a report-driven framework that replaces discrete extraction with a learnable concept bank. By leveraging a frozen medical vision-language encoder (BiomedCLIP), we align organ-level concept embeddings with large-scale clinical corpora through contrastive learning, establishing mutually orthogonal semantic anchors. Our approach explicitly mitigates organ-level semantic collapse and ensures high robustness against diverse clinical synonyms (e.g., "renal" vs. "kidney" ). During inference, a clinical report is embedded and matched against this concept bank to dynamically activate task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules. This decoupled design allows new concepts and experts to be added without retraining existing components, providing a parameter-isolated extension mechanism while keeping previously learned experts unchanged. Evaluated on the AbdomenAtlas 3.0 dataset, ReportMedSAM effectively interprets free-form reports, achieves competitive segmentation accuracy, and demonstrates seamless, non-interfering extension to novel clinical tasks.

</details>


### [22] [Heterogeneous Element-Aware Cross-Version Differencing of Scientific Documents via Layout-Aware Alignment and Structure-Aware Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14117)
*Zhen Yina,Wenkang An,Hao Wang,Keran You*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A layout-aware framework for cross-version scientific document differencing that decomposes pages into semantically typed elements (text, tables, formulas, figures), aligns them via spatial/content/structural compatibility, and performs type-aware difference reasoning, achieving F1 scores of 0.845–0.903 on real-world journal production data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods fail at scientific document differencing because text-sequence-based approaches lose layout/structure information, while image-based methods lack semantic interpretability and are sensitive to rendering variations. There is a need for a method that handles page-structured heterogeneous elements holistically.

Method: The framework decomposes document versions into semantically typed elements, establishes cross-version correspondence via an alignment-first mechanism jointly modeling spatial, content, and structural compatibility, and performs type-aware difference reasoning over aligned element pairs. It supports unified change detection, localization, structure-awareness analysis, and alignment/matching evaluation.

Result: On real-world scientific PDF data from journal proofreading workflows, the framework achieves detection F1 scores of 0.903 (text), 0.855 (tables), 0.862 (formulas), and 0.845 (figures), consistently outperforming element-specific baselines, with additional gains in localization, structure awareness, and matching quality.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous element-aware differencing provides a robust, interpretable solution for scientific document comparison in editorial production. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of cross-version alignment, type-specific representations, structure-aware reasoning, and compatibility-weight design.

Abstract: Cross-version differencing of scientific documents is essential in scholarly publishing and technical documentation, but remains challenging because scientific documents are page-structured artifacts containing heterogeneous elements such as text, tables, formulas, figures, and layout cues. Existing text-sequence-based methods often lose layout and structural information, while image-based methods lack semantic interpretability and are sensitive to rendering variation. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a layout-aware heterogeneous element-aware framework for scientific document differencing. The framework decomposes document versions into semantically typed elements, establishes cross-version correspondence through an alignment-first mechanism that jointly models spatial, content, and structural compatibility, and performs type-aware difference reasoning over aligned element pairs. It supports unified change detection, localization, structure-awareness analysis, and alignment/matching evaluation across text, tables, formulas, and figures. Experiments on real-world scientific PDF data from journal production proofreading workflows show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms element-specific baselines. It achieves detection F1 scores of 0.903, 0.855, 0.862, and 0.845 for text, tables, formulas, and figures, respectively, with further improvements in localization, structure awareness, and matching quality. Ablation and sensitivity analyses confirm the effectiveness of cross-version alignment, type-specific representations, structure-aware reasoning, and compatibility-weight design. These results demonstrate that heterogeneous element-aware differencing provides a robust and interpretable solution for scientific document comparison in realistic editorial production scenarios.

</details>


### [23] [Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14118)
*Micah Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces Budgeted Subset Refinement, a framework for strategically allocating limited refinement effort across a noisy pool of LLM-generated research ideas. The authors show that diversity-aware MMR-k refinement yields the best portfolio-level tradeoffs in terms of research-strong nonduplicate yield, lowest duplication, and cost efficiency, arguing that LLM ideation systems should be evaluated as budgeted allocation systems rather than mere generators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate novel-looking research ideas, but these ideas often lack diversity, resist reliable evaluation, and fail to translate into strong executed projects. Existing work focuses on generation and reranking, but the key bottleneck is how to allocate limited refinement resources across a noisy candidate pool before human researchers engage. This pre-execution scaffolding problem — constructing a strong, diverse, execution-aware portfolio under a fixed rubric — is underexplored.

Method: The authors propose Budgeted Subset Refinement, a family of strategies where only a selected subset of candidates receives refinement (rather than uniform refinement of all candidates). They compare several allocation strategies in a unified shared-candidate-pool benchmark across 10 random seeds and 10 research-ideation environments, including: raw generation + reranking (no refinement), uniform refinement, random-k refinement, and diversity-aware MMR-k refinement. A blinded external-judge robustness check on a balanced 72-item sample validates findings across independent model families.

Result: Raw generation and reranking alone produce zero research-strong nonduplicate ideas. Uniform refinement yields strong individual ideas but is suboptimal for portfolio-level compute allocation. Random-k refinement is a strong low-cost baseline. MMR-k refinement achieves the best overall proxy tradeoff: highest research-strong nonduplicate yield, lowest duplicate rate among successful methods, and best cost per research-strong nonduplicate idea. The external-judge check supports the refinement effect broadly, though per-item rankings among refined strategies vary by judge.

Conclusion: LLM research ideation systems should be evaluated not merely as idea generators but as budgeted support-allocation systems. The claims are scoped to proxy-rated portfolio quality and do not substitute for expert review or execution-grounded validation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate research ideas that appear novel to expert reviewers, but recent work also shows that such ideas often lack diversity, are difficult for LLMs to evaluate reliably, and may fail to translate into strong executed projects. This paper evaluates a controlled proxy benchmark for a pre-execution scaffolding problem: given a noisy pool of LLM-generated research ideas, how should a system allocate limited refinement effort to construct a stronger, more diverse, more execution-aware portfolio for human researchers under a fixed rubric? We introduce Budgeted Subset Refinement, a family of strategies that refine only a selected subset of candidates rather than refining all candidates uniformly. In a unified shared-candidate-pool evaluation across 10 random seeds and 10 research-ideation environments, raw generation and reranking alone produce no research-strong nonduplicate ideas under the benchmark rubric, while refinement is necessary for strong proxy-rated portfolios. Uniform refinement produces strong individual ideas but is not the best portfolio-level allocation of compute. Random-k refinement is a strong low-cost baseline, while diversity-aware MMR-k refinement gives the best overall proxy tradeoff: the highest research-strong nonduplicate yield, the lowest duplicate rate among successful methods, and the best cost per research-strong nonduplicate idea. A blinded external-judge robustness check on a balanced 72-item sample supports the broad refinement effect across independent model families, while showing that per-item rankings among refined strategies vary by judge. These results suggest that LLM research ideation systems should be evaluated not only as idea generators, but as budgeted support-allocation systems. The claims are scoped to proxy-rated portfolio quality and do not substitute for expert review or execution-grounded validation.

</details>


### [24] [Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14147)
*Alex Kwon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A one-line prefill ("Sure, here is") jailbreaks aligned LMs by exploiting a shallow, response-site refusal mechanism. The harm representation remains detectable in prompt-side activations, but refusal is a localized, early-response computation that generic autoregressive conditioning — not safety-specific suppression — can passively override. A prompt-side monitor would be immune to such response-site attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aligned language models can be jailbroken by trivial prefill strings, but the mechanistic reason why this works is unknown. The authors aim to determine where and how refusal fails, whether the harm representation is destroyed or merely bypassed, and what this implies for the architecture of refusal and potential defenses.

Method: The authors use linear probes to read harm representations from activations across four models (1.5B–14B, three families). They localize refusal to an early response window via dose-matched position control, three causal probes (attention knockout, direction restoration, state injection), and base-model comparisons. They measure behavioral compliance, probe accuracy, attention patterns, and logit-trace concentration to distinguish passive autoregressive conditioning from active safety-specific suppression.

Result: Harm representations remain intact (probe accuracy 0.91–0.98) even when behavioral refusal drops to chance. Refusal localizes to the first half of the response; the second half is nearly inert. Injecting the model's own refuse state reverses the jailbreak (74%). Knocking out early-response attention to the prefill collapses harmful continuation.
