Motivation: Outcome-based RL for interactive agents suffers from a supervision gap: sparse trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance on intermediate decisions, leaving token-level policy learning under-supervised.

Method: SEED fine-tunes the policy to analyze completed trajectories and generate natural-language skills capturing reusable workflows, decisive observations, and failure-avoidance rules. The current policy both collects trajectories and extracts hindsight skills, enabling co-evolution. It then re-scores sampled actions under ordinary vs. skill-augmented contexts, converting the skill-induced probability shift into a dense token-level on-policy distillation signal, jointly optimized with outcome-based RL.

Result: Extensive experiments on text-based and vision-based agentic tasks show consistent improvements in performance and sample efficiency, with robust generalization to unseen scenarios.

Conclusion: SEED effectively bridges the supervision gap in outcome-based RL by evolving hindsight skills alongside the policy and providing dense token-level distillation signals, yielding stronger and more sample-efficient interactive agents.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained as interactive agents for long-horizon tasks involving multi-turn interaction, tool use, and environment feedback. Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides a practical optimization paradigm, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards offer limited guidance on intermediate decisions, leaving a supervision gap between episode-level outcomes and token-level policy learning. We propose SEED (SElf-Evolving On-Policy Distillation), a self-evolving framework that converts completed on-policy trajectories into training-time hindsight skills and distills their behavioral effect back into the policy model. SEED first fine-tunes the policy to analyze completed trajectories and generate natural-language skills that capture reusable workflows, decisive observations, or failure-avoidance rules. During RL, the current policy both collects trajectories and serves as the analyzer that extracts hindsight skills from them. Policy updates therefore improve subsequent decision making and skill analysis together, allowing hindsight supervision to evolve with the policy. SEED then re-scores the sampled actions under ordinary and skill-augmented contexts, converting the skill-induced probability shift into a dense token-level on-policy distillation signal. This signal is jointly optimized with outcome-based RL, keeping the auxiliary supervision aligned with the current trajectory distribution. Extensive experiments on text-based and vision-based agentic tasks show that SEED consistently improves performance and sample efficiency, exhibiting robust generalization to unseen scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/SEED.

</details>


### [47] [Show Me How You Reason and I'll Tell You Who You Are: Reasoning Graphs for Robust LLM Authorship Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14905)
*Zlata Kikteva,Artur Romazanov,Annette Hautli-Janisz,Ramon Ruiz-Dolz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a graph neural network approach that extracts reasoning structures from LLM-generated texts (via argument mining) to detect LLM authorship. It significantly outperforms surface-level linguistic baselines, especially under obfuscation attacks like paraphrasing and backtranslation, and generalizes better to unseen model versions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-generated text detection methods rely on surface-level linguistic features, which are brittle against paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. There is a need for deeper, more robust signals of LLM authorship that capture the underlying reasoning structure rather than superficial stylistic patterns.

Method: The authors extract reasoning graphs from text using an argument mining pipeline, which identifies argumentative components (claims, premises) and their relations. These graphs are then processed by a graph neural network (GNN) to learn structural patterns characteristic of LLM-generated reasoning, as opposed to human reasoning. A Longformer model serves as the surface-level baseline for comparison.

Result: The proposed GNN approach outperforms the Longformer baseline by up to 27 percentage points under obfuscation attacks (paraphrasing, backtranslation) and by 19 percentage points when evaluated on texts from unseen LLM versions, demonstrating superior robustness and generalization.

Conclusion: Capturing reasoning structures via argument mining and GNNs provides a more robust and generalizable signal for LLM-generated text detection than surface-level linguistic features, offering a promising direction for authorship attribution in the face of rapidly evolving LLM releases and adversarial obfuscation.

Abstract: Given the current trend to employ large language models (LLMs) in almost any imaginable context, LLM-generated text detection and authorship attribution have become a pressing issue. Prior work has primarily focused on surface-level linguistic features, an approach shown to be susceptible to paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. In this paper, we go beyond the linguistic surface, extracting and analysing reasoning structures in LLM-generated texts with the goal of capturing more complex signals of LLM authorship. We propose a graph neural network approach that leverages reasoning graphs extracted by an argument mining pipeline, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation over a traditional Longformer baseline. Our approach outperforms the baseline by up to 27 percentage points under the obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, and 19 percentage points when evaluated on the texts generated by the unseen model versions, simulating real-world conditions in which new LLM versions are continuously released.

</details>


### [48] [Latent Trajectory Discrimination for AI-Generated Text Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14967)
*Gianluca Bonifazi,Christopher Buratti,Michele Marchetti,Federica Parlapiano,Giulia Quaglieri,Davide Traini,Domenico Ursino,Luca Virgili*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reformulates AI-generated text detection as distinguishing between latent generation trajectories rather than analyzing static documents. It proposes GTCL, a framework that segments documents into ordered units, encodes them in embedding space, constructs sequence-level trajectory representations, and applies contrastive learning to identify geometric regularities of autoregressive generation, achieving consistent improvements over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AIGTD methods treat documents as static objects using aggregate statistics or compressed embeddings, ignoring the inherently dynamic, sequential nature of autoregressive text generation. The authors argue that modeling how textual representations evolve across a sequence (generation trajectories) provides a more principled and discriminative signal for detection.

Method: GTCL (Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning) operates by: (1) segmenting a document into ordered local units, (2) encoding each unit into an embedding space, (3) constructing a structured, sequence-level representation that captures the trajectory of representations, and (4) applying contrastive learning over these trajectories to learn geometric regularities characteristic of autoregressive generation, thereby distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text.

Result: Evaluations on three benchmarks and against multiple detection approaches show that GTCL consistently outperforms baselines, demonstrating that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics yields robust discriminative signals that generalize across models and domains.

Conclusion: Modeling trajectory differences provides a promising, underexplored direction for AI-generated text detection. Explicitly capturing the sequential dynamics of autoregressive generation yields stronger and more transferable detection signals than static representation methods.

Abstract: Most existing approaches to AI-Generated Text Detection (AIGTD) treat documents as static objects and base their decisions on aggregate statistics or globally compressed embeddings. However, this perspective overlooks the inherently dynamic nature of autoregressive generation, where content evolves progressively through the latent space. In this paper, we reformulate AIGTD as the problem of distinguishing between latent generation trajectories. Instead of relying on static representations, we model how textual representations evolve across the sequence. To this end, we propose Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning (GTCL), a framework that segments the document into ordered local units, encodes each unit in an embedding space, and constructs a structured and sequence-level representation. GTCL then applies contrastive learning to these trajectories to learn geometric regularities associated with the autoregressive generation. Evaluations performed on three different benchmarks and several approaches show that GTCL outperforms detection baselines consistently, which implies that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics provides robust discriminative signals across models and domains. These results suggest that modeling trajectory differences could improve detection and open up a dynamic direction that has been underexplored in previous AIGTD literature.

</details>


### [49] [OmniaBench: Benchmarking General AI Agents Across Diverse Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14989)
*Chengyu Shen,Yujie Fu,Gangtao Xin,Yanheng Hou,Wenlong Fei,Guojie Zhu,Jiawei Li,Hongcheng Gao,Runming He,Zhen Hao Wong,Meiyi Qiang,Hao Liang,Zhao Cao,Hao Jiang,Chong Chen,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OmniaBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating general AI agents across 90+ domains with 1,431 tasks. It features a hierarchical domain taxonomy (ToC/ToB/ToE), four task synthesis routes, a ten-dimensional capability framework, and eight difficulty factors. Even top models like Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieve only ~57-58% Overall Pass@1, revealing significant gaps in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks are narrow in scope—limited to specific scenarios, tool ecosystems, or interaction formats—making it impossible to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous real-world application settings. There is a need for a broad, diagnostic benchmark that spans diverse domains and supports fine-grained capability analysis.

Method: The authors derive scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, Web retrieval, and human refinement to build a hierarchical taxonomy spanning ToC (Consumer), ToB (Business), and ToE (Enterprise) with 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains. Executable environments are constructed, and tasks are synthesized via four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program, yielding both single-turn and multi-turn tasks. A ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors enable fine-grained evaluation. The full dataset comprises 1,431 tasks, with a challenging subset of 644 tasks for cost-efficient evaluation and contamination mitigation.

Result: OmniaBench poses substantial challenges: Claude-Sonnet-5 achieves 58.54 Overall Pass@1 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieves 57.14. Analyses reveal clear performance disparities across domains and capabilities, with persistent weaknesses in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction.

Conclusion: OmniaBench provides a broad, diagnostic benchmark that effectively characterizes the capability boundaries of general agents. Current frontier models still fall short, particularly in planning and error correction, highlighting critical areas for future improvement in agent development.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly evolving from text generators into general agents capable of understanding user requests, invoking external tools, and completing complex tasks through interaction. However, existing agent benchmarks often focus on limited scenarios, tool ecosystems, or interaction formats, making it difficult to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous application settings. We introduce OmniaBench, a benchmark for evaluating general agents across diverse scenarios with explicit state spaces. We derive application-oriented scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, Web retrieval, and human refinement, forming a hierarchical taxonomy that spans ToC, ToB and ToE with 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains. Based on this taxonomy, we construct executable environments and synthesize single-turn and multi-turn tasks through four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program. OmniaBench further introduces a ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors to support fine-grained evaluation and analysis. The resulting dataset contains 1,431 tasks, together with a challenging subset of 644 tasks designed to reduce evaluation cost and mitigate potential contamination of the full set after public release. The bench presents substantial challenges to current frontier models, with even Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieving Overall Pass@1 scores of only 58.54 and 57.14, respectively. Further analyses reveal clear differences across domains and capabilities, as well as persistent limitations in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction. OmniaBench provides a broad and diagnostic benchmark for characterizing the capability boundaries of general agents.

</details>


### [50] [Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15092)
*Haocheng Yang,Licheng Pan,Xiaoxi Li,Zhichao Chen,Zhiheng Zhang,Yuan Lu,Haoxuan Li,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Rubrics on Trial is a query-only framework that iteratively builds a rubric set from scratch using synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs, validating each candidate rubric via discriminability checks before inclusion — no external annotations or model training required. It outperforms baselines on 6 of 7 evaluation sets across five preference benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing query-to-rubric generation methods, while avoiding reliance on human-written rubrics or preference data, lack any explicit validation mechanism. A generated rubric may be non-discriminative (fails to distinguish answer quality), over-specific, style-only, or penalize valid alternative strategies — rendering it useless or even harmful for LLM training/evaluation.

Method: The framework evolves a rubric set starting from an empty set. It generates synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs, then screens each candidate rubric through validation checks that test for discriminability, filter out over-specific rubrics, and reject style-only rubrics. Only validated rubrics are added to the set. The entire process uses only the query as input — no human annotations or model fine-tuning.

Result: Rubrics on Trial achieves the best average accuracy across five preference benchmark suites and leads on six of seven individual evaluation sets.

Conclusion: Validating rubrics through discriminability screening is both necessary and effective. A query-only, training-free framework can produce high-quality rubrics that reliably distinguish response quality, outperforming prior approaches that lack such validation.

Abstract: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a rubric set from an empty set without external annotations or model training. It derives supervision solely from synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs and validates each proposed rubric before adding it, screening out non-discriminative, over-specific, and style-only candidate rubrics. Experiments across five preference benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Rubrics on Trial, which achieves the best average accuracy and leads on six of seven evaluation sets.

</details>


### [51] [Grokipedia vs Wikipedia: An LLM-Based Audit of Political Neutrality along Ideologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15146)
*Filippos Vlahos,Guillaume Bied,Tijl De Bie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A political bias analysis comparing Grokipedia (LLM-written by Grok) and Wikipedia across 1,394 politician article pairs finds that all LLM judges, including Grok itself, rate Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias exhibit favorable bias but toward different ideological groups: Grokipedia favors economically right-wing politicians and penalizes socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia shows the opposite pattern.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokipedia was launched in late 2025 as an LLM-generated encyclopedia, motivated partly by claims that Wikipedia suffers from left-wing/liberal bias. This study investigates whether an LLM-written encyclopedia achieves greater neutrality or merely embeds a different ideological slant.

Method: The authors analyze 1,394 article pairs from Grokipedia and Wikipedia, each describing a member of government. Neutrality is assessed along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions using four LLM judges: Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. To account for potential judge bias, the study also examines patterns in the LLMs' judgments themselves.

Result: All four LLM judges, including Grok, consistently rate Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias portray politicians favorably overall but diverge ideologically: Grokipedia exhibits favorable bias toward economically right-wing politicians and penalizes socially liberal ones, whereas Wikipedia shows favorable bias toward socially liberal politicians.

Conclusion: An LLM-written encyclopedia does not inherently deliver greater neutrality; rather, it reflects a different ideological orientation. The finding that Grok itself rates Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia is particularly notable, suggesting that LLM-generated content may embed biases distinct from those found in human-curated platforms.

Abstract: Online encyclopedias shape political opinion and, through it, democratic discourse. In late 2025, Grokipedia was released, an encyclopedia written entirely by the LLM Grok. One motivation behind the project was to provide an unbiased alternative to Wikipedia, which has faced accusations of "left-wing" and "liberal" bias. But does an encyclopedia written by an LLM deliver greater neutrality, or does it simply embed a different ideology? We conduct a large-scale political bias study on Grokipedia and Wikipedia, analysing 1,394 article pairs describing members of government for neutrality along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions employing four LLM judges, Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. As the LLMs could themselves be biased, we also investigate patterns in their judgments. We find all LLM-judges, including Grok, to rate Grokipedia less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias are rated as portraying politicians favourably overall, but towards different ideological groups. Grokipedia particularly favours economically right-wing politicians and penalises socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia is rated as favourably biased towards the latter.

</details>


### [52] [Linear representations of grammaticality in neural language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15175)
*Jane Li,Najoung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether grammaticality is encoded in the internal representations of neural language models using mass-mean probing, finding robust representational separation between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences that generalizes across phenomena and languages, independent of confounding factors like lexical frequency and plausibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on grammatical knowledge in NLMs relies on probability-based measures (comparing likelihoods of grammatical vs. ungrammatical strings), which is problematic because probability conflates grammaticality with lexical frequency, plausibility, and world knowledge. A method is needed that assesses grammatical encoding without depending on string probabilities.

Method: The authors employ mass-mean probing on internal sentence representations of pretrained NLMs to test whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences are linearly separable in representational space. They control for correlated sentence-level confounds and test generalization across different grammatical phenomena and languages.

Result: Grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations across a wide range of pretrained NLMs, with clear representational separation that cannot be fully explained by alternative sentence-level factors. This encoding generalizes across diverse grammatical phenomena and partially across languages, indicating grammaticality forms a coherent representational dimension.

Conclusion: The findings provide new evidence that syntactic knowledge in language models goes beyond surface probabilities, and the probing framework offers a complementary, probability-independent method for evaluating grammatical competence in NLMs.

Abstract: Whether neural language models (NLMs) possess the ability to distinguish strings on the basis of their grammaticality remains a debated topic in the computational linguistics literature. Existing evidence has largely relied on probability-based measures, testing whether models assign higher probabilities to grammatical than ungrammatical strings. However, probability comparisons have been criticized as a measure for grammatical knowledge based on the assumption that grammaticality is inherently entangled with likelihood. Model-assigned probability is a function of many related sentence properties, such as lexical frequency, plausibility, and world knowledge. In this work, we move beyond probability-based evaluations and investigate whether grammaticality is encoded in the internal representations of NLMs. Using mass-mean probing, we test whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences are systematically separated in representational space. We further examine the extent to which these representations are independent of sentence properties that are correlated with grammaticality, as well as their generalization across grammatical phenomena and languages. Our results provide evidence that grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations of a wide range of pretrained NLMs, yielding clear representational separation on the dimension of grammaticality that cannot be fully explained by alternative sentence-level factors. Moreover, this encoding generalizes across a broad range of grammatical phenomena and to some degree, across languages, suggesting that grammaticality constitutes a coherent representational dimension in contemporary NLMs. These findings contribute new evidence to debates about the nature of syntactic knowledge in language models and offer a complementary framework for evaluating grammatical competence that is not dependent on string probabilities alone.

</details>


### [53] [T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15178)
*Ziyang Cai,Xingyu Zhu,Yihe Dong,Yinghui He,Sanjeev Arora*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: T2MLR introduces targeted middle-layer recurrence in Transformers, where a cached representation from the previous token's middle layer is fused into an earlier layer of the current token. This enables latent reasoning states to persist across decoding steps with minimal overhead, consistently outperforming standard Transformers on multi-hop reasoning tasks, and can be retrofitted into existing pretrained models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard autoregressive Transformers compress rich hidden computations through token space at each decoding step, making it difficult for intermediate reasoning states to persist over time. Prior works address this via full-layer recurrence (e.g., looping over all layers), which is computationally expensive. The authors hypothesize that effective latent reasoning can instead emerge from targeted recurrence at middle layers.

Method: T2MLR fuses a cached middle-layer representation from the previous token directly into an earlier layer of the current token position. Crucially, recurrence is applied only to a localized middle-layer block (as little as 20% of the network), rather than looping over all layers. The architecture can also be retrofitted into existing pretrained Transformers with brief finetuning, avoiding pretraining from scratch.

Result: T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer baselines on natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning. Localized middle-layer recurrence often outperforms full-layer recurrence. A 1.7B pretrained Transformer retrofitted with T2MLR and briefly finetuned showed substantial improvements in math reasoning.

Conclusion: Effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers; targeted middle-layer recurrence can be both more effective and more practical, as it can be retrofitted into existing pretrained models with minimal training, lowering the barrier to adoption.

Abstract: Transformer reasoning is limited by autoregressive decoding, which repeat edly compresses rich hidden computation through token space and makes it difficult for intermediate reasoning states to persist across time. We in troduce Transformers with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence (T2MLR), a transformers-based latent reasoning architecture that fuses a cached middle layer representation from the previous token directly into an earlier layer of the current token position, enabling abstract intermediate computation to persist across decoding steps with little inference overhead. Across natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning, T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer base lines. Moreover, applying recurrence to only a localized middle-layer block (as little as 20% of the network) often outperforms full-layer recurrence. Im portantly, T2MLR does not require pretraining from scratch: retrofitting the recurrent pathway into an existing pretrained 1.7B Transformer and briefly finetuning substantially improves math reasoning, lowering the barrier to practical adoption. These results suggest that effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers as in previous works, but can instead emerge more strongly from targeted middle-layer recurrence.

</details>


### [54] [Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15200)
*Haran Raajesh,Kulin Shah,Adam Klivans,Philipp Krähenbühl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper formalizes MDLM generation as a two-stage action MDP with token and masking terms, enabling effective RL optimization that achieves SOTA on GSM8K (87.1%) and MBPP (53.4%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning improves reasoning in LLMs, but extending RL to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) is challenging because log-likelihood is intractable. Existing methods approximate log-likelihood by modeling only token predictions while ignoring the unmasking order, which is a critical component of the generative process.

Method: The authors formalize MDLM generation as a two-stage action Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each step consists of (1) predicting tokens for masked positions and (2) deciding which positions to remask. The policy gradient naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term. Both terms are jointly optimized using reinforcement learning.

Result: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks: 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing both token predictions and masking decisions via the two-stage MDP formulation significantly improves MDLM reasoning performance, enabling RL-based fine-tuning for diffusion language models.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has proven effective for improving reasoning in large language models, but extending it to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) remains challenging due to the intractability of the log-likelihood estimation. Existing approaches approximate this log-likelihood by modeling only the token predictions, ignoring the order in which positions are unmasked during generation. We observe that MDLM generation involves two decisions at each step: what tokens to place at each masked position and which positions to remask. We formalize this as a two-stage action MDP, showing that the policy gradient naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term. Combining optimization of both terms leads to state-of-the-art outcomes on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, with scores of 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP.

</details>


### [55] [Expanding the Lexicon of Ge'ez Based African Languages: A Comparative Study of Amharic and Tigrinya](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15209)
*Hailay Kidu Teklehaymanot,Debela Desalegn Yadeta,Wolfgang Nejdl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VEXMLM extends XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords, improving Amharic and Tigrinya performance and transferring gains to 17 other low-resource African languages across QA, NER, and SA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual PLMs suffer degraded performance on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages due to high OOV rates and excessive subword fragmentation caused by Latin-script-centric tokenizer training. Ge'ez-script languages like Amharic and Tigrinya are particularly affected.

Method: VEXMLM (1) trains a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic/Tigrinya corpora, (2) extends XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords, (3) initializes new embeddings by averaging constituent subword embeddings from XLM-R's original tokenizer, (4) performs continued masked language modeling on the extended vocabulary, and (5) fine-tunes on downstream tasks (QA, NER, SA).

Result: On Amharic/Tigrinya QA: 87.0 EM/90.0 F1 (vs. 66.0/78.0 for XLM-R and 74.0/78.0 for Glot500). On SA: 80.0% accuracy (vs. 77.0% XLM-R, 46.0% Glot500). On NER: OOV-token entity accuracy improved from 81.4% to 94.3% averaged across 11 evaluated languages. Gains transferred to 17 additional unaugmented African languages.

Conclusion: Vocabulary extension with embedding initialization tailored to a specific script, combined with continued pretraining, yields substantial improvements on target languages and positive transfer to typologically related languages, offering an efficient alternative to full pretraining from scratch for low-resource non-Latin-script languages.

Abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models (PLMs) exhibit degraded performance on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages, driven by high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates and excessive subword fragmentation that result from Latin-script-centric tokenizer training. We introduce VEXMLM, a vocabulary-extended variant of XLM-R targeting the two highest-resource Ge'ez-script languages, Amharic and Tigrinya, and further evaluated on 17 additional low-resource African languages (19 total). We train a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic and Tigrinya monolingual corpora, extend XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords derived from this tokenizer, and initialize their embeddings by averaging the embeddings of their constituent subwords under XLM-R's original tokenizer. VEXMLM is trained in two stages: (1) continued masked language modeling over the extended vocabulary on the curated corpora, and (2) supervised fine-tuning on question answering (QA), named entity recognition (NER), and sentiment analysis (SA). On Amharic/Tigrinya QA, VEXMLM achieves 87.0 EM /90.0 F1, versus 66.0 EM/78.0 F1 for XLM-R and 74.0 EM/ 78.0 F1 for Glot500. On SA, VEXMLM reaches 80.0\% accuracy versus 77.0\% (XLM-R) and 46.0\% (Glot500). On NER, VEXMLM raises OOV-token entity accuracy from 81.4\% to 94.3\%, averaged over 11 of the 19 evaluated languages for which OOV analysis was possible. Our contributions are: (i) a vocabulary-extension and embedding-initialization procedure tailored to Ge'ez script; (ii) a two-stage training strategy under which vocabulary and continued-pretraining gains on Amharic/Tigrinya transfer to 17 typologically related, unaugmented African languages; and (iii) an evaluation spanning both intrinsic tokenization metrics (vocabulary coverage, fertility, OOV rate) and extrinsic task performance across all 19 languages.

</details>


### [56] [In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15232)
*Jimmy T. H. Smith,Tarek Dakhran,Alberto Cabrera,Simon S. Lee,Paul Pak,Aditya Tadimeti,Tim Seyde,Maxime Labonne,Alexander Amini,Mathias Lechner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Presents tokenizer expansion, a method to upgrade a pre-trained model's tokenizer in-place by continuing BPE merges on a multilingual corpus. New token embeddings are initialized as the mean of source sub-token embeddings, and a two-stage adaptation recovers quality. Applied to an 8B MoE model, the expanded 128K tokenizer reduces token counts 2.4–4.0× for Hindi, Vietnamese, and Thai, yielding an estimated 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedup on-device.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compact on-device models ship with small vocabularies to keep embedding/LM-head matrices manageable, but this causes severe token fragmentation for languages not prioritized during pre-training. When deployment priorities shift, users of those languages suffer increased latency, compute, and energy costs. The goal is to expand the tokenizer without retraining from scratch, preserving existing model quality while improving multilingual efficiency.

Method: Tokenizer expansion works by continuing the existing BPE merges on a multilingual corpus, ensuring most source tokens remain intact as single tokens and every new token has an exact decomposition into source tokens. Carried-over embedding rows are copied unchanged; new rows are initialized as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. A two-stage adaptation follows: (1) embedding-only training, then (2) full-model continued pre-training, which recovers source-checkpoint quality. Applied to an LFM2-8B-A1B checkpoint to produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer.

Result: The expanded tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in roughly 2.4× and 2.6× fewer tokens than the source (up to 4.0× on Thai). Combining token reductions with measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary, the estimated per-character decode speedup is 2.2–3.7× across reference devices. The two-stage adaptation recovers source-checkpoint quality.

Conclusion: Tokenizer expansion is a practical, in-place recipe for upgrading pre-trained tokenizers to better serve previously under-prioritized languages, offering significant decode speedups on compact on-device models without the cost of pre-training from scratch.

Abstract: A tokenizer fixed at the start of pre-training allocates vocabulary in proportion to the pre-training corpus, reflecting the deployment priorities at that time. When those priorities shift, languages added later are split into many more tokens per word, which can raise latency, compute, and energy consumption for users of those languages. Cloud models can afford a broad vocabulary because the embedding and LM-head matrices are a small fraction of their parameters. On a compact model those matrices are a material share of per-token decode bandwidth, so on-device models ship small vocabularies and accept fragmentation outside a fixed language set. We present tokenizer expansion, an in-place recipe for upgrading a pre-trained model's tokenizer when the model producer controls its design. We continue the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on a multilingual corpus, so most source tokens carry over unchanged as single tokens and every new token has an exact decomposition into source tokens. We copy the carried-over embedding rows unchanged and initialize new rows as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. A two-stage adaptation, embedding-only training then full-model continued pre-training, recovers source-checkpoint quality. We apply the recipe to a continued pre-trained checkpoint of LFM2-8B-A1B, an 8B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model, to help produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer. The expanded tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in roughly $2.4\times$ and $2.6\times$ fewer tokens than the source (up to $4.0\times$ on Thai). Combining these reductions with the measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary, we estimate a $2.2$-$3.7\times$ per-character decode speedup for these languages across our reference devices. We release the model weights and the expanded tokenizer, and report the negative findings that shaped the recipe.

</details>


### [57] [Language Identification via Compositional Data Analysis: A Linear-Time Classifier Based on Log-Ratio Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15238)
*Paul-Andrei Pogăcean,Sanda-Maria Avram*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a language identification method that treats character and bigram frequencies as compositional data on the simplex, applying centered log-ratio (CLR) transformations so that Euclidean distance equals Aitchison distance. Combined with Laplace smoothing, the pipeline achieves robust, efficient, and interpretable language identification across six languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural language identification methods are computationally expensive, while classical n-gram frequency methods are efficient but use distance metrics ill-suited to compositional (proportional) data. The authors aim to bridge this gap by introducing a theoretically sound distance measure—Aitchison distance—for frequency-based language identification.

Method: Character unigram and bigram frequency vectors are treated as compositional data constrained to the simplex. The centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation maps these vectors bijectively onto a (D-1)-dimensional zero-sum subspace of ℝ^D, where standard Euclidean distance corresponds to the Aitchison distance on the simplex. Laplace smoothing handles zero counts (sparsity). The resulting pipeline classifies text by comparing CLR-transformed feature vectors using Euclidean distance.

Result: The CLR-based method achieves robust accuracy across varying text lengths on six languages, with particularly strong performance on longer sequences. It offers a competitive, deterministic alternative to neural methods.

Conclusion: Compositional representations with CLR transformation provide a deterministic, computationally efficient, and interpretable solution for language identification, making it well-suited for low-resource settings where neural approaches are impractical.

Abstract: Language identification is commonly addressed using either neural architectures or statistical n-gram models. Neural approaches typically require substantial computational resources, whereas classical frequency-based methods offer efficient linear-time performance, but rely on distance metrics that are not always appropriate for compositional data.
  This work models character and bigram frequency distributions as compositional vectors constrained to the simplex and mapped via the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation bijectively onto the $(D-1)$-dimensional zero-sum subspace of $\mathbb{R}^D$, where Euclidean distances correspond to Aitchison distances. A pipeline is proposed, combining CLR-transformed unigram and bigram features with Laplace smoothing to address sparsity. The method is evaluated on six languages.
  Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves robust accuracy across different text lengths, with strong performance for longer sequences. These findings indicate that compositional representations provide a deterministic and computationally efficient alternative for language identification, particularly in settings where interpretability and low resource consumption are essential.

</details>


### [58] [TikStance: A Multimodal and Hierarchical Dataset for Multi-target Stance Analysis in TikTok Political Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15240)
*Yazhi Zhang,Fuqiang Niu,Bowen Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TikStance, a multimodal, context-aware dataset of 161 TikTok videos and 13,878 comments (with hierarchical reply trees) covering three U.S. political figures (Trump, Biden, Harris) during the 2024 election cycle. It is designed for stance detection with multi-annotator labels achieving strong inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α > 0.72 across all subsets).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Political discourse has shifted to short-video platforms like TikTok, but existing datasets lack joint audiovisual content and threaded conversational structure, limiting computational analysis of stance in politically relevant multimodal contexts.

Method: The authors collected 161 TikTok videos and their 13,878 associated comments (including nested replies) from September 2023 to January 2025, targeting Donald Trump, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris. Each item (video-to-target and comment-to-target) was labeled by three independent annotators using a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None). Disagreements were resolved through re-annotation, yielding final Krippendorff's α of 0.743 (Trump), 0.723 (Biden), and 0.722 (Harris). The dataset preserves parent-linked comment trees and video metadata for context-aware analysis.

Result: The final dataset achieved high inter-annotator reliability across all three target subsets (α ≥ 0.722). Descriptive analysis revealed target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth, with nested replies comprising 23.3% of all comments, highlighting significant hierarchical conversational structure.

Conclusion: By integrating multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level human annotations, TikStance provides a valuable resource for multimodal stance detection, political communication research, computational social science, and context-aware NLP.

Abstract: Political discourse has increasingly moved to short-video platforms, yet computational analysis of such content remains constrained by the scarcity of datasets that jointly preserve audiovisual information and hierarchical conversations. Here we present TikStance, a multimodal and context-aware dataset comprising 161 videos and 13,876 comments from TikTok, designed for stance detection in political discussions. The dataset covers three major political figures in the 2024 U.S. election cycle--Donald Trump, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris--with content collected between September 2023 and January 2025. Each discussion unit links a host video and its metadata to a parent-linked comment tree, enabling stance analysis within both audiovisual and conversational context. Each item was independently labeled by three annotators using a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None) for video-to-target and comment-to-target stance; items with disagreement were re-annotated, and the final Krippendorff's \(α\) reached 0.743, 0.723, and 0.722 for the Trump, Biden, and Harris subsets, respectively. Descriptive analysis further reveals target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth, with nested replies accounting for 23.3\% of all comments. By combining multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level human annotations, TikStance supports research in multimodal stance detection, political communication, computational social science, and context-aware natural language processing.

</details>


### [59] [Beyond the Leaderboard: Design Lessons for Trustworthy Multimodal VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15241)
*Sushant Gautam,Vajira Thambawita,Michael A. Riegler,Pål Halvorsen,Steven A. Hicks*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Analysis of nine GI endoscopy multimodal AI systems from MediaEval Medico 2025 reveals that while parameter-efficient fine-tuning achieves strong task performance, answer accuracy does not guarantee faithful clinical reasoning. Structured reasoning and explicit grounding correlate with more reliable explanations, motivating evaluation beyond lexical overlap, standardized evidence-linked explanations, and robustness checks for trustworthy healthcare AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Healthcare multimodal AI systems combining visual and textual data must be both accurate and interpretable. Current evaluation practices often overemphasize answer-level metrics (lexical overlap) without assessing whether the reasoning behind answers is faithful, complete, and clinically grounded. There is a gap between high challenge performance and genuine clinical trustworthiness.

Method: The authors conduct a retrospective case study using the MediaEval Medico 2025 GI endoscopy benchmark. They systematically analyze design choices across nine documented multimodal systems along two axes: (1) question-answering performance and (2) explanation quality. The analysis examines how parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones compares with methods enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding, using both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessment of reasoning faithfulness and completeness.

Result: Parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones yields strong challenge performance on answer-level metrics. However, these gains do not consistently translate into faithful or complete clinical reasoning. Methods that enforce structured reasoning and explicit grounding demonstrate more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types. The evidence linking structured reasoning to improved reliability is correlational rather than causal (i.e., no ablation studies confirm this relationship).

Conclusion: The findings call for (1) evaluation frameworks that go beyond lexical overlap metrics, (2) standardized evidence-linked explanations in multimodal medical AI, (3) leakage-aware data governance, and (4) lightweight robustness and calibration checks. These elements collectively support the development of trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI grounded in reliable data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation practices.

Abstract: Healthcare multimodal AI must combine visual and textual evidence while remaining reliable and interpretable. Using MediaEval Medico 2025 as a retrospective GI endoscopy case study, we analyze design choices across nine documented systems for question answering and explanation quality. Parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones provides strong challenge performance, but answer-level gains do not consistently translate into faithful and complete clinical reasoning. Methods enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding show more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types, although the evidence is correlational rather than ablation-based. These results motivate evaluation beyond lexical overlap, standardized evidence-linked explanations, leakage-aware data governance, and lightweight robustness and calibration checks. The findings support trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI based on data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation.

</details>


### [60] [SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15272)
*Yasheng Sun,Zezi Zeng,Yifan Yang,Chong Luo,Wenyi Wang,Ziwei Liu,Jürgen Schmidhuber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciDiagramEdit is a benchmark and skill-evolution framework for instruction-driven editing of scientific figures. It mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories with authors' revision intent, and uses an agentic learning approach where a proposer iteratively refines editing skills from execution traces, progressively improving edit accuracy on held-out data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Editing scientific figures is routine but time-consuming. Automating this via natural language is challenging because figures are dense infographics combining heterogeneous elements (schematics, plots, photos, captions, arrows) under tight visual grammar. Existing approaches lack benchmarks grounded in real revision intents and methods that operate on editable vector sources.

Method: The authors introduce: (1) SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark constructed by mining before/after figure pairs and their associated revision intents from arXiv version histories; (2) a skill-evolution framework that operates on editable vector source files, where an agentic proposer iteratively refines skill specifications over multiple epochs using execution traces from training data, progressively improving the agent's editing capabilities.

Result: The skill-evolution approach progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, demonstrating that natural paper revisions serve as an effective training signal for instruction-driven scientific figure editing.

Conclusion: Natural paper revisions from arXiv version histories provide a viable and effective training signal for automating instruction-driven figure editing. The agentic skill-evolution framework successfully learns to handle the complexity and diversity of real-world scientific figure edits.

Abstract: Editing the figures in a research paper is a routine and time-consuming part of everyday research practice: authors relabel components, rearrange panels, and restyle visuals as they revise their manuscripts. Automating this editing workflow under a natural-language instruction, however, is challenging, because a scientific figure is a dense infographic in which heterogeneous visual elements such as schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows are composed under a tight visual grammar to advance a specific argument. To address this, we present SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark and skill-evolution framework that learns from natural paper revisions and operates on the figure's editable vector source, where users can inspect and co-edit individual primitives alongside the agent. Our benchmark mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each grounded in the authors' own revision intent. To accommodate the diversity of editing instructions, we adopt agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer continually refines the agent's skill specification from execution traces over multiple epochs. The resulting skill progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, providing evidence that natural paper revisions are an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.

</details>


### [61] [Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15277)
*Patrik Wolf,Thomas Kleine Buening,Andreas Krause,Celestine Mendler-Dünner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs violate the law of total probability when making inferences across hierarchical population partitions. Fine-grained subpopulation estimates often outperform direct population-level estimates — a phenomenon dubbed the "macro fallacy" — suggesting models possess relevant knowledge they fail to aggregate consistently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: If in-context learning truly amounts to conditional inference, then LLM probability estimates should obey the law of total probability: prior-weighted conditionals should sum to population marginals. The authors test whether frontier LLMs actually exhibit this basic self-consistency property.

Method: The authors construct binary trees to recursively partition populations into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. They verbalize subpopulation descriptions as prompts, collect LLM conditional estimates, and aggregate them back into population-level estimates via the law of total probability. These reconstructed estimates are compared across granularity levels and benchmarked against human reference data. The protocol spans multiple problem domains and frontier models, with an in-depth study of persona prompting.

Result: Widespread violations of statistical self-consistency are found across all models and domains. A key finding — the "macro fallacy" — shows that estimates reconstructed from fine-grained subpopulation responses better align with human ground truth than direct population-level estimates. This effect is robust to variations in tree structure and task, and can be partially recovered via implicit prompting.

Conclusion: LLMs possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but fail to reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. Statistical self-consistency thus serves as a novel, reference-free evaluation criterion that remains unsaturated by current frontier models, pointing to a fundamental limitation in how LLMs perform conditional inference.

Abstract: In-context learning is commonly interpreted as a form of conditional inference, in which the prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Applying this protocol across problem domains and state-of-the-art frontier models, we show widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. This effect persists across variations in tree structure and estimation task, and can be partially recovered through implicit prompting. Together, these findings suggest that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

</details>

### [62] [Beyond Object Validation: Relational Conformance in Multi-Artifact Agent Releases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14155)
*Tengjiao Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Agent systems rigorously validate inputs and tool calls but often neglect final output packages. The paper documents a real-world failure where a DRSS release self-contradicted (60-point ledger vs. 100-point Gold Path report). It proposes SIP-RC, a relational conformance profile that models releases as evidence-linked graphs with bounded authority, lineage tracking, and independent recomputation. The failure class is established; whether SIP-RC outperforms existing checks remains an open question.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent systems apply extensive validation to inputs, intermediate tool calls, and generated objects, yet the final published package escapes equivalent scrutiny. This gap produces contradictory releases — all local checks passing while the aggregate output is internally inconsistent. The authors seek to formalize this failure class and propose a conformance framework that catches such contradictions by treating a release as a verifiable graph of claims, evidence, and derivations.

Method: The paper examines three case studies: (1) a DRSS release where a 60-point ledger coexisted with a 100-point Gold Path certificate, (2) Schema Docs, where similar faults hardened into product contracts, and (3) Brand Shuttle GEO, where evidence is converted into repair work. From these, the authors derive SIP-RC (Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile), which models a release as a directed graph where claims must point to evidence, decisions carry bounded authority, derived artifacts preserve execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes must match the internally-checked package. A validator recomputes critical decisions on an independent path, and hard failures cannot be averaged or smoothed away.

Result: The paper establishes and formalizes the "contradictory package" failure class with concrete real-world instances. It demonstrates that several SIP-RC mechanisms (evidence linking, lineage tracking, independent recomputation of critical decisions, non-averaging hard failures) are practical to implement. However, the full profile's comparative performance against existing validation approaches is not yet evaluated.

Conclusion: The contradictory-package failure class is real and consequential. SIP-RC offers a principled relational conformance model to address it, with several practical mechanisms demonstrated. The key open question is whether the full profile meaningfully outperforms current validation practices in deployment, which requires further experimentation.

Abstract: Agent systems validate inputs, tool calls, and generated objects. The final package often escapes the same scrutiny. In one DRSS release, the ledger supported 60 points and a failed certificate; the report announced a 100-point Gold Path. Every local gate was green. The package contradicted itself.
  We study that failure alongside Schema Docs, where similar faults became product contracts, and Brand Shuttle GEO, where evidence is turned into repair work. The result is a candidate Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile (SIP-RC). It models a release as a graph: claims point to evidence, decisions carry bounded authority, derived artifacts retain their execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes must match the package that was checked. Hard failures cannot be averaged away, and a validator recomputes critical decisions on a separate path. The paper establishes the failure class and shows that several mechanisms are practical. Whether the full profile performs better than existing checks remains an open experiment.

</details>


### [63] [Natural-Language to SysMLv2 Translation via Conformance-Driven Iterative Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14162)
*Chance LaVoie,Eladio Andujar Lugo,Taylan G. Topcu,Levent Burak Kara*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A conformance-checker-driven framework that wraps LLM-based SysMLv2 generation in a generate-check-repair loop, using a production conformance checker as an oracle. Single-shot generation achieved 51.16% acceptance; the proposed loop achieves 100.00% production conformance across 604 prompt-model cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NL-to-SysMLv2 translation approaches focus on grammar plausibility, but for practical industrial deployment, generated models must pass production-level conformance checking in real modeling environments. This gap between syntactically valid output and tool-acceptable artifacts motivates a framework where production conformance is the explicit termination condition.

Method: A generate-check-repair loop embedding a production SysMLv2 conformance checker. After initial generation, each model is evaluated; deterministic diagnostics from the checker are fed back as revision prompts. Iteration continues until zero conformance errors are reached, using the production checker as the ground-truth oracle rather than relying on grammar alone.

Result: Evaluated on the full SysMBench prompt set (151 prompts) across four LLM backends, yielding 604 prompt-model cases. Single-shot generation achieved 51.16% production-conformance acceptance. The proposed generate-check-repair loop achieved 100.00% conformance, elevating deployability from post-processing to an in-loop control mechanism.

Conclusion: Embedding a production conformance checker as an oracle within a closed-loop generation process reliably converts probabilistic LLM outputs into fully accepted SysMLv2 artifacts. This shifts the goal from grammar plausibility to deployability, making NL-to-model translation viable for industrial MBSE workflows.

Abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) relies on formal system models as primary technical artifacts for representing requirements, structure, and behavior across the system lifecycle. With the standardization of SysMLv2 as a textual language, interest is increasing in translating natural-language descriptions directly into executable models. For practical deployment, generated models must be accepted by industrial modeling environments, not merely satisfy grammar constraints. We present a conformance-checker-driven framework for reliable natural-language-to-SysMLv2 translation that enforces production-level acceptance as the termination condition. The system embeds a SysMLv2 conformance checker within a generate-check-repair loop. Each model is evaluated using the checker, and deterministic diagnostics are incorporated into revisions until zero conformance errors are achieved. Using the production checker as the oracle ensures the framework targets deployability rather than grammar plausibility. We evaluate the approach on the full SysMBench prompt set of 151 prompts across four large language model backends, yielding 604 prompt-model cases. Single-shot generation achieves 51.16% production-conformance acceptance, while our approach achieves 100.00% conformance. By elevating production conformance from a post-processing check to a control mechanism within generation, the framework converts probabilistic outputs into production-accepted SysMLv2 artifacts suitable for loading, visualization, and engineering use.

</details>


### [64] [Towards Reliable AI-Assisted Analog Design: Template-Constrained LLM Agents for SAR ADC Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14165)
*Dimple Vijay Kochar,Hae-Seung Lee,Anantha P. Chandrakasan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ATLAS is an expert-knowledge-grounded, multi-step LLM agentic framework that generates functional SAR ADC schematics capable of passing SPICE simulation validation, addressing the hallucination and failure issues of direct LLM prompting in analog EDA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show strong code generation for digital design but fail in analog EDA due to limited circuit topology understanding and data scarcity. Direct prompting leads to hallucinations and schematics that cannot pass SPICE simulations, creating a bottleneck for LLM application in analog design automation.

Method: ATLAS is an end-to-end, multi-step LLM agentic framework that grounds the LLM with expert knowledge across four stages: planning, selection, parameterization, and iterative modification. It introduces Template-Constrained Generation for a more generalized SAR ADC flow and validates designs across technology nodes and input specifications using SPICE simulations.

Result: ATLAS successfully generates functional SAR ADC schematics that pass rigorous SPICE simulation validation across different technology nodes and input specifications, demonstrating a strong proof-of-concept for LLM-driven analog design.

Conclusion: The expert-knowledge-grounded multi-step agentic approach in ATLAS provides a pragmatic foundation for reliably integrating LLMs into analog design methodologies, overcoming the limitations of direct prompting.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant capability in software code generation, their application to analog Electronic Design Automation (EDA) is bottlenecked. Owing to limited circuit topology understanding and data, directly prompting LLMs and multimodal models leads to hallucinations and failure to produce schematics capable of passing rigorous SPICE simulations, as we show in our work. Instead, we propose an end-to-end, multi-step LLM agentic framework ATLAS, capable of generating a functional Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) that successfully passes simulation validation. To adhere to the rigid constraints of analog design, we utilize expert knowledge to ground the LLM in its planning, selection, parameterization, and iterative modification. As part of ATLAS, we introduce Template-Constrained Generation - which unlike other template-based works - builds towards a more generalized SAR ADC generation flow. We demonstrate a strong proof-of-concept of our framework by developing SAR ADCs across technology nodes and input specs. Overall, our expert-knowledge grounded multi-step agentic ATLAS establishes a pragmatic foundation for integrating LLMs into reliable analog design methodologies.

</details>


### [65] [Stop Means Stop: Measuring and Repairing the Enforcement Gap in Agent-Framework Control Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14166)
*Sajjad Khan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A study exposing that six major open-source LLM-agent frameworks fail to enforce barrier semantics on control primitives like approval gates and cancellation. The authors identify four vulnerability classes--sibling leaks, replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, and timeout zombies--then present SOUNDGATE, a verified external effect gate that blocks all violations while maintaining performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent frameworks provide control primitives (human-in-the-loop approval gates, run cancellation, execution timeouts) whose names and documentation imply that no gated side effect executes while a run is paused, cancelled, or timed out. The authors hypothesize this contract is systematically violated and aim to empirically measure, categorize, and repair these gaps.

Method: Model-free differential probes are used to isolate violations across six open-source frameworks (five with pre-execution gates). Live frontier-model experiments measure leakage rates under a fixed protocol across three schedulers and two language runtimes (215/1200 runs leaked). SOUNDGATE is then introduced: a Rust-based environment-external effect gate enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel. Verification uses Verus, TLA+/TLC (exhaustive to 7.5e7 states), TLAPS, Loom model-checking, and differential conformance testing over 1.2e7 operations.

Result: All six frameworks exhibit at least one violation class; the sibling leak appears in every framework with a pre-execution gate. Frontier models emit leak-triggering plan shapes at up to 14% pooled rates; 215 of 1,200 live runs execute effects during an approval pause. SOUNDGATE blocks every measured violation end-to-end across all six frameworks while releasing legitimate effects, achieving ~1 ms admission latency per write and 12k–26k durable admissions per second.

Conclusion: The implied barrier-semantics contract of LLM-agent control primitives is universally broken in current open-source frameworks. These are not merely theoretical vulnerabilities but are reachable under realistic workloads. SOUNDGATE demonstrates that a formally specified, externally enforced effect gate can close all identified gaps with negligible performance overhead.

Abstract: Production LLM-agent frameworks expose control primitives -- human-in-the-loop approval gates, run cancellation, and execution timeouts -- whose names and documentation imply barrier semantics: while a run is paused, cancelled, or timed out, no gated side effect executes. We show this implied contract holds on none of the six widely used open-source frameworks we test. Model-free differential probes isolate a recurring sibling leak -- an approval gate suspends its own branch while a sibling branch's effect executes during the pause, so a later rejection cannot prevent it -- in every framework shipping a pre-execution gate (five of six), plus three further gaps: replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, and timeout zombies. The hazard is reachable, not merely constructible: under an a-priori-fixed protocol, frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at pooled rates up to 14%, and when live models drive the unmodified frameworks under an approval pause, 215 of 1,200 runs execute their effect during the pause, across three schedulers and two language runtimes. To repair the measured gaps we present SOUNDGATE, an environment-external effect gate in Rust through which every side effect must be admitted, enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel -- one property per violation class -- under a stated complete-mediation contract discharged for network egress by kernel-enforced routes. We verify the properties over a model of the admission core (Verus; TLA+/TLC, exhaustive to 7.5e7 states; TLAPS), model-check the deployed Rust with Loom, and bridge model to code by differential conformance over 1.2e7 operations -- refinement evidence, not a mechanized proof. SOUNDGATE blocks every measured violation end-to-end on all six frameworks while releasing legitimate effects, at about 1 ms admission per write and 12k-26k durable admissions per second.

</details>


### [66] [Structured Feedback Improves Repair in an LLM Agent Loop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14167)
*Jaideep Ray,Ankit Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriHarness introduces a code-controlled agent loop where external validators manage acceptance, budgets, and traces. Structured feedback with failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives dramatically improves LLM retry success (up to +44pp) compared to raw diagnostics, with admissible alternatives accounting for most of the gain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The interface between external validation and the next model call in LLM agent retry loops is underspecified. Current practices lack clarity on what diagnostic information should be fed back to the model after a rejection, limiting retry effectiveness.

Method: The authors introduce VeriHarness, a framework where code controls the agent loop: models generate candidates and external validators control acceptance, call budgets, and traces. They compare raw diagnostics against structured feedback containing three fields: failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Experiments use 50 paired TextWorld games with a four-call cap, testing Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Llama-3.1-8B. Ablations isolate the contribution of each feedback field, and a prose-vs-JSON comparison tests format sensitivity.

Result: Full three-field feedback lifts terminal success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44pp) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42pp). Ablations show admissible alternatives drive most of the gain; location and observed value alone perform near the raw diagnostic baseline. Presenting repair information in prose matches JSON performance, indicating format is not the key factor. Results hold across tested call budgets and a sampled-decoding setting.

Conclusion: Structured feedback that includes admissible alternatives is critical for improving LLM agent retry performance. The representation format (JSON vs. prose) matters less than the informational content, and the benefits are robust across model types, call budgets, and decoding strategies.

Abstract: LLM agents often retry after external validation rejects a candidate, but the interface between validation and the next model call remains underspecified. We introduce VeriHarness, a code-controlled agent loop in which models generate candidates while external validators control acceptance, budgets, and traces. We use it to compare raw diagnostics with feedback that identifies the failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Across 50 paired TextWorld games under a four-call cap, feedback containing all three fields raises terminal success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44 percentage points) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42 points). Ablations locate most of the gain in the admissible alternatives: feedback containing only the location and observed value remains near the raw diagnostic baseline. Presenting the complete repair information in prose instead of a keyed JSON record yields nearly the same success, providing no evidence that JSON syntax itself improves repair. The ordering persists across the tested call budgets and one sampled-decoding setting.

</details>


### [67] [Quantize with Confidence? An Empirical Study of Quantization for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14181)
*Saima Afrin,Md. Zahidul Haque,Antonio Mastropaolo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper empirically evaluates six post-training quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, GGUF) on Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama models across Python and Java benchmarks. It assesses functional correctness, code quality (maintainability, reliability, security, complexity), and robustness under varying prompt complexity (measured via Shannon entropy and token length). Key findings: AQLM matches or exceeds full-precision baselines; QuIP# degrades most, especially on complex prompts; security remains stable across all conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the rise of local inference frameworks like Ollama, developers increasingly deploy large code models on resource-constrained hardware (e.g., laptops). Post-training quantization is essential for reducing memory footprint, yet its impact on generated code — particularly beyond functional correctness — remains poorly understood. There is a need for systematic, multi-dimensional evaluation to guide quantization strategy selection.

Method: The authors empirically evaluate six quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, GGUF) applied to two model families (Qwen2.5-Coder, CodeLlama). Evaluation uses the multilingual McEval and CoderEval benchmarks for Python and Java. Metrics span functional correctness (pass@1), code quality dimensions (maintainability, reliability, security, structural complexity), and a novel robustness analysis under varying prompt complexity — operationalized through Shannon entropy and token length.

Result: AQLM consistently matches or exceeds the full-precision baseline in correctness. QuIP# shows the largest correctness degradation, particularly on complex prompts. Security attributes remain stable across all models, benchmarks, and languages. Robustness to prompt complexity varies significantly across quantization techniques. Different methods exhibit meaningfully different impacts on both correctness and code quality.

Conclusion: Quantization methods differ meaningfully in their impact on code generation quality, and evaluation must extend beyond functional correctness to include maintainability, reliability, security, and robustness. AQLM emerges as the most reliable choice for resource-constrained deployment, while QuIP# should be avoided for complex coding tasks. The findings offer practical guidance for practitioners and underscore the importance of holistic evaluation of quantized code models.

Abstract: The growing adoption of local inference frameworks such as Ollama has made it increasingly common for developers to run large code models on laptops and other resource-constrained hardware. In these settings, post-training quantization is essential for reducing memory footprint and enabling practical deployment, yet its impact on generated code remains insufficiently understood. We empirically evaluate six state-of-the-art quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, and GGUF) on two representative large code model families, Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama, using the multilingual McEval and CoderEval benchmarks for Python and Java. We assess functional correctness (pass@1) together with maintainability, reliability, security, and structural complexity. We also introduce a novel analysis of robustness under varying prompt complexity, characterized by Shannon entropy and token length. Our results show that quantization techniques differ meaningfully in their impact on correctness and code quality. AQLM consistently matches or exceeds the full-precision baseline, whereas QuIP# exhibits the largest correctness degradation, particularly on complex prompts. Security attributes remain stable across models, benchmarks, and programming languages, while robustness to prompt complexity varies across techniques. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting quantization strategies for deploying large code models on resource-constrained hardware and highlight the importance of evaluating quantized models beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [68] [NexForge: Scaling Executable Agent Tasks via Requirement-First Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14186)
*Jiarong Zhao,Zhikai Lei,Zhiheng Xi,Rui Zheng,Hang Yan,Jie Zhou,Qin Chen,Liang He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: NexForge is a requirement-first framework that generates executable agent training data by starting from free-form capability requirements rather than predefined tools or environments. It discovers real-world task distributions, compiles tasks with automatic resource retrieval, and produces training data via teacher rollouts. The approach scales to tens of thousands of tasks, dramatically improving agent performance (e.g., Qwen3.5-35B-A3B from 22.5%→75.3% on Terminal-Bench) and yields Nex-N2, a family of state-of-the-art open-source agent models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent training data generation is bottlenecked by substrate-first methods — tasks are tied to predefined tools, repositories, or skill graphs. Expanding coverage requires manually expanding the substrate, each new domain needs a bespoke pipeline, and resulting task distributions reflect substrate convenience rather than real-world needs. NexForge addresses this by reversing the paradigm to a requirement-first approach.

Method: NexForge employs a four-stage requirement-first pipeline: (1) Research-based demand discovery to identify representative task forms, realistic scenarios, and their prevalence; (2) Distribution-aware task compilation that automatically retrieves or constructs files, repositories, dependencies, and runtime configurations; (3) Teacher rollout collection; and (4) Trajectory distillation.
