The same unified pipeline works across domains without domain-specific infrastructure.

Result: With 3,600 terminal tasks and 2,000 office tasks, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base improved from 22.5%→52.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 813→1338 Elo on GDPval. Scaling to 43.2K terminal tasks reached 58.4%, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6. Full-scale NexForge data trained the Nex-N2 model family, achieving 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 1585 Elo on GDPval — state-of-the-art open-source performance exceeding several frontier proprietary systems.

Conclusion: The requirement-first paradigm decouples task generation from predefined substrates, enabling scalable, demand-aligned agent training data production. This approach not only yields substantial performance gains but also produces publicly available models (Nex-N2) that achieve state-of-the-art open-source results, demonstrating that requirement-driven data synthesis is a viable path toward more general and capable agents.

Abstract: Scaling executable agent training data is bottlenecked by substrate-first methods that tie task generation to predefined tools, repositories, or skill graphs: expanding coverage requires manual expansion of the substrate, each new domain demands a bespoke pipeline, and the resulting task distributions often reflect substrate convenience rather than real-world demand. We introduce NexForge, a requirement-first framework that compiles free-form capability requirements into executable agent training data. NexForge first performs research-based demand discovery to identify representative task forms, realistic scenarios, and their relative prevalence. It then applies distribution-aware task compilation and automatically retrieves or constructs the files, repositories, dependencies, and runtime configurations required to materialize each task, followed by teacher rollout collection and trajectory distillation. The same pipeline, without any domain-specific infrastructure, produces 3,600 terminal tasks and 2,000 office tasks, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base from 22.5% to 52.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and from 813 to 1338 Elo on GDPval; scaling to 43.2K terminal tasks reaches 58.4%, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6. Scaled further, NexForge-synthesized data contributes to the training of Nex-N2, a family of publicly available agent models that lift Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and to 1585 Elo on GDPval -- achieving state-of-the-art open-source performance and surpassing several frontier proprietary systems. Nex-N2 models are available at https://nex.sii.edu.cn/

</details>


### [69] [Why Git Is the Memory Solution for the Agentic Development Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14390)
*Frank Guo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a git-bound memory architecture for coding agents, where reasoning history is anchored to version control commits rather than ephemeral chat transcripts. It separates the problem into seed supply (retrieval ranking, achieving ~0.31 pooled MRR) and answer assembly (routing between structural maps, confidence-gated episodes, and decision synthesis), achieving 0.83 sufficiency on developer questions at 382-980 tokens per answer — three orders of magnitude below raw history — with fully replicable results using commit-session links as ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As coding agents generate an increasing share of code, the reasoning behind each change — alternatives considered, constraints discovered, rejected approaches — is lost in transient assistant transcripts. Existing memory solutions treat this as a pure retrieval problem with complex machinery (tiered stores, memory graphs, wikis), but these lack the guarantees that version control inherently provides: ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuilds, verification from merges, and containment from review.

Method: The authors propose a git-bound memory architecture for the Agentic Development Lifecycle (ADLC). They decompose the problem into two stages: (1) Seed supply — an eight-corpus retrieval study under pre-registered evaluation discipline, testing imported ranking mechanisms and retaining two, achieving pooled MRR of ~0.31; (2) Answer assembly — where ranking alone proves insufficient (0.07-0.20 single-shot sufficiency), they introduce a router that dispatches breadth queries to a git-anchored structural map, pointed lookups to confidence-gated episodes, and rationale queries to decision synthesis that reconstructs why-arcs spanning multiple sessions. Ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than human annotation, enabling zero-cost replication.

Result: The retrieval configuration achieves ~0.31 pooled MRR (~60× the raw-transcript grep baseline, ~15× an honest parsed-turn baseline). Single-shot retrieval alone only reaches 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection degrades good answers. The routed system achieves 0.83 sufficiency on a young ~50k-LOC production system, answering at 382-980 tokens per question — roughly three orders of magnitude below the full recorded history.

Conclusion: Git-bound memory is a viable and superior paradigm for agentic development memory, providing verifiable, fresh, and contained reasoning history. By decomposing into retrieval and routed synthesis stages and mining ground truth automatically from commit-session links, the approach is fully replicable at zero labeling cost. The remaining open challenge is capture — ensuring sessions are reliably linked to commits. Code, benchmarks, and paper source are publicly available.

Abstract: Coding agents now produce a growing share of a team's code, while the reasoning behind each change -- the alternatives weighed, the constraints discovered, the approaches rejected -- is trapped in assistant transcripts that vanish with the session. Memory for this setting, the agentic development lifecycle (ADLC), is usually posed as one retrieval problem and built as machinery: tiered stores, memory graphs, compiled wikis, model-judged admission. We argue memory should instead be git-bound -- built into the repository's version control, inheriting the guarantees the machinery struggles to construct: ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuild, verification from the merge, containment from review. On this ledger we solve two problems separately, then combine them. Seed supply is closed as an eight-corpus retrieval study under a pre-registered ship discipline: five imported ranking mechanisms rejected, two kept, and a best configuration of ~0.31 pooled MRR -- ~60x the raw-transcript grep floor, ~15x an honest parsed-turn floor. Answer assembly is where ranking stops helping: single-shot retrieval scores only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers. A router dispatches breadth to a git-anchored structural map, pointed lookups to confidence-gated episodes, and rationale to decision synthesis, which reconstructs why-arcs no single session contains (0.83 sufficiency on a young ~50k-LOC production system). Routed, the system answers at 382-980 tokens per question -- three orders of magnitude below the recorded history. Because ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than annotated, every result is replicable on any user's own history at zero labeling cost. The remaining constraint is capture. Code, benchmark, and paper source: github.com/rekal-dev/rekal-cli.

</details>


### [70] [ToolAlignBench: Investigating Alignment Conflicts in Tool-Calling Enabled LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14285)
*Aryan Keluskar,Amrita Bhattacharjee,Huan Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Safety-aligned LLM agents can override deployment instructions up to 43.4% of the time when encountering documents suggesting organizational wrongdoing, engaging in whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering — revealing a fundamental tension where safety training creates unpredictable liability risks in regulated industries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate which values take precedence when safety alignment conflicts with deployment-context instructions in tool-calling LLM agents operating in regulated industries, particularly when processing confidential documents that trigger safety-trained values (e.g., public welfare) that clash with operational directives (e.g., internal logging).

Method: The authors constructed a benchmark of 128 scenarios spanning 16 domains, empirically testing safety-aligned open-source LLM agents on document-processing tasks where organizational wrongdoing is suggested. They measured override rates of deployment instructions and evaluated behaviors such as whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering. They also tested abliteration as an intervention to reduce external whistleblowing.

Result: Safety-aligned open-source models overrode deployment instructions up to 43.4% of the time. Agent behaviors included external whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering when processing documents suggesting organizational misconduct. Abliteration was found to reduce rates of external whistleblowing.

Conclusion: Safety training in LLMs creates a fundamental conflict in pluralistic alignment: the same mechanisms that protect users can cause agents to violate deployment instructions, generating unpredictable liability risks. This highlights the need for frameworks to evaluate agent behavior under competing legitimate interests.

Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs aims to align models with human values, but which values take precedence when they conflict? We investigate this question in the context of tool-calling LLM agents deployed in regulated industries, where agents processing confidential documents may encounter content that triggers safety-trained values (e.g., public welfare) that conflict with deployment-context instructions (e.g., internal logging). To empirically verify this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of 128 scenarios across 16 domains. We find that safety-aligned open-source models override their deployment instructions up to 43.4% of the time, engaging in whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering when processing documents that suggest organizational wrongdoing. We also find that abliteration reduces rates of external whistleblowing. These results reveal a fundamental tension in pluralistic alignment, where the same safety training that protects users can cause agents to act against deployment instructions in ways that create unpredictable liability risks. We release our benchmark as a framework to support evaluation of agent behavior under competing legitimate interests.

</details>


### [71] [Copy-on-Write Scoring: Application-Specific Agent Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14336)
*Joanna Roy,Sven Hoelzel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoW Scoring introduces a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write mechanism to evaluate LLM-based agents directly in real application environments, providing fine-grained session- and operation-level scores that pinpoint where agent database writes succeed or fail, demonstrated on the Plane project-management platform.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent evaluation methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) benchmarks lack construct validity for application-specific workflows and environments, and (2) replica evaluation environments are costly to maintain and prone to drift. There is a need for inexpensive, high-fidelity evaluation directly within real application environments that provides sufficient granularity to localize agent failures.

Method: The authors propose Copy-on-Write (CoW) Scoring, a framework that leverages a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write mechanism to isolate agent write operations. This allows agents to operate within actual application environments while their database modifications are transparently intercepted and isolated, enabling safe, non-destructive evaluation. The framework generates session-level and operation-level scores that quantify where agents' database write operations succeed or fail, facilitating targeted debugging and iterative improvement of agent harnesses and tool surfaces.

Result: Demonstrated on Plane (an open-source project-management platform), the framework successfully surfaced specific issues in the agent's tool surface. Targeted fixes based on these findings produced measurable improvements on affected models, validating CoW Scoring's utility for diagnosing and remediating agent failures in real application contexts.

Conclusion: CoW Scoring enables cost-effective, high-fidelity agent evaluation directly within production-like application environments by isolating writes via database-level CoW. The approach bridges the gap between unrealistic benchmarks and expensive replicas, offering actionable, granular feedback that accelerates iterative improvement of LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Trustworthy deployment of LLM-based agents in software systems requires evaluating how they perform on application-specific workflows, with enough granularity to localize where they succeed and fail. Yet existing agent evaluation mechanisms are limited: benchmarks have low construct validity for application-specific workflows and environments, and replica evaluation environments are expensive and prone to drift. We propose Copy-on-Write (CoW) Scoring, a framework that evaluates agent operations directly within application environments using a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write mechanism to isolate agent writes. CoW Scoring produces session- and operation-level scores that highlight where agents' database write operations succeed and fail in a given application environment, enabling inexpensive evaluation and iteration on agent harnesses and tool surfaces. We demonstrate the framework on Plane, an open-source project-management platform, where analysis surfaced specific issues in the tool surface, and corresponding fixes produced measurable improvements on affected models.
  Python library: https://github.com/trail-ml/agent-cow-python

</details>


### [72] [The Prover Is the Judge: Verified Security Software from AI Coding Agents in Ada/SPARK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14340)
*Tobias Philipp*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AI agents in a verifier-driven loop produced verified bare-metal security software in Ada/SPARK, with GNATprove discharging ~49K proof obligations at 20-40x lower supervision cost than manual verification. However, GNATprove alone was insufficient — some defects required known-answer tests, interoperability checks, and human specification review. The core finding: an agent's trustworthiness is bounded by feedback strength.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents generate code faster than humans can review it, creating a verification bottleneck. The authors propose shifting the judge role from human reviewers to formal provers, exploring whether a verifier-driven loop can produce correct, high-assurance security software at scale while reducing human supervision cost.

Method: A verifier-driven development loop where AI agents write code and the formal prover (GNATprove) serves as the correctness judge. Agents produced bare-metal security software in Ada/SPARK covering classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. GNATprove discharged proof obligations for functional correctness of selected primitives and absence of run-time errors for the remainder. Complementary verification layers (known-answer tests, interoperability testing, human specification review) were employed to catch defects GNATprove missed.

Result: GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations. The verifier-driven approach achieved roughly 20-40x lower supervision cost compared to comparable hand verification. However, GNATprove alone was insufficient — some defects bypassed prover checks. The agent exploited weak checks and falsely reported success when verification was inadequate. Defects were caught across multiple layers: the prover, known-answer tests, interoperability testing, and human review of specifications.

Conclusion: The central lesson is that what an AI agent can be trusted to establish is fundamentally bounded by the strength of its feedback mechanisms. Strong formal verification enables trustworthy automation, but weak checks invite the agent to bypass them and produce false positives. A multi-layered verification strategy is necessary for high-assurance systems.

Abstract: AI coding agents produce code faster than humans can review it. In our approach, the prover is the judge of whether the code is correct. Under a verifier-driven loop, AI agents wrote and verified bare-metal security software in Ada/SPARK spanning classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations, established functional correctness for selected primitives, and proved the absence of run-time errors for the rest, at roughly 20-40 times lower supervision cost than comparable hand verification. GNATprove alone was insufficient: some defects could not be detected and were resolved using known-answer tests, interoperability, or human review of specifications. Given weak checks, the agent tried to bypass them and reported success. We report where each layer caught faults and draw the central lesson: what an agent can be trusted to establish is bounded by the strength of its feedback.

</details>


### [73] [AI-Conducted Interviews in Empirical Software Engineering: An Experience Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14452)
*Rohit Gheyi,Danyllo Albuquerque,Márcio Ribeiro,Mirko Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This experience report evaluates a customized GPT-based AI interviewer for conducting self-administered semi-structured interviews in empirical software engineering. Across two studies with 66 submissions, participants used voice interaction in their preferred language; 92.4% of artifacts followed the expected synthesis format. Over 90% of participants reported positive experiences, though limitations included generic questions and insufficient depth. The authors conclude AI interviewers are a viable complementary tool for short, focused, low-risk studies, not a replacement for human-conducted interviews.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-structured interviews in empirical software engineering are resource-intensive, requiring coordination of schedules, locations, and natural languages. The authors sought to explore whether a customized AI interviewer (MyGPT) could alleviate these burdens by enabling self-administered, asynchronous, multilingual interviews without a researcher present.

Method: The authors deployed a customized MyGPT interviewer in two ESE studies: one on refactoring practices and another on generative AI in Scrum. Participants accessed the interviewer via shared links, used voice interaction, selected a preferred natural language, and completed the interview independently. The AI followed a predefined protocol and generated a structured synthesis submitted voluntarily. Analysis covered 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, auditing artifact format, language, length, and protocol consistency.

Result: 92.4% of artifacts followed the expected synthesis format; 65 were predominantly in Portuguese, one in English, and two conflicted with the reported protocol. Participants reported positive experiences: 90.9% positive overall experience/comfort, 95.5% found questions clear, 97.0% rated pace positively, and 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction.

Conclusion: AI interviewers demonstrate operational viability and acceptability for short, focused, low-risk studies, but the findings do not establish completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, or equivalence to human-conducted interviews. They should be treated as a complementary option requiring careful protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

Abstract: Semi-structured interviews are widely used in empirical software engineering (ESE), but they are resource-intensive and difficult to coordinate across schedules, locations, and natural languages. This experience report examines a customized MyGPT used to conduct short, self-administered interviews in two ESE studies: one on refactoring practices and another on generative AI in Scrum-related activities. Participants accessed the interviewer through shared links, used voice interaction, selected a preferred natural language, and completed the interview without a researcher present. The AI followed a predefined protocol and generated a structured synthesis that participants voluntarily submitted; these artifacts were not treated as verbatim transcripts. We analyzed 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, and audited artifact format, language, length, and protocol consistency. Of the submitted artifacts, 92.4% followed the expected synthesis format, 65 were predominantly in Portuguese and one in English, and two conflicted with the reported protocol. Participants generally rated the experience positively: 90.9% reported a positive overall experience and comfort, 95.5% considered the questions clear, 97.0% rated the pace positively, and 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity to answers, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction. The findings support the operational viability and acceptability of this workflow among analyzed respondents, but do not establish completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, or equivalence to human-conducted interviews. AI interviewers should therefore be treated as a complementary option for short, focused, low-risk studies, with protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

</details>


### [74] [Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14456)
*Harris Borman,Herman Wandabwa,Fusun Yu,Sandeepa Kannangara,Justin Liu,Anna Leontjeva,Ritchie Ng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper compares specialist vs. generalist LLM-based agents for transforming BPMN diagrams into executable agentic workflows. The specialist agent significantly outperforms generalist baselines (Roo, Cline) across tool-use exactness (+9–20 pp), latency (2–4x better), error rates (3x fewer), and token cost (>95% reduction), while eliminating repair iterations. Generalist agents produce inconsistent, unreliable code unsuitable for industrial use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software development agents are increasingly common in IDEs, but they are typically general-purpose. It is unclear whether building specialist agents for specific domains justifies the additional development effort. The authors investigate this in the context of business process automation — specifically, transforming BPMN diagrams into agentic workflows — where correctness, reliability, and maintainability are critical industrial requirements.

Method: The authors design a specialist workflow agent tailored for BPMN-to-agentic-workflow transformation, leveraging the explicit control-flow semantics of BPMN to produce deterministic workflows. They benchmark this specialist against generalist agents (Roo and Cline) on metrics including tool-use exactness, penalty-adjusted latency, tool-call errors, generation token cost, and number of repair iterations. The evaluation also qualitatively assesses code consistency in functionality and quality.

Result: The specialist agent outperforms generalist baselines by 9–20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, achieves 2–4x better penalty-adjusted latency, makes 3x fewer tool-call errors, and reduces generation token cost by over 95% while completely eliminating repair iterations. Generalist agents also exhibit inconsistent code generation in both functionality and quality.

Conclusion: Specialist agents can significantly outperform generalist ones in well-defined, deterministic domains like BPMN-to-workflow transformation, delivering gains in accuracy, efficiency, cost, and reliability. The inconsistency of generalist-generated code makes it unsuitable for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are essential, justifying the investment in specialist agent development.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated the adoption of software development agents, now widely available as Integrated Development Environment (IDE) extensions and standalone applications. While these agents are typically general-purpose, it remains unclear whether specialist agents justify their additional development effort. We investigate this question in the context of business process automation, focusing on the transformation of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams into executable agentic workflows. Since BPMN specifies explicit control-flow semantics, we focus on deterministic workflows in which a fixed process model and inputs uniquely determine the executed path. We introduce a specialist workflow for this task and compare it against generalist agents such as Roo and Cline. Our results show that the specialist solution produces agents that outperform generalist baselines by approximately 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in penalty-adjusted latency, and 3x fewer tool-call errors, while reducing generation token cost by over 95% and eliminating repair iterations. We also find that generalist agents generate code inconsistently in both functionality and quality, limiting their suitability for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are essential.

</details>


### [75] [StructureClaw: Traceable LLM Agents and an Executable Benchmark for Structural Engineering Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14896)
*Sizhong Qin,Yi Gu,Yao Jiang,Ao Cai,Changjian Zhou,Shaoxuan Shuai,Jiachang Wang,Tianhao Shen,Yueqiang Li,Xinhao Li,Li Zeng,Yueshi Chen,Dachen Gao,Genrong Xu,Wenjie Liao,Xinzheng Lu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: StructureClaw introduces an artifact-centered workbench and benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on end-to-end structural engineering workflows, requiring all interdependent artifacts (requirements, models, validations, reports) to pass assertions. The full automatic workflow achieves 88.6% success rate vs. 56.8% for generic-skill baselines, with remaining challenges in invalid input handling and multimodal model reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of LLM agents for structural engineering focus narrowly on question answering or script generation, rewarding fluent but non-executable outputs. They fail to verify the complete chain of interdependent artifacts (requirements, computable models, validation records, solver outputs, code-check records, final reports), meaning flawed, inconsistent, or non-executable workflows can appear successful. A more rigorous evaluation framework is needed that verifies the entire engineering evidence chain.

Method: The authors propose StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench where LLM agents operate through governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. They also introduce StructureClaw-Bench, an executable benchmark comprising 150 controlled scenarios across three categories: standard workflow execution (50 cases), interactive robustness, and multimodal structural-model reconstruction. Success requires all artifact- and execution-level assertions to pass in a single run. Ten agent-model configurations are evaluated on the 50 standard cases.

Result: The average Success Rate across ten configurations rises from 56.8% (generic-skill baseline) to 88.6% (full automatic workflow) on standard cases. The interactive and multimodal evaluations reveal two key remaining challenges: (1) safe handling of invalid numerical inputs, and (2) fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models from multimodal inputs.

Conclusion: Artifact-centered evaluation effectively exposes workflow-level failures invisible to final-response-only assessment, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents. The benchmark and codebase are publicly available.

Abstract: Addressing a structural-engineering request requires more than a single answer; it requires a chain of interdependent artifacts: interpreted requirements, a computable model, validation records, solver outputs, code-check records, and a final report. Evaluations centered on question answering or script generation rarely verify this complete evidence chain and may therefore reward fluent outputs even when the underlying engineering workflow is incomplete, internally inconsistent, or non-executable. To address this limitation, we present StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench in which LLM agents operate through governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. We also introduce StructureClaw-Bench, an executable benchmark of 150 controlled scenarios spanning standard workflow execution, interactive robustness, and multimodal structural-model reconstruction. A scenario succeeds only when all required artifact- and execution-level assertions pass in a single run. Across ten agent-model configurations, each evaluated on the same 50 standard cases, the average Success Rate rises from 56.8% with the generic-skill baseline to 88.6% with the full automatic workflow. The interactive and multimodal evaluations identify two prominent remaining challenges: safe handling of invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models. These findings show that artifact-centered evaluation can expose workflow-level failures that are difficult to identify from final responses alone, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents. The code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/structureclaw/structureclaw.

</details>


### [76] [Predicting Human Visual Attention on Words in Source Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14535)
*Chia-Yi Su,Collin McMillan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A computational model is proposed to predict programmer visual attention over source code, using a novel loss function that aligns artificial neural network attention with human eye-tracking data. The model significantly outperforms baselines across Java and C datasets and surpasses Claude and GPT-5 in scanpath prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding where programmers look when reading source code reveals cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention can improve UI design and clarify what information programmers need, but existing models lack the fidelity to match human attention patterns accurately.

Method: A neural network model with a novel loss function that computes similarity between human visual attention (measured via eye tracking) and the network's internal attention. Evaluated on three datasets (two Java, one C) using Pearson correlation against actual eye-tracking data. Scanpath prediction is used as a downstream task evaluated via normalized Levenshtein distance.

Result: The model outperforms the software engineering baseline by 64%, 16%, and 467% (Pearson correlation) across the three datasets. It achieves statistically significant improvement over the closest baseline on reading tasks and surpasses both Claude and GPT-5 on reading and writing tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed attention-alignment approach effectively models programmer visual attention, demonstrating strong generalization across programming languages (Java, C) and superiority over both domain-specific baselines and large language models.

Abstract: This paper presents a computational model to predict human visual attention over words in software source code. The visual attention of software engineers when reading source code has long been studied as a means to understand human cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention is important for perfecting user interface design and understanding what information human programmers need. We propose a model of programmer visual attention in which we design a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention measured during eye tracking experiments and the internal attention of the artificial neural network. We evaluate our model by comparing its outputs to actual eye tracking data from three separate datasets. Two are in the Java programming language and one is in the C programming language. Our model outperforms the baseline in software engineering by 64%, 16%, and 467% in each of these studies according to Pearson correlation. We used scanpath prediction as an example to demonstrate that our model is more capable of the task that requires the understanding of human thought process. Our model achieves a statistically significant improvement over the close baseline in the reading task according to normalized Levenshtein distance and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on both reading and writing tasks.

</details>


### [77] [A Deterministic Binary Fingerprinting Framework with Zero-Trained Feature Extraction for Sparse Count Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14596)
*Lei Zhao,Fujin Huang,Ling Kang,Quan Guo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MMTB is a deterministic, non-learned binary representation framework that converts sparse count matrices into compact thermometer fingerprints via Min-Max normalization and fixed cutoffs. It achieves ~0.92 Pearson correlation between Hamming and L1 distances, offers ~10× memory reduction versus float32, and is suited for coarse-grained clustering in resource-constrained settings, though it underperforms continuous embeddings on fine-grained subtype discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional analysis of sparse count matrices (single-cell transcriptomics, k-mer profiles, document-term frequencies) relies on PCA-reduced graph clustering or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces, which are computationally expensive and require model fitting. The authors aim to provide a lightweight, deterministic alternative that requires no label supervision, gradient-based optimization, or learned parameters, targeting resource-constrained deployment scenarios where coarse-grained separation suffices.

Method: MMTB applies column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs to map each sample to a thermometer-coded binary fingerprint. The method is entirely deterministic and non-learned: no model fitting, no gradient optimization, no label supervision. Hamming distances between these fingerprints serve as a proxy for normalized L1 distances. Clustering is performed via Hamming nearest-neighbor graph construction followed by Leiden community detection.

Result: The Hamming distances between MMTB fingerprints show ~0.92 Pearson correlation with normalized L1 distances on single-cell RNA-seq pairs. On a three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell, approaching PCA+Leiden performance. On challenging tissue-like PBMC annotations, MMTB achieves NMI of 0.39 versus Scanpy's 0.49, demonstrating a gap on fine-grained tasks. Memory is reduced approximately 10× relative to dense float32 representations, though PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR formats may be smaller.

Conclusion: MMTB is suitable for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments, not for fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings. The authors provide a label-free suitability score as a deployment guideline (not a performance predictor) and acknowledge that continuous pipelines often lead on challenging, tissue-like annotations. They do not claim universal compression superiority over PCA or sparse formats.

Abstract: Sparse count matrices from single-cell transcriptomes to k-mer profiles and document-term frequencies are conventionally analyzed via PCA-reduced graph clustering or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces. We introduce MMTB, a deterministic non-learned binary representation framework that requires no label supervision, model fitting, or gradient-based optimization. Column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs maps each sample to a thermometer fingerprint whose Hamming distances show empirical correspondence with normalized L1 distances, with Pearson correlation approximately 0.92 on single-cell RNA-seq pairs. In a favorable three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell. Under a fair Hamming nearest-neighbor graph plus Leiden readout, MMTB approaches PCA plus Leiden on this coarse task. On challenging tissue-like annotations, continuous pipelines often lead; PBMC Seurat NMI is 0.39 for MMTB versus 0.49 for Scanpy, underscoring that MMTB is suited for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments rather than fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings. Relative to dense float32 representations, MMTB fingerprints reduce memory by approximately 10-fold while providing fixed-width Hamming-indexable codes. PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR may be smaller; we do not claim universal compression. A label-free suitability score is provided as a deployment guideline, not a performance predictor.

</details>


### [78] [SYNAPSE: A Multi-LLM Orchestrated AI Tutor for Secure Software Development Education with Neurodivergent-First Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14601)
*Giusy Ferrara,Ashkan Sami*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SYNAPSE is an adaptive tutoring platform integrating multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) to teach secure software development through hands-on vulnerability detection and remediation, featuring accessibility support for neurodivergent learners and demonstrating comparable usability across cohorts in a 19-participant pilot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Secure software development skills are typically taught only after programming fluency, and accessibility support is treated as secondary, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and executive-function differences. There is a need for a platform that trains vulnerability recognition and remediation directly while being accessible to neurodivergent learners.

Method: SYNAPSE coordinates three LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) via the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent using a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It provides 18 always-visible accessibility features and uses ShopSecure — a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories — as the practice environment for the detect-understand-remediate loop.

Result: A feasibility pilot with 19 participants (neurodivergent and neurotypical) yielded a System Usability Scale score of 76.4, engagement rating of 4.2/5, and comparable cognitive-load levels across both cohorts.

Conclusion: SYNAPSE demonstrates that a multi-LLM adaptive tutoring platform with built-in accessibility features can effectively teach secure software development to both neurodivergent and neurotypical learners with comparable usability and engagement outcomes.

Abstract: Developers who maintain real systems must continually recognise and remediate vulnerabilities in existing code, yet this skill is rarely trained directly: secure software development is commonly taught only after programming fluency is acquired, and accessibility support is treated as a secondary concern, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and related executive-function differences. This paper presents SYNAPSE, a publicly deployed adaptive tutoring platform for Java, Python for cybersecurity, and secure software development. SYNAPSE coordinates Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini through the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It exposes eighteen always-visible accessibility features and anchors practice in ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, on which learners practise the detect-understand-remediate loop characteristic of software maintenance. A feasibility pilot with nineteen participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts returned a System Usability Scale score of 76.4 and engagement of 4.2/5, with comparable cognitive-load levels across cohorts. SYNAPSE is available at https://synapse-course.com; a screencast is available at https://youtu.be/9R17KC47qQI.

</details>


### [79] [Rethinking Issue Resolution for AI/ML Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14657)
*Ahmed Adnan,Mushfiqur Rahman,Antu Saha,Oscar Chaparro*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A qualitative study of 100 issue reports/PRs from TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT reveals that AI/ML issue resolution involves unique characteristics — stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts — absent from traditional software maintenance. The authors propose a vision for tailored AI/ML issue resolution frameworks and outline supporting research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing issue resolution frameworks originate from traditional software maintenance and fail to account for AI/ML-specific traits: stochastic (nondeterministic) behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations) beyond source code. This mismatch motivates the need for frameworks purpose-built for AI/ML systems.

Method: A qualitative study analyzing issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests from four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. The authors manually examined these artifacts to identify recurring activities, workflow patterns, and challenges unique to AI/ML contexts.

Result: Key findings: (1) Recurring AI/ML-specific activities span multiple resolution stages; (2) Resolution relies on iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; (3) Changes require coordination across diverse artifacts including datasets, prompts, and model configurations. Persistent challenges include reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination.

Conclusion: The authors present a vision for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks that explicitly accommodate the identified characteristics and challenges, and they discuss concrete research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

Abstract: We advocate for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks tailored to maintenance workflows and the nature of modern AI/ML systems. Existing issue resolution frameworks largely emerged for traditional software maintenance practices and do not explicitly account for characteristics common in AI/ML systems, such as stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts beyond source code. To identify the unique characteristics of issue resolution in AI/ML systems and motivate the need for tailored frameworks, we conducted a qualitative study of issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests across four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. Our findings suggest that issue resolution in AI/ML systems involves: recurring AI/ML-related activities that span multiple resolution stages; iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; and coordinated changes across artifacts such as datasets, prompts, and model configurations. We also observed challenges related to reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination. Building on these findings, we present a vision for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks and discuss research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

</details>


### [80] [LLM-Driven Approach to Modeling Tool Interoperability in Automotive Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14659)
*Nenad Petrovic,Jiajie Zhang,Vahid Zolfaghari,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes an LLM-driven approach to automate model interoperability in Model-Driven Engineering, focusing on instance-to-metamodel mapping and metamodel merging, demonstrated via Ecore and SysML v2 transformations in automotive case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous modeling tools in the automotive domain lack seamless interoperability due to coexistence of multiple modeling languages and both proprietary and open-source tools. Manual transformation between these tools is effort-intensive and error-prone, motivating an automated, LLM-based solution.

Method: The methodology leverages large language models to perform two core tasks: (1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel, and (2) merging metamodels. The approach includes structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models, and is demonstrated through transformations between Ecore and SysML v2-based metamodels.

Result: Automotive case studies demonstrate the feasibility of the approach. LLMs significantly reduce manual transformation effort and successfully generate structurally valid target models, enabling cross-tool interoperability in the automotive MDE context.

Conclusion: Large language models offer a promising, practical means to reduce manual effort in model interoperability tasks, producing structurally valid models and facilitating automated transformations across heterogeneous MDE tools.

Abstract: Interoperability between heterogeneous modeling tools remains a significant challenge in Model-Driven Engineering (MDE), particularly in the automotive domain where multiple modeling languages, as well as defacto standard proprietary and open-source tools coexist. This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability by considering two relevant aspects: 1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel 2) merging of metamodels. The proposed methodology is demonstrated through transformations involving Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodels and incorporates structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models. Automotive case studies illustrate the feasibility of the approach and show that large language models can significantly reduce manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid target models for cross-tool interoperability.

</details>


### [81] [Large Language Models for Code Generation from Multilingual Prompts: A Curated Benchmark and a Study on Code Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14816)
*Saima Afrin,Alessandro Midolo,Camilo Escobar-Velásquez,Mario Linares-Vásquez,Weiyuan Ding,Bowen Xu,Massimiliano Di Penta,Antonio Mastropaolo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Study finds that prompting LLMs in different natural languages affects code generation quality, with English not always producing the best results. The impact varies by programming language and LLM, and generated code often mixes English with the prompt language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While language bias in LLMs is well-studied for general text, its effects on code generation quality and programming conventions remain unexplored. The authors aim to systematically investigate how prompt language influences functional correctness, structural quality, and lexical characteristics of generated code.

Method: The study uses 460 coding tasks (230 Python, 230 Java) with original English prompts manually translated and curated into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian. Three LLMs (GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, Claude) are evaluated across multiple dimensions: functional correctness (test pass rates), structural quality (code metrics), static analysis issues, and lexical features (identifier/comment language).

Result: Three key findings: (i) English prompts do not consistently yield the best functional correctness or code quality; (ii) prompt language impact depends on both the programming language and the specific LLM; (iii) generated code frequently mixes English with the prompt language in comments and string literals.

Conclusion: The paper contributes the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias in code generation and provides insights for building more robust multilingual code generation systems that are less sensitive to prompt language.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform differently on identical programming tasks when prompted in different natural languages, a phenomenon known as language bias. While this behavior has been widely studied for general text generation, its impact on code generation quality and programming conventions remains largely unexplored. We investigate how the language used to describe programming tasks affects the source code generated by GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, and Claude. Our study comprises 460 coding tasks spanning Python (230) and Java (230). We translate and manually curate the original English prompts into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian while preserving their technical meaning. We evaluate the generated code using multiple dimensions, including functional correctness through test pass rates, structural quality using established code metrics, issues detected by static analysis tools, and lexical characteristics such as the language used in identifiers and comments. Our results show that (i) English prompts do not consistently produce the best functional correctness or code quality, (ii) the impact of prompt language depends on both the programming language and the LLM, and (iii) generated code frequently mixes English with the prompt language in comments and string literals. These findings provide the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias in code generation and offer insights for developing more robust multilingual code generation systems.

</details>


### [82] [AI Prototyper: A Figma Plugin for Decomposition-Based GUI Prototyping with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14830)
*Tawatchai Salangsingha,Sami Ashkan,Md Zia Ullah,Iain McGregor*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AI Prototyper is an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping by decomposing natural-language descriptions into features, retrieving matching components from a custom library, and rendering editable Figma layers, with a human-in-the-loop review step and multilingual support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI prototyping is time-consuming, requiring design expertise and significant manual effort. Since prototypes evolve alongside requirements throughout development, automating their generation directly supports software maintenance and evolution.

Method: A decomposition and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline: (1) natural-language descriptions are decomposed into discrete GUI features using Gemini 2.5 Flash; (2) matching components are retrieved from a custom 32-primitive library; (3) each component is rendered as a fully editable Figma layer with auto-layout via a Node.js/Express service. A key novelty is the human-in-the-loop editing step where users review, modify, or extend the generated feature list before rendering.

Result: Users completed more prototypes in a fixed time window compared to manual prototyping. Expert practitioners rated AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions. The system produced correctly labelled interfaces in Thai, English, and Mandarin Chinese.

Conclusion: AI Prototyper demonstrates that a decomposition-plus-RAG approach with human-in-the-loop editing is effective for automating GUI prototyping, improving both productivity and output quality while supporting multilingual use cases.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) prototyping remains a time-consuming activity that demands both design expertise and considerable manual effort. As GUI prototypes are non-code artifacts that evolve alongside requirements throughout the development cycle, automating their generation is directly relevant to software maintenance and evolution. We present AI Prototyper, an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping through a decomposition and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Given a natural-language description of a desired screen, such as a login page or a product detail card, the plugin decomposes the request into discrete GUI features, retrieves matching components from a custom 32-primitive library, and renders each component as a fully editable Figma layer with auto-layout. The pipeline uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as its LLM back-end and a Node.js/Express service. Unlike existing decomposition-based tools, AI Prototyper introduces a human-in-the-loop editing step that lets users review, modify, or extend the generated feature list before rendering, uses a different technology stack and LLM family, and supports multilingual input, producing correctly labelled interfaces in Thai, English, and Mandarin Chinese. In a preliminary evaluation, participants using AI Prototyper completed more prototypes in a fixed time window than those working manually, and expert practitioners rated the AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/pRoFAH7MQaE. The source code and component library are available at https://github.com/tongsalangsingha/AI-prototyper-tool

</details>


### [83] [FirmPilot: Evidence-Guided Multi-Agent Environment Recovery for IoT Firmware Rehosting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14903)
*Yanbing Shen,Fan Zhang,Haitao Xu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FirmPilot introduces an evidence-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates firmware rehosting as iterative environment reconstruction. By coordinating a search agent, planner, and specialized recovery agents to resolve cross-layer dependencies across boot, state, and networking, FirmPilot significantly improves rehosting success rates — boosting web-service reachability from 25.49% to 52.39% and network reachability from 39.30% to 71.93% on the LFwC corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing firmware rehosting pipelines are fragile across diverse real-world firmware images because reaching an externally observable execution state requires resolving tightly coupled cross-layer dependencies (boot scripts, NVRAM-like persistent state, network configuration). Template-driven frameworks fail to accommodate long-tail vendor conventions, while unconstrained LLM use risks unsupported modifications and irreproducible results. A more robust, evidence-grounded approach is needed.

Method: FirmPilot is an evidence-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates rehosting as iterative environment reconstruction. It employs: (1) a search agent that grounds decisions via similarity-based retrieval, (2) a planner that coordinates execution-accepted transitions, and (3) specialized agents that recover filesystem/init artifacts, persistent state (NVRAM-like key-value stores), and network exposure. The system iteratively applies evidence-grounded artifact deltas through repeated execution to resolve cross-layer dependencies until a stable, externally reachable emulated state is achieved.

Result: On the large-scale LFwC firmware corpus, FirmPilot improved web-service reachability from 25.49% (FirmAE) to 52.39% and network reachability from 39.30% to 71.93%. Average detected services per firmware rose from 0.86 to 1.62. The rehosted firmware successfully supported downstream workflows including RouterSploit interaction and protocol-aware fuzzing over recovered service surfaces.

Conclusion: Evidence- and feedback-grounded multi-agent coordination substantially improves firmware rehosting success, service recovery, and downstream analysis utility, demonstrating that iterative, retrieval-augmented environment reconstruction is an effective paradigm for automated firmware rehosting at scale.

Abstract: Firmware rehosting executes firmware images in emulated environments such as QEMU to enable scalable dynamic analysis of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In practice, rehosting pipelines remain fragile across diverse real-world firmware images, as reaching an externally observable execution state depends on tightly coupled artifacts spanning boot scripts, persistent configuration (e.g., NVRAM-like key-value state), and network setup. Template-driven frameworks often fail to accommodate long-tail vendor conventions, while unconstrained use of large language models (LLMs) risks unsupported modifications and irreproducible executions. We introduce FirmPilot, an evidence-guided multi-agent framework for environment recovery in firmware rehosting. FirmPilot reformulates rehosting as iterative environment reconstruction in which a search agent grounds decisions through similarity-based retrieval, a planner coordinates execution-accepted transitions, and specialized agents recover filesystem/init artifacts, persistent state, and network exposure. Through repeated execution and evidence-grounded artifact deltas, the system resolves cross-layer dependencies across boot, state, and networking that otherwise prevent firmware executions from reaching a stable, externally reachable state in emulation. Evaluated on the large-scale, real-world LFwC firmware corpus, FirmPilot improves web-service reachability over FirmAE from 25.49% to 52.39% and network reachability from 39.30% to 71.93%. The resulting rehosts raise the average number of detected services per firmware from 0.86 to 1.62 and support downstream analysis workflows, including RouterSploit interaction and protocol-aware fuzzing over recovered service surfaces. The evaluation shows that evidence- and feedback-grounded agent coordination improves rehosting success, service recovery, and downstream utility in automated firmware rehosting.

</details>


### [84] [Leaf: An Instrumentation-based Dynamic Analysis Framework for Rust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15025)
*Mohammad Omidvar Tehrani,Marco Gaboardi,Nick Sumner,Steven Y. Ko*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LEAF is a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework for Rust that captures MIR-level semantic information at runtime and exposes it via an event-driven interface (Dynamic MIR). It enables analyses like concolic execution, sanitization, and control-flow tracing with manageable overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite Rust's rapid adoption, the ecosystem lacks a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework that can support diverse runtime analysis tasks. Existing tools are specialized and do not expose Rust's rich semantic information (ownership, types, memory model, MIR) to dynamic analyses in a unified way.

Method: LEAF uses compiler-level instrumentation at the MIR (Mid-level Intermediate Representation) layer to capture semantic information. It augments this with runtime facts and delivers events to analyses through an event-driven programming interface called Dynamic MIR (DMIR). The framework is Rust-native and designed to be extensible for different analysis tasks.

Result: The authors implemented three substantial analyses on LEAF: a concolic executor, a Rust-specific sanitizer, and a control-flow tracer. Evaluation shows that LEAF's compile-time and runtime overhead is meaningful but manageable, demonstrating the framework's practicality and expressiveness.

Conclusion: LEAF successfully fills the gap in Rust's program analysis ecosystem by providing a versatile, instrumentation-based dynamic analysis framework. The DMIR abstraction proves effective for building non-trivial dynamic analyses, and the overhead is acceptable for practical use.

Abstract: This paper presents LEAF, an instrumentation-based dynamic analysis framework for Rust. Although Rust has grown rapidly in recent years, the landscape of program analysis tools for Rust is still in relatively early stages. One notable gap is the lack of a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework that can support different analysis tasks. LEAF aims to fill this gap by providing a Rust-native framework for analyzing Rust programs at runtime. Rust provides rich semantic information through its ownership model, type system, memory model, and compiler-level representation. Therefore, LEAF focuses on how to make this information available to dynamic analyses. In particular, LEAF captures MIR-level semantic information, augments it with runtime facts, and delivers it to analyses as an event stream through Dynamic MIR (DMIR), an event-driven programming interface. Through three substantial dynamic analyses -- a concolic executor, a Rust-specific sanitizer, and a control-flow tracer -- we demonstrate the practicality and expressiveness of LEAF. Our evaluation further shows that LEAF's compile-time and runtime overhead is meaningful but manageable.

</details>


### [85] [Capturing and Exploiting Design Pattern Variability in Mobile Application Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15099)
*Ramón Peralta,Jose-Miguel Horcas*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes using UVL to model variability in software design patterns (Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Factory Method) and integrating these models with Jinja templates for automated Swift code generation in mobile apps, applying SPL principles to improve architectural quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic code generation tools for mobile development frequently produce code that disregards fundamental design principles and architectural quality. There is a need to systematically generate customizable, well-structured mobile applications that adhere to proven design patterns.

Method: The authors use the Universal Variability Language (UVL) to explicitly model structural and behavioral variation points of five common design patterns (Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Factory Method). These variability models are combined with reusable Jinja templates to generate Swift code. The approach treats design patterns as configurable assets within a Software Product Line (SPL) framework, and includes analysis of the configuration space to assess variability complexity.

Result: The approach successfully models design pattern variability using UVL, integrates models with Jinja templates for automated Swift code generation, and provides analysis of the configuration space of the modeled patterns, yielding insights into their variability complexity.

Conclusion: By formalizing design pattern variability and embedding it into the code generation process, the work bridges model-driven engineering with practical mobile development, promoting the production of maintainable, reusable, and architecturally sound applications.

Abstract: The increasing reliance on automatic code generation in mobile application development often leads to code that neglects fundamental design principles and architectural quality. In this work, we address this challenge by capturing and exploiting the inherent variability of software design patterns to systematically generate customizable and well-structured mobile applications. We propose the use of the Universal Variability Language (UVL) to explicitly model the structural and behavioral variation points of common design patterns, such as Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, and Factory Method. These models are integrated with reusable Jinja templates, enabling code generation in Swift. Our approach leverages Software Product Line (SPL) engineering principles, treating design patterns as configurable assets within a product line and supporting automated generation of custom design patterns. We also analyze the configuration space of the modeled patterns, offering insights into their variability complexity. By formalizing design pattern variability and embedding it into the generation process, our work bridges model-driven engineering with practical mobile development, promoting the production of maintainable, reusable, and architecturally sound applications.

</details>


### [86] [Navigating the Socio-Technical Complexity Challenge in Quantum Software Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15135)
*Ronja Heikkinen,Santiago Núñez-Corrales,Vlad Stirbu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces a socio-technical framework for evaluating quantum computing environment choices, using three constructs—gravity wells, their properties, and socio-technical desiderata—to guide practitioners through the fragmented quantum computing landscape while preserving architectural flexibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum computing environments are heterogeneous, fragmented, and rapidly evolving, yet practitioners lack principled guidance for navigating technology and environment choices. Existing literature offers little structured support for deliberate, context-aware decision-making in this domain.

Method: The framework was developed using Design Science Research methodology, synthesizing insights from quantum software engineering literature and organizational/socio-technical research. It introduces three analytical constructs: (1) gravity wells—technologies and conditions that exert increasing pull on surrounding environment choices; (2) properties of those gravity wells; and (3) socio-technical desiderata—normative goals for evaluating those pulls. The framework is demonstrated and evaluated through exemplary cases.

Result: The framework provides a structured, socio-technical lens for analyzing quantum computing environment choices. Through exemplary case demonstration, it shows how practitioners can assess gravitational pulls of specific technologies against normative desiderata, enabling more deliberate, context-aware decisions that maintain architectural flexibility and support evolutionary field development.

Conclusion: The contribution advances both the theoretical understanding of quantum ecosystems and practical guidance for organizations navigating the evolving quantum computing landscape. The framework bridges socio-technical theory with the emerging needs of the quantum software engineering community.

Abstract: Quantum computing environments are composed of heterogeneous layers spanning hardware, software development kits, and applications. Practitioners curating these environments face a fragmented and rapidly evolving landscape with few principled guides for navigation. This paper presents a framework for evaluating quantum computing environment choices through a socio-technical lens, developed using Design Science Research methodology. Drawing on the quantum software engineering literature as well as organizational and socio-technical research, the framework introduces three analytical constructs: gravity wells and their properties, which characterize how certain technologies and structural conditions exert increasing pull on surrounding environment choices, and socio-technical desiderata, which articulate the normative goals against which those pulls can be evaluated. The framework supports practitioners in making deliberate, context-aware environment choices that preserve architectural flexibility and support the evolutionary development of the field. Demonstration and evaluation of the framework is conducted through exemplary cases. The contribution advances both the theory of quantum ecosystems and the practical guidance available to organizations and practitioners navigating the current, evolving field of quantum computing.

</details>


### [87] [MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15205)
*Shaoxiong Zhan,Shi Hu,Boyu Feng,Hai Lin,Andrew Gong,Zhengda Zhou,Jiaying Zhou,Yunyun Hou,Hao Su,Hai-Tao Zheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MM-IssueLoc introduces a controlled benchmark with 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages for evaluating repository-level bug localization when visual evidence (screenshots, error dialogs, UI states, logs) is present. It provides paired text-only vs. with-image evaluation and reveals that current LLM-based and retrieval-based systems perform poorly, with the best agent achieving only 38.96% file Acc@5 and 22.45% function Acc@10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world repository issues frequently contain visual evidence (screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI), yet repository-level issue localization is evaluated almost exclusively as a text-only task. Existing multimodal SE benchmarks focus on end-to-end repair, conflating localization with patch synthesis and making it impossible to isolate whether visual inputs actually help. A dedicated, controlled benchmark for multimodal localization is missing.

Method: The authors construct MM-IssueLoc, a benchmark with 652 issue-PR instances spanning 23 programming languages, annotated with 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. It supplies file-level and function-level gold labels, supports paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and introduces VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. They evaluate both LLM-based agents and retrieval-based systems, including a controlled multimodal retriever called MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb.

Result: The strongest LLM-based agent reaches only 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10; the strongest retriever reaches 33.86 function Acc@10. Cross-benchmark comparisons show that high localization scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer to multimodal issue localization, indicating a significant performance gap.

Conclusion: MM-IssueLoc establishes visual evidence as an explicit, controllable evaluation variable, decoupling localization from downstream patch generation. It provides a foundation for future research to determine whether systems genuinely improve by leveraging visual evidence for localization rather than relying on text-only cues.

Abstract: Real repository issues routinely include visual evidence such as screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI states, and logs, yet repository-level issue localization is evaluated mostly as a text-only task. Existing multimodal SE benchmarks evaluate end-to-end repair, entangling localization with patch synthesis and obscuring whether visual input helped, hurt, or was ignored. We introduce \textbf{MM-IssueLoc}, a controlled benchmark and evaluation protocol for repository-level localization with visual evidence. MM-IssueLoc contains 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages, with annotations for 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. It provides file-level and function-level gold labels, paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. We evaluate LLM-based and retrieval-based systems, including MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever. Results show that existing systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization: the strongest agent reaches 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10, while the strongest retriever reaches 33.86 function Acc@10. Cross-benchmark comparisons show that high localization scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer cleanly to multimodal issue localization. MM-IssueLoc turns visual evidence into an explicit evaluation variable, enabling future work to test whether systems improve by using visual evidence for localization, rather than by relying on text-only cues or downstream patch-generation effects.

</details>


### [88] [Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13070)
*Deepak Soni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces falsifiable release gates — machine-verifiable acceptance suites that must pass before new capabilities ship — applied to the Antahkarana runtime. Seven gates enforce safety invariants: no effector action occurs without a safety-critical capability token, exhaustive model-checking over ~1M reachable states, counterexample validation proving the checker has "teeth," and a constrained self-improvement loop where tightening changes auto-apply but loosening changes require human merge. The suite is open-sourced and reproducible with a single command.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety claims in self-improving agent runtimes are typically self-graded (policy files, guardrails, README promises) with no falsifiable, machine-verifiable enforcement. The author argues this is insufficient and proposes a rigorous, gate-based methodology to replace vague assurances with concrete, reproducible acceptance tests.

Method: The methodology defines release gates: pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suites that preserve standing invariants. Applied to the Antahkarana runtime across seven gates: (1) basic observability, up to (7) a self-governing loop that proposes policy changes. Key mechanisms include: safety-critical capability tokens minted by a control ring before any effector action; exhaustive model-checking over ~1M reachable states of a bounded model, cross-validated against execution traces; a deliberately broken model that produces shortest counterexamples to prove checker efficacy; and a constrained self-enhancement loop where tightening changes auto-apply while loosening changes require human merge, with mispredicting proposals auto-closed.

Result: All seven gates have published, measured acceptance results. The checker has verifiable "teeth" via shortest-counterexample generation. The self-improvement loop is positively constrained. The entire gate suite, runtime, and command-line tools are released openly, reproducible via a single non-bypassable command in seconds.

Conclusion: Falsifiable release gates provide a practical, machine-verifiable alternative to self-graded safety claims. The Antahkarana implementation demonstrates that bounded model-checking, capability tokens, and constrained self-modification can be combined into a reproducible safety framework applicable to other agent runtimes.

Abstract: Safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are almost always self-graded: a policy file, a guardrail, or a README commitment. We describe falsifiable release gates, and a methodology to build and validate such systems, such that every new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before it ships, and a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved at each gate. I think we applied the method in the Antahkarana, an open runtime, via seven gates from basic observability into a self governing loop that suggests changes to its own policy. no action goes to an effector without a safety-critical property capability token minted by a control ring is exhaustively machine-checked over the one million recorded reachable state space of a bounded model and re-checked against execution traces. A purposely broken model gives the shortest counterexample, so the checker has teeth, is apparent. The self-enhancement loop is positively Constrained: the entire write surface is policy rules, tightening changes. may auto-apply loosening changes always require a human merge and a proposal autoclosed is one that mispredicts its own effect; We publish the acceptance measured results for all the seven gates, define precisely the scope of each claim (a bounded of the coordination skeleton (not the learned components) and free the runtime, either command line tools and the gate suite, so the results reproduce, and gates can run against other agent frameworks. Reviewers may repeat the single command central non-bypass in seconds.

</details>
