### [89] [World-Model-Aware Responsibility Allocation in Heterogeneous Logistics Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14550)
*Artan Markaj,Niklas Jobs,Felix Gehlhoff*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: WMARF proposes dynamic authority allocation between autonomous logistics equipment and central control based on world-model quality, preventing deadlocks caused by model divergence that static authority schemes cannot handle. A proximity-triggered handoff is validated via VDA 5050 discrete-event simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In mixed-autonomy logistics systems, authority between autonomous logistic equipment (ALE) and central control systems (CS) is fixed at design time. When the ALE's local world model and the CS global model diverge, both act on incompatible beliefs, producing deadlocks that traditional resource-based deadlock handling neither explains nor prevents. This creates a fundamental gap: the best decision-maker depends on who holds the most current world model, yet authority cannot shift dynamically.

Method: The authors propose the World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF), which dynamically assigns authority based on two factors: (1) CS world-model quality and (2) equipment automation level. Deadlocks are classified by the state of authority — none, in transition, or divergent. Validation uses discrete-event simulation of two ALE converging on a semi-automated transfer point, reproduced over the VDA 5050 interface standard, where a proximity-triggered handoff prevents a divergence deadlock that occurs under static control.

Result: Under static control, a divergence deadlock occurs when ALE and CS world models are incompatible. With WMARF, a proximity-triggered handoff dynamically shifts authority to the entity with the superior world model, preventing the deadlock. The scheme remains valid as autonomy increases because authority follows information quality rather than relying on a shared protocol.

Conclusion: Authority in mixed-autonomy logistics should follow world-model quality rather than be statically assigned. WMARF's dynamic handoff mechanism prevents divergence deadlocks and scales with increasing autonomy levels, offering a principled alternative to fixed-design-time authority allocation in systems governed by standards like VDA 5050.

Abstract: Logistics systems increasingly mix \emph{autonomous logistic equipment} (ALE) with non-autonomous machinery under a central control system (CS), where the best decision-maker depends on who holds the most current world model, yet authority is fixed at design time. When an ALE's local model and the CS global model diverge, both act on incompatible beliefs and produce deadlocks that resource-based handling neither explains nor prevents. We propose the World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF), which assigns authority dynamically from CS world-model quality and equipment automation level, and classifies deadlocks by the state of authority -- none, in transition, or divergent. In a discrete-event simulation of two ALE converging on a semi-automated transfer point, reproduced over the VDA~5050 interface, a divergence deadlock under static control is prevented by a proximity-triggered handoff. Because authority follows information quality rather than a shared protocol, the scheme stays valid as autonomy grows.

</details>


### [90] [Multi-Scale Equilibrium under Variable Indicator Dimensionality: Faithful Reduction of Dynamic Attractors in Urban Mobility Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14815)
*Ali Ghoroghi,Yacine Rezgui,Afrouz Ghaemi,Cristina De Nardi,Andrei Hodorog*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper formally analyzes the mismatch between high-dimensional equilibrium models of urban mobility and the variable data availability across cities. It develops a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor framework with a fast performance layer and a slow strategic layer, then derives conditions under which lower-dimensional indicator projections remain faithful to the full equilibrium structure. Key results include projectability conditions with error bounds, preservation of the two-layer fixed point, retained Fisher information under measurement models, and a one-sided restoration-time bias. The framework helps city authorities decide which indicators are essential to monitor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban mobility equilibrium analysis operates in a high-dimensional indicator space, but real-world data availability varies dramatically across cities and disruption scenarios (e.g., natural disasters, infrastructure failures). There is no formal treatment of when a reduced set of observable indicators can faithfully represent the full equilibrium dynamics, creating risk that cities make decisions based on incomplete or misleading indicator sets.

Method: The authors construct a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor with two coupled layers: (1) a fast performance layer that relaxes toward an indicator-dependent target, and (2) a slow strategic layer that supplies a joint traffic-modal-learning fixed point. Antifragility is classified via a statistical decision rule on the post-to-baseline performance ratio. They then mathematically derive four results on lower-dimensional projections: exact/approximate projectability conditions with explicit error bounds, contraction boundary for fixed-point preservation, Fisher information retention under a measurement model, and a one-sided restoration-time bias. A simulation study on three stylized pilot-city configurations validates the theoretical results.

Result: Four main theoretical results were established: (1) conditions for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor with an explicit error bound; (2) preservation of the coupled two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary; (3) any indicator support retains Fisher information and decision power under a measurement model on observable urban indicators; and (4) reduced monitoring can only understate recovery duration (one-sided restoration-time bias). Simulation on three stylized pilot-city configurations verified each result and demonstrated that two observable channels suffice for the candidate classification target where the indicator catalogue permits.

Conclusion: The framework provides city authorities with a principled, mathematically grounded basis for deciding which indicators must be maintained in their monitoring systems. It demonstrates that lower-dimensional indicator sets can remain faithful to the full equilibrium structure under specific, derivable conditions, reducing monitoring costs without sacrificing analytical fidelity.

Abstract: Equilibrium analysis of urban mobility systems is formulated in a high-dimensional indicator space, whilst data availability varies sharply across cities and disruption contexts. This paper gives a formal treatment of that mismatch. It presents a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor for disrupted urban mobility, in which a fast performance layer relaxes towards an indicator-dependent target, a slow strategic layer supplies a joint traffic, modal and learning fixed point, and antifragility is classified through a statistical decision rule on the post-to-baseline performance ratio. It then characterises when a lower-dimensional indicator projection is faithful to this equilibrium structure, establishing four results: conditions for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor with an explicit error bound; preservation of the coupled two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary; the retained Fisher information and decision power of any indicator support under a measurement model on observable urban indicators; and a one-sided restoration-time bias, whereby reduced monitoring can only understate recovery duration. A simulation study on three stylised pilot-city configurations verifies each result, and shows that two observable channels suffice for the candidate classification target where the indicator catalogue permits. The framework gives city authorities a principled basis for deciding which indicators must be maintained.

</details>


### [91] [Randomized routing strategies of fleets of CAVs may prove market efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14859)
*Grzegorz Jamróz,Łukasz Gorczyca,Rafał Kucharski*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper examines the market structure for competing CAV fleet operators in future cities. It finds that randomized CAV routing creates unpredictable travel times for human-driven vehicles (HDVs), which can be more efficient when human drivers exhibit diverse attitudes toward CAVs. The authors propose augmenting market-share objectives with system-wide travel time metrics to curb antisocial strategies and foster welfare-oriented competition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As future cities will feature a mix of human-driven vehicles (HDVs) and connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) operated by competing fleet companies, there is a need to understand what market structure aligns fleet operator incentives with city-wide goals such as minimizing congestion and travel time.

Method: The authors propose a market model where CAV fleet operator revenue is proportional to market share. They develop multiple routing algorithms and benchmark scenarios to compare performance. Key algorithms include randomized CAV routing (producing unpredictable HDV travel times) and routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium. The interaction between HDV driver attitudes and CAV routing strategies is analyzed for efficiency.

Result: Randomized CAV routing, which yields unpredictable travel times for HDVs, proves more efficient than system-optimum/user-equilibrium-proportional routing when human driver attitudes toward CAVs are sufficiently diverse. This diversity causes heterogeneous behavioral responses that randomized strategies can exploit to improve overall system performance.

Conclusion: To prevent fleet operators from adopting antisocial randomized strategies purely for market share gain, the market design should incorporate a mean system-wide travel time objective alongside the market-share objective. This dual-objective mechanism steers competition toward socially welfare-oriented cooperation.

Abstract: In future cities every driver may own a vehicle which could be either independently driven (HDV), or autonomously routed and piloted (CAV). The autonomous operations could be handled by a few competing companies. What is the market structure which would make this market aligned with city goals? In this paper we discuss a variant of the emerging market of collectively routed fleets of CAVs, where revenue for fleet operators is proportional to market share. We provide benchmark scenarios to compare the routing algorithms. We present several routing algorithms and demonstrate that, when the attitudes of human drivers towards CAVs exhibit significant diversity, randomised CAV routing, resulting in unpredictable travel times for HDVs, is more efficient than routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium. Based on this, we propose to improve the design of the market by augmenting the market-share objective with mean systemwide travel time in order to limit antisocial randomised strategies of fleet operators and drive the competition towards social welfare oriented cooperation.

</details>


### [92] [The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14865)
*Lucas Bergholdt Hansen,Federico Torrielli,Filippo Tonini,Lukas Galke Poech*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The Energy Society is a minimal multi-agent simulation where LLM agents' inference costs (tied to model size) directly impact survival. The study compares competitive vs. cooperative incentives, finding that larger models consume disproportionate energy, cooperation leads to altruistic donation behaviors, and design elements like inter-agent recommendations and memory support coordination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings where incentives shape behavior, yet the interaction between inference cost (token generation) and agent survival incentives remains underexplored. The authors aim to create a controlled testbed where the cost of "thinking" is literally tied to continued agent existence.

Method: The Energy Society model: agents spend energy proportional to model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate at zero energy. Experiments compare competitive and cooperative objectives against baselines and control variants, with ablations on action recommendations and memory mechanisms.

Result: (1) Larger models consistently consume more energy than they gain, even when token cost is not size-dependent. (2) Cooperative incentives lead agents to donate energy to reactivate others, sometimes sacrificing their own survival, and alter job allocation patterns. (3) Action recommendations support coordination and ambitious job selection; memory helps agents calibrate risk. (4) Direct sabotage is rare, but subtle self-serving behaviors emerge in competitive settings.

Conclusion: The Energy Society provides a compact, open-source testbed for studying how token costs and group incentives interact under survival pressure, revealing that cooperative incentives and communication mechanisms significantly shape emergent multi-agent behavior.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

</details>


### [93] [Stigmergic Graph Memory: An Environment-Aware Approach for Many-to-Many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15182)
*Aditya Dutta,Joon-Seok Kim*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: SGM introduces a decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and edges to rank endpoint selection and route preferences in MAPD, yielding 20.5–36.7% throughput gains over baselines across all tested conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-guidance methods for MAPD influence routing only after goals are fixed, leaving endpoint instantiation uninformed by recent traffic. There is a need to incorporate recent execution feedback into the goal-selection phase to reduce congestion proactively.

Method: Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM): a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges. These signals rank feasible source-destination pairs and route preferences before path planning, without altering collision constraints or planner validity.

Result: Across five layouts, three load levels, and 25 seeds per condition, SGM outperformed two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines in all 15 map-load conditions, achieving paired throughput gains of 20.5–36.7%.

Conclusion: Recent execution memory improves warehouse throughput not by modifying how agents travel to fixed goals, but by shaping which feasible goals enter the planner in the first place.

Abstract: Automated fulfillment warehouses must continuously assign and execute pickup-and-delivery work while avoiding congestion. In many-to-many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD), a request specifies a stock-keeping unit rather than fixed endpoints, requiring the controller to select an agent, source, and destination before path planning. Existing graph-guidance methods primarily influence routing after goals are fixed, leaving endpoint instantiation uninformed by recent traffic. We introduce Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM), a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges to rank feasible endpoints and route preferences without altering collision constraints or planner validity. Across paired request streams on five layouts, three load levels, and 25 seeds per condition, SGM outperforms two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines in all 15 map-load conditions, with paired throughput gains of 20.5-36.7%. These results show that recent execution memory can improve warehouse throughput by shaping which feasible goals enter the planner, not only how agents travel to already fixed goals.

</details>
