TL;DR: RegNetAgents is a multi-agent AI framework that identifies and ranks cancer gene regulators by integrating bulk tumor and single-cell regulatory networks, demonstrating significant enrichment for known cancer genes across breast and colorectal cancers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches lack a unified, structured framework for query-driven identification of regulatory candidates across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks (bulk tumor vs. single-cell). There is a need for interpretable, AI-assisted integration of TCGA and single-cell regulatory data with downstream cancer relevance filtering and mechanistic interpretation.

Method: RegNetAgents implements a multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow that: (1) performs dual-network classification on TCGA-derived ARACNe and GREmLN single-cell networks; (2) filters candidates using OncoKB cancer gene annotations; (3) assigns mode-of-action (MoA) labels to tumor-derived regulatory relationships; (4) ranks candidates by cross-network evidence consistency (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only); and (5) provides extended evaluation modules for oncogenicity, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability. The system is accessible via a Python API and MCP client.

Result: Across 11 BRCA and 12 COAD focal genes, RegNetAgents-identified candidates were significantly enriched for OncoKB-annotated cancer genes. TCGA-derived candidates: Stouffer Z = 6.69 (BRCA) and 6.95 (COAD). GREmLN-derived candidates: Z = 5.51 (BRCA) and 7.06 (COAD). All p < 0.0001. Housekeeping and non-driver control gene sets showed no enrichment, confirming signal specificity.

Conclusion: RegNetAgents provides an interpretable, AI-driven framework for cross-network regulatory candidate discovery in cancer genomics, bridging bulk and single-cell regulatory data with structured biological interpretation.

Abstract: We introduce RegNetAgents, an AI-oriented multi-agent framework for structured, query-driven regulatory candidate identification across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks. The system enables unified analysis of bulk tumor and single-cell-derived ARACNe networks by integrating TCGA-derived cancer networks with large-scale single-cell regulatory networks from the GREmLN project. For a given focal gene, the framework performs dual-network classification, cancer gene filtering using OncoKB annotations, and mode-of-action (MoA) assignment for tumor-derived regulatory relationships. Candidates are ranked by evidence consistency across networks (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only). The system is implemented as a multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow, accessible through a unified Python API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client, operating as a downstream analytical layer over precomputed regulatory networks rather than a network inference method. Across eleven breast cancer (BRCA) and twelve colorectal cancer (COAD) focal genes, RegNetAgents identifies candidate regulators significantly enriched for OncoKB-annotated cancer genes. TCGA-derived candidates show strong enrichment (Stouffer Z = 6.69 for BRCA and 6.95 for COAD), while GREmLN-derived candidates also demonstrate significant enrichment (Z = 5.51 for BRCA and 7.06 for COAD; all p < 0.0001). No enrichment is observed in housekeeping or non-driver control gene sets, supporting signal specificity. An extended module enables structured evaluation of oncogenic potential, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability, supporting end-to-end interpretation from candidate identification to biological hypothesis generation. RegNetAgents establishes an interpretable AI framework for cross-network regulatory candidate identification in cancer genomics.

</details>


### [117] [DialogueVPR: Towards Conversational Visual Place Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14115)
*Yukun Song,Changwei Wang,Xingtian Pei,Shibiao Xu,Wenhao Xu,Shunpeng Chen,Yu Zhang,Ke Zhang,Rongtao Xu,Xuxiang Feng,Pengyang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a paradigm shift from static retrieval to interactive, dialogue-driven reasoning for language-guided geo-localization, introducing Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), a new benchmark (DlgQuest-Cities), and a framework combining a cross-modal retriever with a questioner trained via supervised fine-tuning and GRPO-based reinforcement learning, significantly outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-guided geo-localization methods rely on a static, one-shot retrieval paradigm that cannot handle the ambiguity and incompleteness of real-world natural language descriptions. Human spatial communication is inherently interactive and dialogue-driven, motivating a shift to reasoning-based retrieval.

Method: Introduces Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR) with a unified framework coupling a cross-modal multi-level retriever with an intelligent questioner called DQ-pilot. DQ-pilot is trained via a curriculum: supervised fine-tuning on DQ-cities-20k, followed by reinforcement refinement on DQ-cities-10k using GRPO. Two task-aligned metrics guide training: Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) for curriculum sampling and Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) as a reward measuring retrieval improvement from each question.

Result: The reasoning-based interactive approach significantly outperforms static retrieval baselines on the newly introduced DlgQuest-Cities benchmark.

Conclusion: Dialogue-driven reasoning retrieval represents a more effective paradigm for language-guided geo-localization, better handling real-world ambiguity than static one-shot methods. The DlgQuest-Cities benchmark, DQ-pilot questioner, and associated training metrics (DDI, PRG) establish a strong foundation for future interactive localization research.

Abstract: Inspired by how humans communicate spatial information, language-guided geo-localization has gained significant traction for its intuitive and practical value. Despite this progress, most methods still rely on a static, one-shot retrieval paradigm, which fails to handle the ambiguity and incompleteness inherent in real-world natural language descriptions. We propose a paradigm shift to reasoning retrieval and introduce Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), which casts localization as an interactive, dialogue-driven reasoning process. To support this new task, we present DlgQuest-Cities, the first large-scale dialogue-based benchmark for place recognition, and a unified reasoning framework that couples a cross-modal multi-level retriever with an intelligent questioner, DQ-pilot. DQ-pilot is trained in a curriculum: supervised fine-tuning on a curated DQ-cities-20k subset followed by reinforcement refinement on a harder DQ-cities-10k split via GRPO. Two task-aligned metrics guide learning: a Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) for curriculum sampling and a Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) reward that directly measures retrieval improvement induced by a question. Experiments show this reasoning-based approach significantly outperforms baselines. The code and model are available at https://github.com/Graysonggg/DlgPR.

</details>


### [118] [Interpretable Language Model for Closed-Loop Type 1 Diabetes Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14126)
*Maya Sarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-T1D distills an RL-based insulin controller into fine-tuned LLMs (LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B), achieving superior glycemic control (73.5% TIR) with natural-language explanations and formal safety guarantees against hallucinations, validated on the FDA-approved UVA/Padova simulator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement Learning-based Artificial Pancreas Systems for Type 1 Diabetes are effective but operate as black boxes, undermining trust among patients and clinicians. There is a need for controllers that combine high precision with transparent, human-understandable decision-making.

Method: First, an expert RL policy is trained for insulin dosing. Its knowledge is then distilled via fine-tuning into two 8B-parameter LLMs (LLaMA 3.1 and Qwen3). The resulting LLM controllers output both insulin decisions and natural-language rationales. Formal safety verification is applied to guard against hallucinations.

Result: The LLM controllers achieve 73.5% Time in Range on the FDA-approved UVA/Padova T1D simulator, outperforming the original RL expert, while providing plain-language explanations and passing strict formal safety verification.

Conclusion: Distilling RL policies into LLMs yields a transparent, high-performance insulin delivery controller that matches or exceeds RL-only systems in efficacy while offering interpretability and verified safety, representing a promising step toward trustworthy closed-loop diabetes care.

Abstract: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is a chronic, life-threatening autoimmune condition characterized by the complete destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. While Artificial Pancreas Systems (APS) powered by Reinforcement Learning (RL) have shown promise in automating insulin delivery, their ``black-box'' nature makes it hard for patients and doctors to trust them fully. This paper presents LLM-T1D, a promising approach that combines the precision of RL with the clear, human-like reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) to create a more transparent and reliable insulin pump controller. By training an expert RL system and distilling its knowledge into fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1 8B and Qwen3 8B models, we developed a controller that not only surpasses the RL system's performance but also explains its decisions in plain, understandable language. Tested on the FDA-approved UVA/Padova T1D simulator, the LLM controllers deliver excellent blood sugar control (73.5% Time in Range) while maintaining strict formal safety verification against hallucinations.

</details>


### [119] [Orchestrating Power Grid Studies with Multi-Agent AI and MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14158)
*Jérôme Picault,Clément Goubet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This position paper proposes integrating Large Language Models with power-grid simulation tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), introducing pypowsybl-mcp as an MCP-based interface that exposes simulation capabilities to AI agents, enabling agent-assisted grid studies with human-in-the-loop supervision in Transmission System Operator contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transmission System Operators require more interactive, auditable, and scalable environments for conducting power-grid studies. The authors see an opportunity to leverage Agentic AI and standardized tool-calling protocols (MCP) to bridge Large Language Models with numerical grid simulation tools, reducing manual overhead while maintaining human oversight.

Method: The authors (1) identify industrial requirements for agent-assisted grid studies in TSO contexts; (2) develop pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface that exposes selected pypowsybl simulation capabilities as standardized tool calls for AI agents; (3) propose principles for human-in-the-loop and multi-agent workflows; and (4) outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics with practitioner feedback.

Result: As a position paper, this work presents pypowsybl-mcp as a concrete first-step testbed rather than final experimental results. It demonstrates the feasibility of exposing power-system simulation functions (setup, execution, analysis, result retrieval) through MCP-standardized tool calls and lays out a roadmap for evaluation.

Conclusion: MCP-based tool integration represents a promising direction for building interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments. The pypowsybl-mcp interface serves as an initial platform to explore how AI agents can assist with power-grid simulations under structured human supervision.

Abstract: This position paper explores how Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) can support power-grid studies in a Transmission System Operator (TSO) context. We focus on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision. We identify key industrial requirements for agent assisted grid studies and introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface exposing selected capabilities of our simulation tool, pypowsybl to AI agents. This first step provides a testbed to study how agents can setup simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls. We also discuss principles for human-in-the-loop, multi-agent workflows and outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback. The paper positions MCP-based tool integration as a step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments.

</details>


### [120] [Human AI Construction of Bayesian Networks for Operational Decision Support -- A Virtual Survey Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14141)
*Kumar Rahul,Shovan Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel methodology using Large Language Models with a panel of AI agents and trimmed-mean aggregation is proposed to build Bayesian Belief Networks, bridging expert judgment and data-driven learning. Applied to modeling customer intention in alternative healthcare, it reveals subjective norms have stronger causal impact than self-efficacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian Belief Networks are valuable for decision-making under uncertainty, but constructing their structures and estimating parameters is challenging — researchers are forced to choose between subjective expert judgment or requiring large datasets for learning. No existing approach effectively bridges these two extremes.

Method: The authors propose using Large Language Models (LLMs) as a panel of AI agents, each embodying specific personas and contextual knowledge, to estimate probabilistic parameters for BBNs. A trimmed-mean rule is applied to filter noise from the aggregated probability estimates. A six-step BBN framework is developed to operationalize this approach.

Result: Applied to modeling customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system, the model shows that self-efficacy, while appearing important, has a small actual causal impact. Subjective norms exert a much stronger effect. The most effective intervention strategy combines improving both confidence and community norms simultaneously.

Conclusion: LLM-based panels with robust aggregation can successfully bridge expert elicitation and data-driven BBN construction. Combining confidence-building with normative interventions yields the greatest impact on customer intention in alternative healthcare contexts.

Abstract: Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs) are powerful tools for decision-making under uncertainty. However, building their structures and estimating parameters are difficult. Currently, researchers must choose between relying on expert judgement or using large datasets to learn the structure and parameters of the network. We propose a new methodology using Large Language Models to bridge the gap between expert opinion and data-driven learning. This approach uses a panel of AI agents to estimate probabilities based on specific personas and context. We then apply a trimmed-mean rule to remove noise from these responses. We develop a six step BBN framework and illustrate it to model customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system. The model reveals that while self efficacy appears to be a major factor, its actual causal impact is small. In contrast, subjective norms have a much stronger effect in modelling customers' intention. The most effective strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms simultaneously.

</details>


### [121] [ReasFlow: Assisting Reasoning-Centric Scientific Discovery in Applied Mathematics via a Knowledge-Based Multi-Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14178)
*Yutong He,Daibo Li,Guohong Li,Jiahe Geng,Zhengyang Huang,Can Ren,Zekun Zhang,Yifan Liu,Shuchen Zhu,Hengrui Zhang,Boao Kong,Ming Sun,Shu Li,Chenyi Li,Jiang Hu,Kun Yuan,Zaiwen Wen,Pingwen Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReasFlow is an end-to-end autonomous agent system for theory-driven scientific discovery that adopts a human-AI collaborative paradigm. It features internal verification loops for logical coherence and automated knowledge retrieval for self-improvement, unifying literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation. Deployed to generate five complete research papers, it achieves top scores among open-access baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated research systems focus on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery underexplored. Key gaps include difficulty verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning for autonomous frontier exploration, and scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature.

Method: ReasFlow operationalizes a human-Principal-Investigator / AI-graduate-student collaborative paradigm. It incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors before human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation.

Result: Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric.

Conclusion: ReasFlow demonstrates that autonomous agents can be extended into theory-driven, mathematically rigorous scientific discovery through verification loops and knowledge retrieval mechanisms, with public access provided via the ReasLab platform.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models have fueled autonomous AI agents capable of tackling complex scientific tasks, yet existing automated research systems remain predominantly focused on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery, particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge, largely underexplored. Key challenges include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for autonomous frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature. We introduce ReasFlow, an end-to-end autonomous agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that operationalizes a collaborative paradigm where the human expert acts as Principal Investigator while the agent executes rigorous derivations as a capable graduate student. ReasFlow incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors prior to human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that proactively surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics, substantially reducing expert intervention. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single system. Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform, providing a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research. Github repo: https://github.com/ReasLab/ReasFlow.git.

</details>


### [122] [Capability from Access Structure, Not Scale: Lower Bounds and Pre-Registered Tests for Hybrid Sequence Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14144)
*Wenhui Chen,Jianlin Chen,Ziyao Lin,Chi Man Vong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH) argues that while neural network representations converge with scale (Platonic Representation Hypothesis), capabilities do not — instead they converge toward a specific architectural class called the "access-complete hybrid," which combines a compressive O(1)-state channel with a scalable verbatim-index channel. Three fundamental resource walls (Shannon, horizon, circuit) block any architecture lacking both channels, and small-scale pre-registered experiments support the predicted bifurcation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that scaling models leads to convergent representations, but this paper identifies a critical gap: representational convergence does not imply capability convergence. The authors seek to establish the architectural prerequisites for genuine capability convergence, distinguishing what is freely given by scale from what must be explicitly engineered through access structure.

Method: The paper proceeds through three complementary approaches: (1) information-theoretic lower bounds establishing three "resource walls" (Shannon wall for architectures lacking O(N) state, horizon wall for fixed-window models, circuit wall for fixed-depth attention-only models conditional on TC0 ≠ NC1); (2) a constructive demonstration that a hybrid architecture (compressive O(1)-state channel + scalable verbatim-index channel) crosses all three walls, proving strict super-additivity; (3) pre-registered small-scale experiments with criteria frozen before data collection, testing exact-retrieval error, state-tracking bifurcation, and a conjunction witness task.

Result: The predicted "scissors gap" was measured: exact-retrieval error of 0.994 versus 0.000 when a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer. The state-tracking bifurcation landed at the pre-registered boundary. A conjunction witness showed an irreducibly two-channel solution. One prediction failed with reversed direction and is reported transparently.

Conclusion: Representational convergence emerges freely from scale, but capability convergence requires purchasing specific access structure — namely, the dual-channel hybrid architecture. The access-completeness principle rests on proved information-theoretic lower bounds, while the broader field-level convergence trend remains an economics-motivated conjecture requiring further validation.

Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that as models scale, representations of heterogeneous networks converge toward a shared model of reality. We propose its sequel and boundary, the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH): under a fixed per-token inference budget, representational convergence does not entail capability convergence. Capability instead converges toward a class, the access-complete hybrid: any architecture holding both a compressive O(1)-state channel and a scalable verbatim-index channel. We anchor it on a witness task, the Newton's-apple problem in an infinite stream, and name three resource walls: a Shannon wall barring any o(Nb)-state architecture, a horizon wall barring any fixed window, and a circuit wall barring fixed-depth attention-only composition (conditional on TC0 != NC1). Under an explicit separability assumption a hybrid crosses all three by paying each wall's price, so capability is strictly super-additive under composition. We separate what we prove from what we conjecture: the access-completeness principle rests on information-theoretic lower bounds and pre-registered experiments, while the field-level convergence trend is an economics-motivated conjecture. We report the first pre-registered small-scale tests under criteria frozen before the data: the predicted scissors gap is measured (exact-retrieval error 0.994 vs. 0.000 once a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer), the state-tracking bifurcation lands at the registered boundary, and a conjunction witness shows an irreducibly two-channel solution; one prediction failed with its direction reversed and is reported as such. Representational convergence is given freely by scale; capability convergence must be purchased by access structure.

</details>


### [123] [Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14256)
*Genglin Liu,Muye Zhang,Krishnamurthy Viswanathan,Nichole J. Hansen,Blaž Bratanič,Nathan L Clement,Shalini Ghosh,Ariel Fuxman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an automated, multi-agent red-teaming framework that iteratively synthesizes adversarial multimodal examples to uncover safety policy violations in MLLMs. Using these examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time retrieval reduces the False Negative Rate from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark, without any human labeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs deployed for content safety and moderation are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation cannot scale to handle the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats, necessitating an automated approach to discover boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases.

Method: The authors propose an agentic red-teaming framework with three components: (1) a high-reasoning Architect agent that proposes novel hypotheses and mutates past attempts in an iterative strategy, (2) an advanced image generator to synthesize adversarial examples, and (3) a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters. The synthesized adversarial examples are then used as in-context demonstrations via test-time retrieval to improve the target model's robustness.

Result: The framework autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations without human intervention. Using the synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations, the target model's False Negative Rate (FNR) dropped from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark.

Conclusion: Automated, agentic red-teaming with iterative hypothesis-driven synthesis can effectively surface multimodal safety vulnerabilities at scale. Test-time retrieval of these adversarially generated examples significantly improves MLLM robustness without relying on costly human annotation.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed for nuanced content safety and moderation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation fail to scale against the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats. In this paper, we propose an automated, agentic red-teaming framework that systematically synthesizes difficult examples using an iterative strategy that proposes novel hypotheses as well as mutating on past attempts. Leveraging a multi-agent architecture that consists of a high-reasoning Architect agent, an advanced image generator, and a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters, our system autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases without any human intervention. By employing these carefully synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time Retrieval, we substantially improve the target model's robustness, reducing the False Negative Rate (FNR) from 41.2% to 24.5% in a public image safety benchmark without relying on any human labeling.

</details>


### [124] [ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14145)
*Weiting Liu,Jieyi Bi,Wanqi Zhou,Jianfeng Feng,Yining Ma,Ai Han,Wenlian Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tool-augmented LLM agents suffer from behavioral inertia when their toolset is expanded—they default to familiar tools. The authors propose ToolAnchor, which injects counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points to break this inertia, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes successful interventions through agentic post-training, achieving competitive performance across GAIA, BrowseComp, and VDR-Bench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When new tools are introduced, agents exhibit behavioral inertia—they fall back on familiar tools and reasoning patterns, failing to leverage new capabilities. Retraining from scratch on the expanded toolset is often impractical. The work aims to enable efficient toolset expansion without full retraining.

Method: ToolAnchor, a three-stage framework: (1) A teacher model hypothesizes counterfactual anchor contexts—alternative reasoning paths that incorporate new tools—at critical decision points where the agent's trajectory failed. (2) These counterfactual interventions are verified via student model rollouts to confirm they recover failed trajectories. (3) Successful interventions are internalized through agentic post-training, fine-tuning the agent to naturally adopt the expanded toolset. The approach bridges static post-training and dynamic adaptation.

Result: Extensive evaluations across three benchmarks—GAIA (general AI assistant), BrowseComp (textual search), and VDR-Bench (visual search)—demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets compared to baseline agents that suffer from behavioral inertia.

Conclusion: ToolAnchor effectively bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic toolset adaptation. By breaking behavioral inertia through counterfactual anchoring, the framework enables scalable agentic reinforcement learning, offering a practical path for deploying LLM agents with evolving tool capabilities without requiring full retraining.

Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [125] [SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14494)
*Yiming Zhang,Koji Tsuda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAGA introduces schema-aware grounding for LLM-based interactive KBQA, replacing type-blind property retrieval with type-constrained exploration. It achieves top F1 on 9/9 and top exact-match on 8/9 benchmarks across Wikidata and Freebase, while reducing empty-result queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interactive LLM agents for KBQA ground properties using only lexical relevance and instance-level observations, ignoring entity types, property domains/ranges, and expected answer types. This "type-blind grounding" expands the search space and produces semantically incompatible triple patterns that yield empty results. The authors aim to make KB grounding schema-aware to reduce this failure mode.

Method: SAGA is a training-free framework that converts property exploration into schema-constrained grounding. It maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively using empirical and trace-local evidence.

Result: SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine benchmark settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight of nine settings across Wikidata and Freebase. It also reduces empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

Conclusion: Schema-aware grounding significantly improves interactive text-to-SPARQL generation by preventing semantically invalid property selection, reducing empty results, and boosting overall accuracy without requiring additional training.

Abstract: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

</details>


### [126] [AI Agents Do Not Fail Alone:The Context Fails First](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14275)
*Fouad Bousetouane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Context engineering quality is an independent, measurable leading indicator of AI agent reliability. Using ProofAgent-Harness with multi-juror scoring across seven criteria, the authors show context scores predict behavioral outcomes (hallucination, manipulation resistance, instruction following, tool use) without circular reliance on those same behavioral metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agent evaluation focuses on behavioral outcomes but neglects the quality of the context (instructions, tools, memory, guardrails, etc.) that shapes agent behavior. Context engineering remains unmeasured, making it impossible to audit or preflight agent reliability before deployment. The authors aim to validate context quality as an independent leading indicator, distinct from downstream behavioral metrics.

Method: The authors developed ProofAgent-Harness, an open-source evaluation infrastructure using multi-juror, consensus-based scoring. Context quality is assessed across seven criteria: role clarity, guardrail coverage, instruction consistency, tool schema quality, grounding sufficiency, injection hardening, and token efficiency. Critically, context scores are isolated from behavioral metrics and release decisions to avoid circular validation. A controlled study was conducted across regulated agent domains, holding frontier LLM agents fixed while varying only the operating context, to test whether context-quality criteria predict corresponding behavioral outcomes.

Result: Context-quality criteria consistently predicted their corresponding behavioral outcomes: grounding sufficiency predicted hallucination resistance, guardrail coverage predicted manipulation resistance, instruction consistency predicted instruction following, and tool-schema quality predicted tool use.

Conclusion: Context measurement is a validated preflight signal for agent reliability. Context engineering should be positioned as an auditable, independent layer of agent evaluation and governance, decoupled from behavioral outcome metrics.

Abstract: Context engineering has become central to building reliable AI agents, yet it remains largely unmeasured. Agents do not fail in isolation: their behavior is shaped by the instructions, tools, memory, retrieved knowledge, guardrails, and untrusted inputs accumulated in their context. When this context is weak, agents drift, hallucinate, misuse tools, ignore constraints, become vulnerable to injection, and waste tokens. This paper validates context-engineering quality as an independent leading indicator of agent reliability. We implement the measurement in ProofAgent-Harness, an open-source infrastructure for AI agent evaluation that uses multi-juror, consensus-based scoring. The harness assesses context across seven criteria: role clarity, guardrail coverage, instruction consistency, tool schema quality, grounding sufficiency, injection hardening, and token efficiency. Crucially, the context score is isolated from behavioral metrics and release decisions, enabling a non-circular validation. Through a controlled context-quality study across regulated agent domains, holding frontier LLM agents fixed and varying only their operating context, we show that context-quality criteria consistently predict their corresponding behavioral outcomes. Grounding sufficiency predicts hallucination resistance, guardrail coverage predicts manipulation resistance, instruction consistency predicts instruction following, and tool-schema quality predicts tool use. These findings establish context measurement as a validated preflight signal for agent reliability and position context engineering as an auditable layer of agent evaluation and governance.

</details>


### [127] [Enhancing Small Language Models Reasoning through Knowledge Graph Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14149)
*Dimitrios Kelesis,Konstantinos Bougiatiotis,Georgios Paliouras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic agentic framework that equips small language models (SLMs) with tool-based access to symbolic triplet extraction and RGCN-driven expert hints, tested on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. While hints yield 1.5–2× gains, the system is bottlenecked by extraction errors and compounding failures in multi-hop reasoning, with noisy self-generated facts sometimes degrading performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are costly and environmentally taxing, making SLMs an attractive sustainable alternative. However, SLMs struggle with complex, multi-hop logical reasoning tasks. The authors aim to bridge this gap by augmenting SLMs with neuro-symbolic tools, investigating whether structured symbolic guidance can compensate for the limited inherent reasoning capacity of small models.

Method: The authors design a minimalist agentic framework around SLMs (Gemma 3 1B/4B, Llama 3.2 3B) with two specialized tool calls: (1) `extract_facts` for symbolic triplet extraction from natural language narratives, and (2) `get_hint` for querying a pre-trained Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN) that provides expert relational reasoning hints. Evaluation is conducted on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark under two configurations — an Oracle scenario using ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario where the SLM relies on self-extracted facts — to isolate the effects of extraction quality versus reasoning capability.

Result: RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5–2× performance improvement over story-only baselines. However, overall system performance is constrained by an extraction bottleneck: errors in early-stage triplet extraction compound across multi-hop reasoning chains (sequential deductive fragility). A notable "distraction effect" emerges in certain architectures, where noisy self-extracted facts degrade performance even when expert hints are available.

Conclusion: The work characterizes fundamental challenges in symbolic grounding for low-resource agentic systems, highlighting that expert symbolic guidance is beneficial but insufficient when extraction fidelity is low. The authors propose iterative verification as a roadmap for improving robustness in future neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. Our approach transforms the SLM into a minimalist agent utilizing two specialized tool calls: extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction and get_hint for expert reasoning via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). We evaluate these models across two configurations, both in an Oracle scenario with ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge. Our results reveal that while RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5 - 2x performance gain over story-only baselines, the system is constrained by the extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early extraction errors compound over multi-hop chains. Furthermore, we identify a "distraction effect" in specific architectures where noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite the presence of expert hints. This work characterizes the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and provides a roadmap for iterative verification in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

</details>


### [128] [Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14553)
*Artan Markaj,Raphael Höfer,Felix Gehlhoff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a middleware that represents high-level human intentions as persistent, first-class runtime objects using LLMs grounded in OWL ontologies. It detects goal conflicts between autonomous subsystems at registration time and explains them in natural language, shifting assurance from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution intention-level checking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In modern industrial environments, multiple autonomous subsystems (schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets) share physical resources but operate with their own goals. High-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, leaving no component able to verify whether execution still aligns with original intent. Goal conflicts are discovered only after causing missed targets or shutdowns, motivating a need for persistent, explainable intention representations and pre-execution conflict detection.

Method: The IAL is a domain-agnostic middleware with three core components: (1) an LLM grounded in a formal OWL ontology that parses natural-language goals into structured, machine-readable intentions; (2) a consistency monitor that detects conflicts between intentions at registration time, before any execution occurs; and (3) a transparency module that explains detected conflicts in natural language. The approach treats intentions as first-class, persistent runtime objects.

Result: A proof-of-concept demonstration shows two autonomous agents registering conflicting production and energy intentions. The IAL successfully flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer, validating the pre-execution detection capability.

Conclusion: The IAL shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking, enabling earlier and more interpretable conflict resolution in shared-resource industrial settings.

Abstract: Modern industrial environments increasingly run many autonomous subsystems at once - schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets - each pursuing its own goals while sharing the same physical resources. Because high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, no running component can tell whether it is still doing what was actually intended, and goal conflicts surface only after they have caused a missed target or a shutdown. We propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domainagnostic middleware that represents intentions as first-class, persistent, and explainable runtime objects: a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses naturallanguage goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time, before execution, and a transparency module explains them in natural language. We report a first proof of concept in which two autonomous agents register conflicting production and energy intentions, and the IAL flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer. The result is a mechanism that shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

</details>


### [129] [SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15257)
*Yuyao Zhang,Junjie Gao,Zhengxian Wu,Jiaming Fan,Jin Zhang,Shihan Ma,Yao Yao,Weiran Qi,Chuyan Jin,Guiyu Ma,Xingzhong Xu,Kai Yang,Ji-Rong Wen,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchOS is a multi-agent framework that externalizes search progress into explicit shared state (Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, Failure Memory) to prevent repetitive loops in LLM-based information-seeking, achieving SOTA on WideSearch and GISA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents performing web search accumulate long interaction histories and fail to track progress. When searches return poor results, both single- and multi-agent systems fall into repetitive query loops, wasting search budgets and degrading output quality. There is no explicit, persistent mechanism for agents to know what has been tried, what evidence exists, and what remains uncovered.

Method: The authors (1) formalize open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations; (2) introduce Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM) with four components: Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, and Failure Memory; (3) apply pipeline-parallel scheduling to overlap sub-agent execution and refill freed slots with tasks targeting coverage gaps; and (4) build a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model-tool interactions, records grounded evidence, detects stalls/budget exhaustion, and provides a hierarchical skill system (strategy and access skills) to avoid repeating failed search patterns.

Result: SearchOS achieves leading results on all metrics across the WideSearch and GISA benchmarks when compared against single-agent and multi-agent baselines.

Conclusion: Explicit, persistent, shared state management via SOCM combined with pipeline-parallel scheduling and a middleware harness enables robust multi-agent information-seeking that avoids repetitive failure loops and maximizes search budget efficiency.

Abstract: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

</details>


### [130] [Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301)
*Shahin Hossain,Tukhbita Afroz Nawmi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study developed and validated the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four types of GenAI reliance (Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, Dialogic) among undergraduates. Validated with 382 survey respondents and 14 interviews at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution, the scale demonstrated a five-factor structure (Strategic split into Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation), acceptable reliability (ω = .75–.88), scalar invariance across demographic groups, and meaningful associations with AI literacy and writing outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing measures of GenAI reliance were developed inductively for discrete problem-solving tasks and validated with homogeneous samples, leaving a gap for theoretically grounded instruments that capture how—not just whether—undergraduates rely on GenAI in academic writing. Understanding reliance types is critical for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity.

Method: The GenAI-RTS was developed from a four-type theoretical framework. Validation followed the multisource Standards framework: a survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution provided data for confirmatory factor analysis (testing six competing models), reliability estimation (omega), measurement invariance testing (across gender, first-generation status, STEM/non-STEM), and Rasch analysis. Fourteen purposively sampled students were interviewed for qualitative triangulation.

Result: A five-factor model (Strategic split into Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation, plus Instrumental, Dependent, Dialogic) showed best fit (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Reliability ranged from ω = .75–.88. Scalar invariance held across all tested groups—the first such evidence for a GenAI reliance instrument. Rasch analysis recommended a five-point response format. Strategic reliance correlated positively with AI literacy, and reliance types differentiated students on multiple writing process and outcome variables.

Conclusion: The GenAI-RTS provides a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated tool for identifying undergraduate reliance profiles, supporting research, assessment, and AI literacy interventions in academic writing contexts.

Abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in undergraduate academic writing, how students rely on these tools, rather than simply whether they use them, has become a central question for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity. Existing measures of reliance were developed inductively, focused on discrete problem-solving tasks, and validated mainly with homogeneous samples. This study developed and validated the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four theoretically derived types of GenAI reliance: Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic. Validation followed the multisource framework of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, drawing on a survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution and interviews with 14 purposively sampled students. Confirmatory factor analyses of six competing models supported a five-factor structure in which Strategic Reliance comprises two facets, Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation, alongside Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic factors (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Subscale reliability was acceptable to good (omega = .75-.88), and scalar measurement invariance held across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors, to our knowledge the first such evidence for a GenAI reliance instrument. Rasch analysis indicated that a five-point response format would improve category functioning. Strategic reliance was positively associated with AI literacy, and the reliance types differentiated students across multiple writing process and outcome variables. The GenAI-RTS offers researchers and educators a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated instrument for identifying undergraduate reliance profiles and supporting research, assessment, and AI literacy intervention.

</details>


### [131] [MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14159)
*Yue Huang,Wenjie Wang,Han Bao,Yuchen Ma,Xiaonan Luo,Yi Nian,Haomin Zhuang,Zheyuan Liu,Yue Zhao,Xiangliang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemoHarness is an adaptive framework that learns from its own execution experience to optimize agent harnesses across six editable control dimensions, using a dual-layer experience bank for case-specific and global patterns. It improves over fixed harnesses on shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks without test-time labels or additional search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic improvement methods for LLM-based agents focus on narrow artifacts like prompts or workflows, while the agent harness—the external control layer managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling—remains a single static configuration despite strongly influencing agent behavior. There is a need for harnesses that adapt per-case using past execution experience.

Method: MemoHarness decomposes the agent harness into six editable control dimensions. It maintains a dual-layer experience bank: per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns. At test time, it retrieves relevant experience from this bank to adapt the harness to each case, requiring no test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. The framework learns from its own prior executions.

Result: MemoHarness outperforms fixed harness baselines across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks. It demonstrates selective transfer capability to unseen benchmark suites and base models. The additional context remains cost-competitive when retrieved experience is largely cacheable.

Conclusion: Execution experience is a practical substrate for building adaptive agent harnesses that outperform static configurations. The authors leave broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

Abstract: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

</details>


### [132] [Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14673)
*Leanne Tan,Rohan Jaggi,Shaun Khoo,Roy Ka-Wei Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Kaleidoscope is a workflow for contextual functional evaluation of AI applications that combines persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, human review, and reliability-gated automated scoring using LLM judges, piloted across four organizational use cases with promising results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public benchmarks rarely match an AI team's specific users, context, or policies. Human review is tedious and doesn't scale. These challenges are especially acute in the public sector, where applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. There is a need for a practical, inspectable, iterative evaluation workflow that bridges this gap.

Method: Kaleidoscope integrates four components: (1) persona-based test case generation tailored to application context; (2) application-specific contextualized rubrics for scoring; (3) human annotation providing reviewable labels; and (4) LLM judges that automate scoring only when their agreement with human labels exceeds a configured reliability threshold. The approach was piloted in a three-week study across four organizational use cases, with custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions.

Result: The three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs (spanning 4 domains, 14 evaluation dimensions) demonstrated that the reliability-gated automated scoring approach is viable. Results highlight useful features for achieving end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

Conclusion: Kaleidoscope offers a practical, inspectable, and iterative evaluation workflow for product teams, particularly those operating under policy and governance constraints. The reliability-gated mechanism ensures automated scoring is only used when trustworthy, making it suitable for real-world deployment where evaluation must be both scalable and dependable.

Abstract: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

</details>


### [133] [When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14169)
*Javier Aguilar Martín*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-synthesized Code World Models (CWMs) can achieve near-perfect transition accuracy yet fail catastrophically in planning because rare but pivotal dynamics are missed. The paper formally characterizes this "verified-vs-correct gap," derives a quantitative danger law, shows the problem stems from rule translation (not inference), and demonstrates the same mechanism in imperfect-information settings with a provable coverage bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The prevailing practice evaluates LLM-synthesized world models by transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. The authors argue this is the wrong adequacy metric for planning: a model can be near-perfect on random samples yet miss exactly the rare dynamics that determine game outcomes, rendering it useless for downstream planning.

Method: The paper proceeds in four parts: (1) End-to-end demonstration of the verified-vs-correct gap using a CWM synthesis pipeline, measuring both transition accuracy and actual play performance; (2) Derivation of a quantitative danger law, danger = play_cost × (1−rarity)^N, with empirical bounding of play cost; (3) Ablation across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples) to test whether more data repairs the gap; (4) Extension to imperfect-information CWMs, proving a coverage bound (N ≳ b^{d_max}) and constructing Beacon, a hand-crafted verified-but-wrong inference function.

Result: (1) A CWM passed a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and ≥98% state-accuracy on the planner's search distribution, yet lost systematically due to <1% pivotal errors (play cost 0.091, 95% CI [0.065, 0.117], n=4800). (2) The danger law is proven exact for the gate-miss factor and empirically bounded for play cost. (3) LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not inference — the omitted rule was never inferred across models or data regimes. (4) In imperfect-information settings, a size-N gate is identifying only when N ≳ b^{d_max}; Beacon passes the gate yet loses every game.

Conclusion: Adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by direct play performance, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions. The verified-vs-correct gap is structural, not fixable by scaling data, and applies to both fully-observed and partially-observed settings.

Abstract: Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

</details>


### [134] [RxBrain: Embodied Cognition Foundation Model with Joint Language-Visual Reasoning and Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14187)
*Haotian Liang,Mingkang Chen,Yufei Huang,Yuchun Guo,Xiaomeng Zhu,Xiangli Shi,Kaixuan Wang,Yunxuan Mao,Weijie Zhou,Ling Chen,Shirong Zeng,Yueyu Long,Yuchen Si,Yajuan Zhu,Xingyu Zhou,Minghui Wang,Wanjia He,Xin Yang,Lingzhu Xiang,Zhiqing Liu,Bohan Ma,Xiran Huang,Tianshuo Yang,Zhiheng Liu,Xuantang Xiong,Zisheng Lu,Ping Luo,Yao Mu,Han Hu,Zhengyou Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RxBrain is an embodied cognition foundation model that unifies language and visual reasoning in a single planning sequence, where language provides abstract task structure and visual imagination grounds it in physical state predictions. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, it supports multimodal understanding and generation, and can be extended to robot action generation without large-scale action pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current models suffer from a disconnect: vision-language models focus on scene understanding and textual decisions, while generative world models only predict future visual states. Neither approach tightly couples high-level task reasoning with the physical states agents must achieve. RxBrain addresses this gap by jointly representing embodied plans through complementary language (abstract structure) and visual imagination (physical grounding).

Method: RxBrain uses a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting language, image, and video understanding/generation. An automatic pipeline converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps aligned with visual state transitions. The model produces plans as a single sequence where textual reasoning (task decomposition, temporal order, constraints) and visual components (world state prediction, subgoal planning) are interleaved. The authors also introduce RxBrain-Bench for evaluating joint textual-visual plan representation.

Result: RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation capabilities while producing plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. Extended to continuous robot action generation, it demonstrates promising real-robot performance without requiring large-scale action-data pretraining.

Conclusion: RxBrain represents an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition by tightly coupling language-based planning with visual world state prediction in a unified architecture, enabling agents to connect high-level reasoning with physical task execution.

Abstract: Embodied cognition requires agents to connect high-level task reasoning with the physical states to be achieved. We introduce Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model with joint language-visual reasoning and imagination. Unlike vision-language models that emphasize scene understanding and textual decision making, or generative world models that mainly predict future visual states, RxBrain represents embodied plans in a single planning sequence where language and visual imagination play complementary roles. Language provides the abstract structure of a plan, including task decomposition, planning primitives, constraints, temporal order, and decision logic, while visual imagination grounds this structure through world state prediction and joint subgoal planning, associating each planning step with intermediate and final physical states. RxBrain adopts a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports language, image, and video understanding and generation within one model. To train this capability, we build an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps and aligning them with visual state transitions. We further introduce RxBrain-Bench to evaluate whether models can represent embodied plans through joint textual and visual components rather than separate understanding or generation. Experiments show that RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, and produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. We also extend RxBrain to continuous robot action generation, where it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining. These results provide an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

</details>


### [135] [Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15202)
*Hoang-Loc Cao,Van Pham,Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,Phuc Ho,Veronica Whitford,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A self-evolving annotation framework that combines LLM-assisted labeling with expert verification to create DSM-5-TR-aligned depression datasets, using a dual-memory architecture to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve annotation quality, consistency, and explainability without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mental health datasets suffer from poor annotation quality: labels lack structured evidence, symptom-level justification, and traceable alignment with DSM-5-TR criteria, undermining transparency and model interpretability in XAI systems for depression research.

Method: A three-stage annotation framework: (1) candidate evidence selection from textual records, (2) criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and (3) case-level synthesis producing diagnostic labels and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture (Example Memory + Reflection Memory) internalizes expert feedback to iteratively refine future annotations without retraining. The system also exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories for full auditability.

Result: In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the framework improved annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort. The dual-memory mechanism is described but its multi-cycle evaluation is deferred to future work.

Conclusion: The proposed expert-in-the-loop framework offers a promising direction for building higher-quality, DSM-5-TR-aligned, and auditable depression datasets. Full validation of the dual-memory feedback mechanism across multiple cycles remains as future work.

Abstract: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in building reliable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems for mental health research. In depression-related datasets, labels are often assigned without structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable alignment with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), limiting both transparency and downstream model interpretability. We propose a self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that combines large language model (LLM)-assisted labeling with expert verification. The framework is intended to support the construction of explainable, DSM-5-TR-aligned datasets rather than to perform clinical diagnosis. It operates in three stages: candidate evidence selection from textual records, criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and case-level synthesis that produces label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture, composed of Example Memory and Reflection Memory, is designed to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve future annotations without retraining. We describe this mechanism and leave its evaluation across multiple feedback cycles to future work. In addition to final labels, the framework exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories, enabling comprehensive auditability. In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the proposed approach improves annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort.

</details>


### [136] [Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15176)
*Patrick Phuoc Do,Chau M. Ta,Chaoli Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks six multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on a standardized scientific visualization literacy test and finds that while Gemini exceeds the human baseline, all models exhibit highly uneven performance across different visualization techniques and task types, with open-source models falling below human performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLM evaluations for visual interpretation are overly focused on chart-centric assessments, leaving scientific visualization (SciVis) literacy largely unexamined. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a rigorous, human-normed benchmark to assess whether MLLMs truly understand complex scientific visualizations.

Method: The authors benchmark six MLLMs (three closed-source, three open-source) using the scientific visualization literacy assessment test (SciVis LAT), a standardized instrument with 49 items derived from 18 scientific visualizations spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. A closed-world evaluation protocol is used, and model performance is compared against data from 485 human participants.

Result: Gemini outperforms all other models and exceeds the human mean, while all open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is uneven: models excel on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding tasks but struggle with texture-based and integration-based visualizations and quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation.

Conclusion: SciVis literacy constitutes a necessary and currently under-explored dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. The uneven performance across techniques and tasks highlights specific weaknesses that future MLLMs must address to achieve robust scientific visualization understanding.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

</details>


### [137] [How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14197)
*Jason Miklian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI answer engines hallucinate more about conflicts with thinner documentary records, creating structural vulnerability to disinformation via Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Analysis of 1,048 source websites confirms GEO is already occurring, with state-partisan digital capture growing rapidly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether LLM hallucinations about peace and conflict issues follow discernible patterns, and to understand how these patterns shape the evolving global conflict information environment.

Method: The authors queried five leading AI answer engines with a battery of questions about 28 distinct conflicts, producing 5,460 answers which were scored against documented evidence. They further analyzed 1,048 websites that the LLMs sourced conflict facts from to detect GEO and state-partisan manipulation.

Result: Thinner retrievable records around a conflict correlate strongly with increased hallucination (invention, misattribution, miscounting). These thin records create structural exposure to mis/disinformation because they are easiest to manipulate via GEO. Analysis confirmed GEO source optimization is already underway, and state-partisan digital capture, while incipient, is rapidly expanding.

Conclusion: The findings signal the rise of GEO-enabled information warfare. The authors advocate for a return to deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI cannot replicate, and identify future research opportunities in this rapidly evolving domain.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment?
