To this end, we propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. A key insight is to utilize the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics. Specifically, a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) is designed to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enables joint modeling of spectral and semantic features within a shared representation space. Furthermore, a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism is introduced to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets demonstrate that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

</details>


### [160] [RetroAgent: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured Memory for Agentic Retrosynthesis Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14512)
*Yanqiao Zhu,Jingru Gan,Xiaoqi Sun,Fang Sun,Yidan Shi,Md Mofijul Islam,Chao Shang,Wenhao Gao,Connor W. Coley,Yizhou Sun,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RetroAgent is an LLM-based agent for multi-step retrosynthesis that combines symbolic tree search with structured memory and chemistry tools, enabling globally-informed decisions and outperforming prior methods on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-step retrosynthesis involves a vast combinatorial search space. Traditional methods use tree search with offline value networks that score candidates in isolation without holistic route reasoning, while recent LLM-based approaches use overly simple interfaces that restrict search space exploration. There is a need for an agent that can reason about the full search state — explored routes, alternatives, and intermediate properties — to make globally informed decisions.

Method: RetroAgent bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning via a harness with structured memory and chemistry tools. The agent maintains awareness of the full search state (explored routes, available alternatives, intermediate molecule properties), allowing it to ground decisions in both global search progress and domain knowledge, rather than scoring candidates in isolation.

Result: RetroAgent achieves strong performance and generalization on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution retrosynthesis benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining LLM reasoning with structured memory and symbolic search capabilities.

Conclusion: Integrating LLM agents with structured memory and symbolic search tools represents a promising direction for complex chemical planning tasks, overcoming the limitations of both traditional offline-scoring methods and simplistic LLM interfaces.

Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization.

</details>


### [161] [WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524)
*Adnan Labib,Yixuan Huang,Jiahui Wu,John Maurice Gayed,Zheng Yuan,Qiao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WrAFT is a modular automated writing evaluation system that achieves SOTA essay scoring (QWK 0.84, RMSE 0.44) and highly rated multi-level feedback (93-96% approval) using fine-tuned LLMs on TOEFL essays.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated writing evaluation systems often lack reliable scoring combined with comprehensive, quality feedback. The authors aim to build a tool that delivers both accurate scores and effective feedback across surface-level and deep-level dimensions for argumentative essays.

Method: WrAFT uses a modular design separating scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback (macro and micro). Multiple LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7) were evaluated via direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores (0-5 scale) was used for training and evaluation. Scoring performance was measured by QWK and RMSE; feedback quality was assessed through human evaluation.

Result: Scoring: QWK of 0.84 and RMSE of 0.44 against official TOEFL scores (0-5 scale). Feedback human approval: 96.14% for surface-level, 93.03% for deep-level macro, and 94.69% for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive public web interface was deployed.

Conclusion: WrAFT demonstrates that a modular LLM-based AWE system can achieve both high-accuracy automated essay scoring and pedagogically effective, human-approved feedback, making it a viable tool for real-world writing assessment and instruction.

Abstract: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

</details>


### [162] [Are LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Production-Ready? A Trace-Driven Benchmark and Optimization Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14541)
*Lingyun Yang,Yuxiao Wang,Shenghao Liang,Linfeng Yang,Daocheng Ying,Chunbo You,Rui Zhang,Luping Wang,Yinghao Yu,Guodong Yang,Liping Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Atrex-Bench is a production-derived GPU kernel benchmark sampled from real inference traces, weighted by serving time. Current coding agents achieve only ~10% of hardware roofline, with inflated pass rates from PyTorch fallbacks. The co-released Atrex-Kernel-Agent uses profile-driven iterative optimization with a layered knowledge base to close this gap, matching or exceeding hand-tuned kernels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks use synthetic or curated problems that do not reflect real deployed inference workloads. This creates a misleading picture of coding agent capabilities — models appear competent but actually rely on PyTorch fallbacks rather than generating performant kernels, and their true performance relative to hardware limits (roofline) on production operators is unknown.

Method: The authors construct Atrex-Bench by sampling 30 operators and 440 shapes directly from full-cluster production inference traces on compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem is weighted by its share of observed GPU time (adjusted by application card-hours and separated by serving phase), with per-problem roofline ceilings. They also build Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), which combines: (1) iterative measure-revise search, (2) optimization dropout to escape stalled contexts, and (3) a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base containing 298 reference-kernel files, 244 optimization documents, and external upstream references for API/ISA lookup.

Result: Evaluation of six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows the best vanilla model reaches only ~10% of hardware roofline on production operators. Much of the apparent pass rate stems from PyTorch fallbacks rather than model-authored kernels. In a controlled case study, AKA converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or surpass hand-tuned production baselines.

Conclusion: Production-derived benchmarking reveals a significant gap between current coding agents and hand-tuned production kernel performance. Profile-driven optimization agents with rich domain knowledge bases can bridge this gap, outperforming vanilla models that rely on framework fallbacks.

Abstract: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks draw problems from synthetic or curated sources that diverge from deployed workloads. We present Atrex-Bench, a benchmark whose 30 operators and 440 shapes are sampled directly from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem carries an importance weight derived from its share of observed GPU time, weighted by application card-hours and computed separately for the serving phases in which it runs, together with a per-problem roofline ceiling, so the aggregate score emphasizes the kernels that consume the most serving time. Evaluating six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows that even the best vanilla model reaches only ${\sim}10\%$ of the hardware roofline on production operators; and correctness alone overstates capability, since much of the apparent pass rate comes from PyTorch fallbacks rather than kernels the model wrote. To close this gap, we co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel-optimization agent that combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout for escaping stalled search contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-knowledge documents, plus external upstream reference projects for API/ISA lookup). In a controlled case study, the agent converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.

</details>


### [163] [Seeing the End at Step Zero: Accelerating Diffusion MLLMs via MLP Sparsity-Aware Truncation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14557)
*Qicheng Zhao,Qi Sun,Zheyu Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Seer is a training-free framework that accelerates Diffusion Multimodal LLMs by detecting the semantic boundary at the first denoising step via MLP activation sparsity shifts, enabling one-shot truncation of redundant [EOS] padding and achieving up to ~31× throughput gains with no performance degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DMLLMs suffer from inefficient inference due to fixed-length generation constraints: outputs are padded to a predefined maximum length, causing substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. The actual output length is unknown a priori, creating a need for dynamic early termination.

Method: The authors observe that DMLLMs exhibit a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity at the first denoising step, which implicitly reveals the valid semantic boundary. Seer leverages this via an SNR-based criterion to detect the boundary and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix. For batched serving, a hybrid execution strategy maximizes throughput while accommodating dynamic sequence lengths.

Result: Seer accelerates throughput by up to ~31×, robustly maintains performance across 9 benchmarks, and even yields slight accuracy improvements on complex visual tasks (e.g., DocVQA from 63.52 to 63.66) by mitigating noise leakage.

Conclusion: Seer provides a highly efficient, plug-and-play, training-free solution for DMLLM acceleration, effectively eliminating padding waste without compromising model performance.

Abstract: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) are highly effective for multimodal reasoning, yet their inference efficiency is significantly hindered by fixed-length generation constraints. Since the actual output length is unknown, output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, resulting in substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. In this work, we discover that DMLLMs implicitly reveal their valid semantic boundary at the very first denoising step through a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity. Leveraging this observation, we propose Seer, a training-free framework that detects this boundary using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-based criterion and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. To preserve these theoretical gains during batched serving, Seer incorporates a hybrid execution strategy that maximizes throughput while seamlessly accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experimental results demonstrate that Seer effectively eliminates padding waste, accelerating throughput by up to $\sim$31$\times$. Across 9 benchmarks, Seer robustly maintains overall performance and even improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by mitigating noise leakage (e.g., DocVQA score increases from 63.52 to 63.66), offering a highly efficient, plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

</details>


### [164] [Collaborative Spatial Learning with Multi-LLM Agents in Networked Social Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14574)
*Hao He,Chris J. Kuhlman,Xinwei Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents exhibit a significant network-efficiency effect on the Mason–Watts search task only when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, with Bayesian optimization agents outperforming LLM agents overall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether groups of LLM agents reproduce the network-efficiency effect observed in humans on collective problem-solving tasks, and to benchmark LLM agent performance against mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents and human experimental data.

Method: Groups of 16 LLM agents and mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents were evaluated on the Mason–Watts two-dimensional search task across all eight Mason–Watts network topologies, with and without a first-round randomization instruction. Performance was compared along dimensions of exploration–exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

Result: LLM agents showed a significant network-efficiency effect only under the first-round randomization condition; this simple instruction improved collective payoff by over 3× the estimated payoff difference across topologies. Bayesian optimization agents achieved higher payoffs than LLM agents on the spatial search task.

Conclusion: LLM agents can exhibit human-like network-efficiency effects but are sensitive to initialization conditions. Simple prompting strategies can dramatically improve collective performance, yet mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents remain superior on this class of spatial search problems.

Abstract: Collective problem solving often requires that group members consider the tradeoff between exploitation of known solutions and exploration for new ones, where information of known solutions can be disseminated among individual members through communication networks. The Mason--Watts experiment (PNAS 2012) showed that human groups in shorter-path networks outperform those in longer-path networks on a two-dimensional search task. In this work, we focus on the investigation of such network-efficiency effects in the setting of a group of large language model (LLM) agents. Specifically, we consider groups of sixteen LLM agents playing the Mason--Watts experiment on the eight Mason--Watts network topologies. Moreover, we develop mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents such that the performance of LLM agents can be compared with both the mechanistic agents and the human experimental data. Our computational experiments indicate that the LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, but not under the default initialization. In this experiment, adding a one-sentence first-round randomization instruction improves collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across the eight network topologies. Also, the Bayesian optimization agents obtain higher payoffs than the evaluated LLM agents on this spatial search task. We further compare the agents' exploration--exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

</details>


### [165] [Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14581)
*Sinyoung Ra,Jonghun Kim,Hyunjin Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a multi-LLM cooperative system to generate a paired 3D MRI-text dataset for brain oncology (glioma and meningioma), then builds a 3D vision-language model that outperforms existing 2D and 3D methods on report generation and visual question answering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical VLMs focus on 2D images (e.g., chest X-rays) and cannot be easily extended to 3D imaging due to the scarcity of paired 3D imaging-text data. This gap limits the application of VLMs in volumetric medical imaging domains such as brain oncology.

Method: A cooperative multi-LLM system is used where several LLMs collaboratively generate and cross-verify radiology reports for 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases, producing a high-quality paired 3D MRI-text dataset. This dataset is then used to train a VLM that tokenizes 3D MRI volumes and aligns them with text instructions for report generation and VQA.

Result: The proposed VLM outperformed other 2D and 3D baseline methods on both report generation and visual question answering tasks, demonstrating superior diagnostic and descriptive capabilities in brain oncology.

Conclusion: The cooperative LLM-based dataset creation pipeline effectively addresses the 3D image-text data scarcity problem, and the resulting VLM improves report quality, aiding better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

</details>


### [166] [MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14582)
*Junjie Zhang,Jiayu Liu,Wenbin Liu,Zhenya Huang,Doudou Wang,Yan Jiang,Leiye Xu,Tao Xiong,Wen Huang,Qi Liu,Guoping Hu,Enhong Chen,Mengping Zhang,Xiangdong Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MathCoPilot is a human-in-the-loop system for interactive theorem proving in Lean 4, where mathematicians guide high-level proof strategy while AI agents handle formalization, verification, and knowledge retrieval. The authors benchmark four LLMs on FormalMATH and real PDE theorems, finding strong undergraduate-level performance but significant gaps on domain-specific problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based theorem provers operate as fully autonomous agents, which is insufficient for real mathematical research that requires deep domain expertise and iterative human reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap by introducing a symbiotic human-AI collaboration paradigm where mathematicians retain strategic control while AI handles labor-intensive formalization and verification.

Method: MathCoPilot integrates three components: (1) an interactive workbench with a living proof blueprint for stepwise human inspection and refinement; (2) automated proving skill orchestration combining adaptive knowledge base search with Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval with automated formalization into a verified Lean 4 knowledge base. Four LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and one unnamed) are evaluated on a FormalMATH subset and two real PDE theorems, measuring both proof generation success and error-detection capability.

Result: State-of-the-art LLMs achieve high success rates on undergraduate-level problems under favorable autoformalization conditions. However, substantial challenges persist for domain-specific PDE theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding, indicating a gap between formal manipulation and deep conceptual reasoning.

Conclusion: Current LLMs, even the strongest, are not yet capable of independently tackling research-level mathematics in formal proof systems. The human-in-the-loop paradigm embodied by MathCoPilot offers a more viable path forward, combining human mathematical insight with AI automation for formalization and verification tasks.

Abstract: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

</details>


### [167] [SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14616)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Haotian Xia,Akshaya Bharadhwaj,Anay Putty,Anirudh Ravishankar,Jaewoong Lee,Jinglin Xiao,Kyumin Andrew Shim,Mishika Ahuja,Nisarga Patil,Leo Liu,Zhuohan Liu,Weining Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SportD is a benchmark of 478 soccer decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup, evaluating whether vision-language models (VLMs) can make strategically optimal on-ball choices (shoot vs. pass). The best VLM selects the highest-valued action only 31.4% of the time (vs. 38.9% for pros), exhibits systematic bias toward low-variance/low-reward actions, and partially imitates suboptimal human play patterns rather than evaluating counterfactuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs have advanced in visual interpretation, but their capacity for strategic decision-making in dynamic, value-measurable environments remains untested. Soccer offers a uniquely quantifiable setting where every action (shoot vs. pass) can be evaluated via possession-value models that estimate scoring probability changes, enabling rigorous measurement of decision quality and regret.

Method: The authors introduce SportD, a benchmark of 478 on-ball decision events from the 2022 FIFA World Cup, each accompanied by preceding video frames. Every action choice is scored against a possession-value model that identifies the action maximizing the attacking team's scoring probability. Metrics include optimal-action accuracy and regret (value forfeited relative to optimal). Three frontier VLMs are evaluated and compared against professional players' actual decisions, with analysis of action distributions (shot frequency, pass progressiveness) and imitation of suboptimal human choices.

Result: The best VLM achieves 31.4% optimal-action accuracy versus 38.9% for professional players, with all models incurring significantly higher regret. VLMs systematically prefer lower-variance, lower-reward actions: they shoot less often and choose less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or real players. Models reproduce the human player's specific action above chance even when suboptimal, suggesting pattern imitation rather than genuine counterfactual evaluation.

Conclusion: Current VLMs lack robust strategic reasoning in physically-grounded, value-quantifiable domains. SportD establishes a framework for measuring this capability, revealing that models lean on familiar action patterns rather than principled evaluation of alternatives. The benchmark offers a pathway for developing and testing VLMs with stronger forward-planning and counterfactual reasoning abilities.

Abstract: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

</details>


### [168] [Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14635)
*Yufeng Ji,Wenhao Tang,Haoyi Niu,Koushil Sreenath,Yi Wu,Zhongyu Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Action QFormer, a query-based interface that reorganizes multimodal representations for action prediction in VLA models, addressing the tension between action-compatible representation learning and preservation of language/object grounding capabilities. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, it boosts task success from 18.8% to 56.3%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior VLA models treat action supervision merely as a downstream objective, but the authors argue it actively shapes inherited multimodal representations. They identify a critical tension: action supervision is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but applying it too directly destabilizes language-side processing and object grounding in the multimodal pathway. This motivates a need for better architectural mediation between inherited representations and action learning.

Method: The authors propose Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that sits between the inherited multimodal backbone and the action generation head. It uses instruction-conditioned queries to selectively reorganize multimodal information into action-facing representations, decoupling action supervision's direct impact on upstream representations while still enabling effective action learning.

Result: In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation: average closed-loop task success improved from 18.8% to 56.3%; fixed-instruction action-generation correctness rose from 22.5% to 75.5%; out-of-distribution instruction generations were nearly eliminated. Analyses show Action QFormer reduces broad upstream representation rewriting under action supervision while preserving targeted, constructive adaptation.

Conclusion: Improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones but also better mechanisms for selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how action supervision shapes it. Action QFormer demonstrates that architectural mediation between multimodal representations and action learning is a promising direction.

Abstract: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

</details>


### [169] [Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14641)
*Remo Pareschi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes the analytic mode of abductive reasoning as a risk-sensitive, non-greedy framework where latent causal factors coexist under epistemic governance. The core κ-τ apparatus manages hypothesis interaction and commitment thresholds, while causal clusters with a two-level architecture prevent premature convergence and causal misattribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing abductive reasoning systems tend toward greedy, premature commitment to single explanations, lacking mechanisms to suspend decomposition, manage competing hypotheses, and calibrate commitment to decision stakes — especially critical in high-stakes domains like epidemiology and cybersecurity.

Method: The κ-τ apparatus: κ encodes epistemic interaction among hypotheses (intra-cluster κ* for within-cluster interactions, inter-cluster κ** for between-cluster interactions); τ sets a context-sensitive commitment threshold. Causal clusters serve as structured objects recording latent factors, their weights, and interaction structures. The two-level architecture governs when suspended decomposition resolves into committed conclusions.

Result: Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework produces legible suspended decompositions — competing explanatory scenarios weighted by plausibility and paired with discriminating evidence — enabling sound action under ambiguity without premature convergence.

Conclusion: The analytic mode of abduction, when equipped with the κ-τ apparatus and causal cluster architecture, provides a coordination object for human-AI reasoning that structurally resists premature convergence, offering decision-makers actionable, ambiguity-preserving explanations rather than a single imposed answer.

Abstract: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $κ$-$τ$ apparatus: $κ$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $τ$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $κ^*$, inter-cluster $κ^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

</details>


### [170] [TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14658)
*Mingze Xu,Yinghui Li,Jiayi Kuang,Zhanhui Kang,Di Yin,Ying Shen,Xing Sun,Yuxing Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopoAgent introduces a self-evolving topological framework for multimodal scientific reasoning that replaces linear planning with dynamic DAG-based graph evolution, featuring atomic decomposition and adaptive fission to overcome visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs struggle with rigorous scientific reasoning because monolithic, linear planning suffers from three key issues: (1) visual-semantic misalignment across modalities, (2) long-context hallucinations from accumulated irrelevant history, and (3) brittle execution due to fixed, coarse task granularity that cannot adapt when tool capabilities are exceeded.

Method: TopoAgent operates through three core mechanisms: (1) a front-end decomposer that fractures complex scientific queries into visually-grounded atomic units; (2) organization of these atoms into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on inter-atom dependencies, ensuring strict context isolation so each reasoning step is shielded from irrelevant historical noise; and (3) adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically detects bottleneck nodes at runtime and splits them into finer-grained sub-atoms when the current granularity exceeds tool capability boundaries.

Result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, validating its effectiveness as a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

Conclusion: TopoAgent establishes that replacing linear reasoning trajectories with a self-evolving topological graph architecture — combining DAG-based context isolation with runtime adaptive fission — constitutes a superior paradigm for scientific reasoning, offering robustness, noise resistance, and self-correction capabilities absent in existing linear agent frameworks.

Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

</details>


### [171] [SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14661)
*Zhihan Jiang,Meng Li,Shenghao Liu,Keran Li,Ruiben Zhou,Xianjun Deng,Shuai Wang,Haipeng Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SmartRAG is a fully on-device framework for deploying LLM assistants on mobile devices, decomposing intelligence into four modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking). It features EvoNER for continual entity recognition and MRGraph for knowledge storage, enabling a 1.7B-parameter model to rival up to 18× larger models on multi-hop QA benchmarks while running entirely on smartphones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLMs as personal assistants on mobile devices requires privacy, low latency, and offline availability, but giant models exceed edge-hardware budgets. The authors argue that model compression alone is insufficient; instead, on-device intelligence must be decomposed into complementary functional roles to balance capability and computational cost.

Method: SmartRAG comprises four modules: (1) Perception, centered on EvoNER — a continually learnable NER that expands its label inventory via teacher-distilled updates without retraining the backbone LLM; (2) Memory, using MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph; (3) Focus, with a hybrid retrieval pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search; and (4) Thinking, where the on-device LLM is invoked only for labeling, planning, and answer synthesis. The backbone is a quantized 1.7B-parameter model.

Result: On four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA), SmartRAG achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18× larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency constraints.

Conclusion: Decomposing on-device intelligence into coordinated functional roles — rather than relying solely on model compression — enables small, quantized LLMs to deliver competitive multi-hop reasoning on mobile devices, preserving privacy, low latency, and offline operation.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

</details>


### [172] [Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14682)
*Harikrishnan P M,Goutham Vignesh,Ganesh Parab,Saisubramaniam Gopalakrishnan,Vishal Vaddina,Varun V,Rohit Agrawal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Perception-RFT introduces a GRPO-based RL framework for multimodal document QA that directly aligns visual features with structured grounding outputs, bypassing reasoning tokens. It finds that reasoning traces are suppressed during training at the 4B scale, yielding 60%+ inference token reduction and identifying a novel "Grounding Divergence" trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal document QA faces a bifurcation: SFT requires large annotated datasets and plateaus, while reasoning-centric RL inflates inference costs with verbose intermediate traces that provide no clear benefit. The authors aim to resolve whether explicit reasoning is necessary for visual grounding and to characterize the optimization dynamics of RL-based multimodal post-training.

Method: Perception-RFT applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, training the model to directly map visual features to structured grounding outputs without intermediate reasoning tokens. A reasoning variant is constructed under identical reward settings for controlled comparison. Analysis is conducted on Qwen3-VL-4B, examining SFT saturation, cold-start RL instability, and the trade-off dynamics using two OOD benchmarks (4,828 samples). An early SFT→RL transition strategy is also tested.

Result: Reasoning-enabled models suppress their traces during training and converge to direct perception-based policies, reducing inference token length by >60%. Reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability extend to the multimodal domain. A newly identified "Grounding Divergence" reveals a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL optimization. Early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

Conclusion: Explicit reasoning traces are unnecessary and counterproductive for multimodal visual grounding at the 4B scale. Direct perception-based RL (Perception-RFT) yields superior efficiency and performance. The discovered Grounding Divergence and data-efficient SFT→RL transition strategy offer practical insights for future multimodal post-training pipelines.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

</details>


### [173] [InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14683)
*Hao Yang,Yanyan Zhao,Kewei Zhao,Hongbo Zhang,Tian Zheng,Yusheng Liu,Xing Fu,Bichen Wang,Yu Zhang,Hao He,Zhen Wu,Xuda Zhi,Yongbo Huang,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InCarEmo is a multimodal dataset for in-cabin affective computing that integrates RGB/infrared video, audio, and dialogue text across diverse driving scenarios, supporting emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing in-cabin affective computing datasets are limited to visual modalities and lack conversational/linguistic cues, hindering comprehensive understanding of driver emotion and state. A multimodal dataset capturing vision, audio, and dialogue is needed.

Method: The authors collected scripted in-cabin scenarios under diverse lighting and driving conditions, capturing synchronized RGB video, infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text. They constructed both Chinese (original) and English (auxiliary) benchmarks and established a unified evaluation framework with unimodal and multimodal baselines, including modality-missing and noise-condition analyses.

Result: Multimodal fusion outperforms unimodal approaches across all three tasks. However, significant challenges persist under real-world noise and low-light conditions, as revealed by modality-missing and robustness analyses.

Conclusion: InCarEmo provides a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable in-cabin affective understanding. The dataset and benchmarks aim to advance safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction by enabling multimodal, human-centric emotion and state recognition.

Abstract: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

</details>


### [174] [AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14756)
*Zahratu Shabrina,Muhammad Asa,Jin Rui,Lu Yin,Stephen Law*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) can classify building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from Google Street View images with ~70% accuracy, with Chain-of-Thought prompting yielding the most stable performance. AI focuses on visual indicators while human experts emphasize contextual/domain knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether Vision-Language Models can automate building-typology classification at scale from street-level imagery, a task traditionally requiring costly and time-consuming manual expert annotation.

Method: Multiple state-of-the-art VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) were prompted to infer three building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from GSV images. Different scaling strategies and prompting techniques were compared. VLM predictions were benchmarked against ground-truth labels from human experts (civil engineers and architects). Keyword probability analysis of AI-generated explanations was used to probe reasoning patterns and identify drivers of agreement/disagreement with experts.

Result: Chain-of-Thought prompting provided the most stable performance across models. VLMs achieved ~70% average accuracy in building-typology classification. AI reasoning predominantly relied on visual indicators, while human experts leveraged broader contextual cues and domain knowledge alongside visual signals.

Conclusion: VLMs show strong potential as scalable, complementary tools for urban analysis, particularly in pattern recognition and object identification tasks. They can serve as collaborative assistants to human experts rather than replacements, with their visual reasoning strengths complementing human contextual knowledge.

Abstract: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

</details>


### [175] [Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14782)
*Rachel Adams,Fola Adeleke,Ayantola Alayande,Selamawit Engida Abdella,Ana Florido,Nicolás Grossman,Leah Junck*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GIRAI 2026 evaluates 135 countries on responsible AI governance using 38 indicators. While 126 countries now have some AI policy, frameworks remain largely non-binding—especially in the Global South (78% vs 42% in the Global North). Only 18% of countries mandate public disclosure of government algorithms, and 35 countries show credible evidence of deploying unacceptable-risk AI systems. The findings call for a shift from policy adoption to enforceable, rights-based protections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether countries' commitments to responsible AI translate into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms—rather than remaining hollow framework adoptions—grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI.

Method: GIRAI 2026 employs a global network of 135 country-level researchers who collected and assessed 68,138 data points across 38 indicators organized into three pillars: (1) government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), (2) civil society engagement (5), and (3) enabling conditions (15), along with documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI. Data spans November 2023 to September 2025, with countries ranked on a 0–100 composite score.

Result: Key findings: (1) 126 of 135 countries have at least one AI policy or initiative, signaling expanding governance. (2) Global South countries contributed 203 of 306 new indicator cases since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks are non-binding vs. 42% in the Global North. (3) Transparency and Explainability is the strongest-performing indicator (58% of countries have some framework), but only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. (4) Credible evidence of government-deployed unacceptable-risk AI was found in 35 countries.

Conclusion: Responsible AI governance must evolve beyond symbolic framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, adequately resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress mechanisms to close the gap between stated commitments and meaningful protections.

Abstract: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

</details>


### [176] [Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14791)
*Darius Lim,Nathan Leow,Xin Wei Chia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores using transcoders (specifically per-layer transcoders, PLTs) to analyze deceptive behavior in the Qwen3-4B language model. By constructing attribution graphs and performing feature steering, the authors identify deception-related features that causally influence deceptive outputs, demonstrating that transcoders are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability and early detection of malicious behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deceptive behavior in language models presents significant safety and security risks. Understanding the internal mechanisms underlying such behavior through mechanistic interpretability is crucial for monitoring and mitigating these risks. Transcoders offer a promising circuit-level analysis framework, but their application to deception detection remains underexplored.

Method: The authors apply pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) to a Qwen3-4B model. They construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, enabling circuit-level analysis. Feature steering and circuit analysis are then used to identify and validate a dictionary of deception-related features by observing predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive model responses.

Result: A dictionary of deception-related features was identified. These features exert stronger causal influence on deceptive outputs and produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses when steered, confirming that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms rather than superficial patterns.

Conclusion: Transcoders, particularly PLTs, are effective tools for circuit-level mechanistic interpretability of deceptive behaviors. The findings support the use of transcoder-based monitoring for early detection of security vulnerabilities and malicious behaviors in language models.

Abstract: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

</details>


### [177] [CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14800)
*Miguel Lopez-Duran,Julian Fierrez,Aythami Morales,Daniel DeAlcala,Gonzalo Mancera,Javier Irigoyen,Ruben Tolosana,Oscar Delgado,Francisco Jurado,Alvaro Ortigosa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrimeNER Demo is an AI platform for extracting crime-related entities from documents using pretrained NER models with two granularity levels, supporting user-provided fine-tuning data. It targets researchers and law enforcement with an end-to-end annotation pipeline, publicly available on GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of accessible, domain-specific NER tools tailored to crime-related information extraction. The authors aim to promote crime-domain NER research and provide a practical, customizable tool for both researchers and law enforcement agencies to automatically extract structured crime information from unstructured documents.

Method: The platform provides pretrained NER models trained on the CrimeNER database with two levels of entity granularity. It offers a fine-tuning capability allowing users to upload their own annotated data for domain-specific adaptation. An automatic pipeline handles end-to-end extraction and annotation of crime entities from input documents.

Result: The resulting system is a publicly available demo platform (on GitHub) that includes pretrained crime-domain NER models, a fine-tuning interface for custom user data, and an automated extraction/annotation pipeline, accompanied by a tutorial and video demonstration.

Conclusion: CrimeNER Demo successfully delivers a flexible, practical NER tool for the crime domain, lowering the barrier to entry for crime-related information extraction and encouraging further research through its open, customizable architecture.

Abstract: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

</details>


### [178] [Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14886)
*Chien-Liang Liu,Tsao-Lun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAPTOR introduces a self-supervised pretraining method that learns reachability estimates between entities to guide RL-based multi-hop reasoning on temporal knowledge graphs, improving both training efficiency and accuracy over sparse-reward RL baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-based multi-hop TKG reasoning suffers from sparse rewards and inefficient exploration due to a vast, time-evolving action space. This hinders both training efficiency and final predictive performance.

Method: RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration) is a self-supervised pretraining framework that trains an agent to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to a target entity. This injects a reachability-aware inductive bias, reducing wasteful exploration and providing a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning.

Result: On ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets, RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines.

Conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning in TKG extrapolation, addressing core exploration inefficiencies through reachability-aware pretraining.

Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

</details>


### [179] [Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14957)
*Besim Shala,Peter Mandl,Andreas Humpe,Martin Häusl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-based system for detecting online firestorms on Reddit, operating in two modes: retrospective thread classification and sequential early warning using sliding windows. The system estimates negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count, achieving strong classification performance and high-recall early detection after only a few comments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing firestorm detectors rely on volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features, which only indirectly capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussions. There is a need for approaches that directly model semantic context in thread dynamics for more accurate and timely detection.

Method: A prompt-engineered LLM operates in two modes: (1) a retrospective global mode that classifies complete Reddit threads by aggregating local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment; (2) an early warning mode that processes threads sequentially using a sliding window calibrated against thresholds, where the LLM estimates three indicators — negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count — to trigger alerts.

Result: On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance. The early warning mode attains high recall and successfully detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors.

Conclusion: LLMs are effective not only for static, retrospective classification but also as repeated, context-aware estimators for real-time monitoring of social media discourse, enabling timely intervention in emerging firestorms.

Abstract: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

</details>


### [180] [Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14970)
*Paul Darm,Cem Alpturk,Kenneth Ulrich,William Duncan,Ali Anwar,Annalisa Riccardi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper combines Implicit Function Theorem-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP and LLMs to generate real-time natural language explanations for industrial process optimisation, achieving >0.99 correlation with KernelSHAP at 40× speedup on an HPGR control problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A trust gap exists between optimisation algorithm designers and plant operators who must act on recommendations. While SHAP has improved interpretability for ML predictions, optimisation outputs lack similarly effective explanation methods. Operators need real-time, understandable explanations to trust and act on automated optimisation recommendations.

Method: The approach integrates three components: (1) Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) applied to optimality conditions to compute exact parameter sensitivities ∂p*/∂x analytically, (2) GradientSHAP using these sensitivities for efficient feature attribution, and (3) Large Language Model-based narrative generation converting SHAP attributions into natural language explanations tailored for operators.

Result: On an industrial HPGR control optimisation problem with 22 features, the IFT-based GradientSHAP achieves SHAP attributions with >0.99 correlation compared to KernelSHAP while providing over 40× speedup, enabling real-time explanation generation. The approach was validated on industrial scenarios with domain expert feedback.

Conclusion: IFT-based sensitivity analysis combined with SHAP and LLM narrative generation provides a practical, real-time explainability solution for industrial optimisation, bridging the trust gap between automated systems and human operators without sacrificing attribution fidelity.

Abstract: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

</details>


### [181] [CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14975)
*Yuan Gao,Wenjun Yu,Jun Jiang,Yunfan Li,Xinyu Guo,Shugong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CFM-Bench is a unified, multi-domain, multi-task benchmark for channel foundation models that standardizes evaluation across diverse channel configurations, downstream tasks, and data partitions, enabling fair comparison of CFM transferability while prohibiting pretraining on benchmark splits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current CFM evaluations are fragmented: each study uses custom data, configurations, partitions, and metrics, making it impossible to rank CFMs or compare them fairly against task-specific baselines. A standardized benchmark is needed to unify evaluation and isolate the effect of pretrained channel representations.

Method: The authors introduce CFM-Bench, which curates six channel configurations (3GPP statistical simulation, two ray-tracing pipelines, industrial/aerial measurements, and vehicular multimodal simulation). Data partitions isolate complete trajectories, sessions, links, or spatial regions. No benchmark split may be used for pretraining; the training split is exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. All development data must be disclosed, and test units are prohibited during training. Six task groups span three CFM application dimensions: PHY channel intelligence, RAN decision intelligence, and ISAC.

Result: CFM-Bench provides a standardized evaluation substrate covering CSI feedback, channel extrapolation (frequency and temporal), propagation-state classification, beam prediction (current and future), and localization (single-frame and temporal), enabling reproducible comparison of channel representation transferability across models, domains, and tasks.

Conclusion: CFM-Bench fills a critical infrastructure gap in CFM research by decoupling pretraining from evaluation, standardizing multi-domain multi-task assessment, and enforcing strict data hygiene rules, thereby enabling rigorous, reproducible, and fair benchmarking of channel foundation models.

Abstract: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

</details>


### [182] [Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14984)
*Mahmoud Ibrahim,Bart Elen,Chang Sun,Gokhan Ertaylan,Michel Dumontier*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Synthetic data from a demographically-conditioned generative model can both mitigate training bias and reliably detect evaluation bias in medical image classifiers, particularly for minority subgroups where real test sets lack sufficient samples for statistically meaningful fairness audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fairness audits of medical image classifiers suffer from a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in test sets are too small to produce tight confidence intervals, making it impossible to reliably detect the very biases audits aim to uncover. The authors propose leveraging synthetic data to address both sides of this problem.

Method: Using a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator conditioned on demographic attributes, the authors generate synthetic chest CT images for COVID-19 classification. For mitigation, they compare sequential pretraining (synthetic pretraining → real fine-tuning) against joint augmentation (mixing synthetic and real data). For detection, they compare per-subgroup performance estimates from synthetic test cohorts against a well-powered real oracle using Spearman rank correlation on MCC and Recall across five minority cohorts and five classifier seeds.

Result: For mitigation, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, achieving better than full-real baseline performance at approximately 100× real-data efficiency. For detection, the synthetic estimator achieves Spearman ρ = 1.00 on both MCC and Recall against the real oracle, and provides reliable per-cell estimates precisely where the small real test set runs out of samples.
