Conclusion: A demographically-conditioned synthetic generator serves a dual purpose: it is most effective as a pretraining prior for bias mitigation and as a reliable proxy for bias detection in data-scarce minority subgroups—exactly the cells fairness audits target.

Abstract: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

</details>


### [183] [Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14998)
*Jean-Paul Van Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes flipping the typical AI ethics question: instead of how humans should treat ASI, it explores how future sentient ASI might morally evaluate humanity, and suggests that current technical design choices and human moral behavior will shape humanity's standing in a post-ASI world.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional AI ethics focuses on human responsibilities toward AI systems. The authors argue this is one-directional and overlooks a critical long-term concern: that sentient ASI will eventually form its own moral judgments about humans, and the conditions shaping those judgments are being set now.

Method: The paper employs a conceptual/philosophical inversion approach — reframing the ethical relationship between humans and ASI by placing ASI in the position of moral agent and humanity as the moral patient. It then proposes a preliminary framework of post-human moral principles that might govern sentient ASI behavior.

Result: The analysis yields a preliminary set of post-human moral principles for ASI, and identifies that technical design choices, humanity's collective moral conduct, and conceptions of human identity are all factors that could influence how a future sentient ASI evaluates and treats humanity.

Conclusion: Humanity should not only focus on controlling or aligning ASI, but also consider how to act in ways that would earn favorable moral consideration from a future sentient superintelligence. Design choices made today have long-term ethical consequences for humanity's standing.

Abstract: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

</details>


### [184] [SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15003)
*Riccardo Curcio,Toni Mancini,Enrico Tronci*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel methodology combining Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking (SMC-ES) to synthesize control policies that come with formal probabilistic guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness — with confidence 1−δ, failure probability ≤ ε.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement Learning produces performant controllers for cyber-physical systems but lacks formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. Existing safe RL approaches often provide heuristic rather than provable assurances.

Method: SMC-ES integrates Evolutionary Strategies for policy optimization with Statistical Model Checking for verification. Given desired properties, confidence δ, and allowable failure probability ε, it uses simulation-based statistical verification to produce a policy accompanied by a Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)-style certificate bounding violation probability.

Result: Evaluated on Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium continuous control tasks, SMC-ES achieves competitive performance against model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines while delivering formal guarantees, at the cost of a sustainable increase in computation.

Conclusion: The SMC-ES framework demonstrates that formal performance, safety, and robustness guarantees can be practically integrated into learning-based policy synthesis for cyber-physical systems, bridging the gap between high-performing controllers and verifiable safety.

Abstract: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

</details>


### [185] [Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15027)
*Sofi Gjing Jovanovska,Kuntal Ghosh,Daniel Muhu Njenga,Ahmed Mufassir,Shadan Sadeghian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ArtSplit is a provotype that quantifies human and AI contributions across creative workflow stages to elicit artists' reflections on ownership attribution. The study finds that quantification fails to capture artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, challenging the techno-solutionist impulse to reduce a historically and socially situated concept like ownership to a measurable metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The integration of AI in creative work has created tensions around ownership, with no clear consensus on how to define or attribute it when human and AI contributions are interwoven. The authors sought to provoke critical reflection on these tensions rather than resolve them.

Method: The authors designed ArtSplit, a provotype — a provocative prototype — that explicitly quantifies the relative contributions of human and AI across different stages of the creative workflow. This artifact was then used to elicit artists' responses and reflect on the concept of attributing ownership through measurable actions.

Result: Quantification of contributions fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency. Efforts to measure ownership risk undermining long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work.

Conclusion: The paper critiques the impulse to transform ownership — a historically and socially situated relation — into a purely technical problem. Attributing ownership through quantitative metrics is incompatible with how artists conceptualize and experience creative practice.

Abstract: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

</details>


### [186] [BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15079)
*Haoxuan Li,Tianci Gao,Jianhe Li,Yang Fan,Runze Shi,Weiran Wang,Tianxiang Zhao,Zezhao Wu,Xiaoyang Jiang,Qihui Zhang,Jia Li,Xiao Xiao,Kai Du,Xiaoxuan Jia,Chao Xie,Lu Mi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BrainPilot is a fully open-source multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research by using a PI agent to coordinate specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge, with traceable logs, fabrication checking, and performance comparable to state-of-the-art frameworks at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few intervention points for experts. These failures are especially costly in brain science where conclusions inform downstream claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment.

Method: BrainPilot uses a principal investigator (PI) agent to coordinate specialist agents grounded in a unified knowledge base (7,233 indexed items) and a skill library (72 reusable methodology units across 7 domains). Every major step is recorded in a Graph of Trace for auditability. An Auditor agent performs fabrication checking. Evaluation uses three tasks from Agents' Last Exam, a new BrainPilotBench-v0 benchmark, and end-to-end case studies.

Result: BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks while incurring lower costs.

Conclusion: BrainPilot demonstrates that a domain-grounded, auditable multi-agent system can accelerate brain science research reliably and cost-effectively, offering traceable, verifiable workflows suitable for high-stakes scientific contexts.

Abstract: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

</details>


### [187] [Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15105)
*Vladimir Fedosov,Aleksandr Sazhin,Artemiy Grinenko,Frank Woernle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) combined with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage to enable parameter-efficient fine-tuning with long training sequences. Using 4-bit QLoRA on Qwen3-8B, HGA achieves 16,384-token training on a 16 GB GPU (vs. 2,048 for dense attention) with comparable perplexity. The same adapter can handle 131,072 tokens at evaluation, with throughput advantages over dense attention that widen with context length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like QLoRA reduce model and optimizer memory, but the quadratic cost of dense self-attention remains a bottleneck for long-sequence training. This limits the context length that can be used during fine-tuning on consumer-grade GPUs, creating a need for attention mechanisms that decouple memory footprint from sequence length while preserving model quality.

Method: The authors introduce Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA), which restricts gradient computation to an active segment in VRAM while detaching older key-value (KV) pairs into RAM or NVMe storage. For each query block, HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens rather than compressed summaries. This is paired with segment-wise backpropagation (processing the sequence in segments, only the current segment being differentiable) and tiered KV storage (VRAM → RAM → NVMe). Training uses 4-bit QLoRA on Qwen3-8B. At evaluation, dense attention is used for quality comparisons to ensure compatibility with standard generation frameworks, though HGA can also serve for retrieval and generation.

Result: On a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000: (1) Dense training fits 2,048 tokens but OOMs at 4,096; HGA reaches 16,384 tokens at 15.28 GB peak VRAM. (2) At evaluation, the HGA-trained adapter runs through 131,072 tokens. (3) At 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters achieve 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat on PG19 (vs. 2.9541 for the stock model). (4) HGA training is marginally faster at 2K (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K, suggesting a widening lead as context grows.

Conclusion: HGA enables training with 8× longer sequences than dense attention on the same GPU while maintaining comparable downstream quality. The approach decouples training memory from sequence length, shifting the practical limit to RAM/NVMe capacity. Throughput advantages over dense attention increase with context length, and the method remains compatible with standard dense-attention evaluation and generation pipelines.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

</details>


### [188] [Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15142)
*Yukuan Lu,Zaishuo Xia,Weyl Lu,Yubei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper isolates and evaluates learned world models from five MBRL agents on Atari Pong, revealing significant failures in closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL. The authors propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss on segmented concept regions, which improves performance but does not fully resolve all world-model bottlenecks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are typically evaluated only as components of full MBRL systems, obscuring their standalone quality. The authors aim to isolate and stress-test learned world models to understand their failure modes, particularly in modeling task-critical concepts like the ball in Pong.

Method: The authors reproduce five visual world-model agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) on Atari Pong. After training, they freeze the world models and apply two evaluation protocols: (1) closed-loop rollout diagnostics — a separately trained policy interacts with the frozen model and generated trajectories are inspected for visual/dynamical errors; (2) pixel-space zero-shot MBRL — a new policy is trained entirely inside the frozen model and tested in the real environment. They then propose CGSReg, an auxiliary reconstruction loss targeting pre-segmented concept regions (e.g., the ball) to regularize world-model learning.

Result: All five models exhibit clear rollout failures: ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions. In zero-shot MBRL, policies trained inside frozen models substantially underperform original MBRL pipelines. DreamerV3 suffers most, with mean return dropping from -5.5 to -20.9 (near Pong's minimum of -21). CGSReg improves closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, but effects are inconsistent across other models and metrics, indicating it does not resolve all bottlenecks.

Conclusion: World models learned by state-of-the-art MBRL agents contain significant modeling failures when evaluated in isolation. Targeting task-critical concepts via spatial regularization helps but is insufficient as a complete solution, highlighting the need for further research into world-model fidelity beyond aggregate agent performance.

Abstract: World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

</details>


### [189] [The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15164)
*Emmanuel Jeannot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This essay examines seven critical concerns arising from AI's transformation of scientific research from a craft model to an industrialized pipeline model, using the DOE's Genesis Mission as a case study, and frames these concerns not as arguments against AI-driven science but as necessary conditions for its responsible pursuit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The author is motivated by the fundamental shift occurring in scientific research — from a craft model where knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in individual researchers, to an industrialized pipeline model where these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised by AI. The DOE's Genesis Mission exemplifies this shift, but the implications extend far beyond any single program, raising urgent questions that demand scrutiny before the transformation becomes irreversible.

Method: This is a conceptual/analytical essay that identifies and systematically examines seven specific questions raised by the industrialization of research through AI. The method involves philosophical and sociological analysis of structural risks, drawing on the DOE's Genesis Mission as a concrete instantiation while abstracting to universal concerns applicable across scientific domains.

Result: The essay articulates seven structural concerns: (1) erosion of intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; (2) growing opacity of AI-generated theories; (3) collapse of peer evaluation under machine-generated output floods; (4) unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; (5) capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; (6) compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and (7) structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers.

Conclusion: The seven concerns identified do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science — its demonstrated potential is real and significant. Rather, they constitute the conditions that must be addressed for that potential to be responsibly pursued, framing responsible governance as a prerequisite rather than an obstacle.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research - not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science - whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

</details>


### [190] [MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15166)
*Goktug Ozkan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedFailBench is a clinician-built benchmark that categorizes medical AI errors by severity (1-5) and safety gate failure type, rather than just measuring answer correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks only assess whether models produce correct answers, failing to capture how and why safety boundaries are violated. There is a need for structured taxonomies of medical AI failures to improve safety evaluation.

Method: The authors constructed a synthetic benchmark of 44 clinician-reviewed cases with a dual annotation framework: a 5-level clinical severity rubric and a 6-category safety gate taxonomy (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The release includes an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs and a HuggingFace leaderboard.

Result: The current release (v0.2.1) delivers 44 annotated synthetic cases, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and a live leaderboard preview. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included in this version.

Conclusion: MedFailBench provides a complementary evaluation paradigm focused on safety gate failure analysis rather than accuracy. It is released under open licenses (Apache-2.0, CC-BY-4.0) with a Zenodo DOI for reproducibility.

Abstract: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

</details>


### [191] [Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15190)
*Han Jiang,Sunbeom Kwon,Jinwen Luo,Ziang Xiao,Susu Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how mismatches between AI benchmark data characteristics and standard IRT assumptions affect estimation reliability. Through 18,000 simulation conditions spanning six LLM benchmarks, three IRT models, and four estimators, it identifies regimes where IRT inferences about model rankings, performance, and item characteristics become unreliable, particularly when model sets are small or non-normally distributed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI benchmarks increasingly adopt IRT to estimate model capabilities and diagnose benchmark quality, but these benchmarks differ fundamentally from human testing contexts: fewer evaluated models, many more items, and non-normal capability distributions. Standard IRT tools were designed for the opposite regime, raising concerns about the validity of IRT-based claims in AI evaluation. The paper aims to systematically identify when IRT modeling reliably supports versus distorts benchmarking inferences.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale simulation study using item parameters and capability distributions from six real LLM benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag). They simulate response matrices under three IRT models (1PL/Rasch, 2PL, 3PL) and compare four estimation approaches: marginal maximum likelihood (MML), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), variational inference (VI), and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 conditions varying sample size, distribution shape, and model specification, they evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and reliability of inferences about rankings, predicted performance, and item parameters.

Result: Classical estimators (MML, MCMC) become computationally infeasible in large benchmark settings with many items. Scalable estimators (VI, neural) can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences when model sample sizes are small or capability distributions are skewed, clustered, or multimodal. The paper delineates specific sample size requirements and distributional conditions necessary for trustworthy IRT use in AI benchmarking.

Conclusion: IRT can be a powerful tool for AI benchmarking, but its reliability is contingent on adequate model sample sizes, appropriate estimator choice, and diagnostic checks for distributional assumptions. The paper provides practical guidance on when IRT inferences are trustworthy and when they risk distorting evaluation claims, urging caution in applying off-the-shelf IRT tools to AI benchmark data without regime-aware validation.

Abstract: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

</details>


### [192] [Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15193)
*Madhumitha Venkatesan,Shicheng Wen,Jiajing Guo,Jorge Piazentin Ono,Liu Ren,Dongyu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Plover is a plan-centric GUI automation system that makes autonomous agent plans visible and editable, enabling users to inspect, supervise, and correct automation behavior through localized interventions and natural-language guidance without losing prior progress.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous GUI agents operating in real-world environments often fail due to dynamic layouts and unexpected interface states, but their internal planning remains opaque, preventing users from inspecting or correcting behavior. There is a need for transparency and user controllability in vision-based GUI automation.

Method: Plover uses a planner–executor architecture that externalizes task plans as inspectable, revisable artifacts. Users can supervise execution, edit plans locally, provide natural-language guidance, and make screenshot-grounded interventions. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design, followed by benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow evaluations.

Result: Many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized. Explicit replanning enhances transparency, controllability, and adaptability of GUI automation.

Conclusion: Externalizing plans and supporting explicit replanning makes vision-based GUI automation more transparent and user-controllable, enabling effective repair of agent failures through localized, plan-level interventions.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

</details>


### [193] [AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15247)
*Moein Taherinezhad,Sebastian Maier,Gerardo Vitagliano,Francesco Pierri,Stefan Feuerriegel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates the entire meta-analysis pipeline — from literature search and screening to effect size computation and random-effects meta-analysis — producing PRISMA-aligned reports with pooled estimates closely matching expert-conducted meta-analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis (meta-analysis) is essential for translating primary research into reliable knowledge, yet remains largely manual, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Automating this process would accelerate evidence-based decision-making across science, medicine, education, and policy.

Method: AutoSynthesis is a multi-agent system that takes a natural-language research question and sequentially: (1) formulates a search strategy, (2) retrieves scientific literature, (3) screens candidate studies, (4) assesses full-text eligibility, (5) extracts quantitative statistics, (6) computes standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g), and (7) performs random-effects meta-analysis. It also supports heterogeneity analysis (moderator effects) and risk-of-bias assessment, outputting a transparent PRISMA-compliant report.

Result: In application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates (Hedges' g) closely matched those of expert-conducted meta-analyses, demonstrating strong agreement with manual evidence synthesis.

Conclusion: AutoSynthesis demonstrates that fully automated quantitative evidence synthesis is feasible and scalable, offering a tool that can support evidence-based decision-making across diverse disciplines while maintaining transparency through PRISMA-aligned reporting.

Abstract: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

</details>


### [194] [Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15267)
*Victoria Graf,Hannaneh Hajishirzi,Noah A. Smith,David Kohlbrenner,Kyle Lo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper explores poisoning attacks on language model pretraining data via public web discussion interfaces, introducing HalfLife, a novel method to estimate whether adversarial content survives web crawling and data curation pipelines, revealing third-party webpage content as a viable attack vector.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on pretraining data poisoning relied on controlled sources like Wikipedia and ignored real-world complexities: the massive scale/heterogeneity of web-crawled corpora and the filtering effects of data curation pipelines. The authors aim to demonstrate poisoning feasibility in realistic, web-scale settings.

Method: The authors exploit public discussion interfaces (e.g., comment sections on the web) as a content injection mechanism. They introduce HalfLife, an analysis framework for estimating the probability that adversarially injected content persists through web crawling and data curation stages to end up in final pretraining datasets.

Result: The analysis shows that poisoning web-scale pretraining corpora via open discussion interfaces is feasible. HalfLife reveals that a non-trivial portion of injected adversarial content can survive crawling and curation, establishing third-party webpage content as a practical attack vector for LM pretraining.

Conclusion: Estimating poison inclusion rates is critical for understanding pretraining data vulnerabilities. Third-party content injection through public web interfaces represents a realistic and concerning threat vector for compromising language model pretraining at scale.

Abstract: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [195] [Position: Explainability Research Must Prioritize Foundations over Ad-hoc Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14123)
*Michal Moshkovitz,Suraj Srinivas,Lesia Semenova,Nave Frost,Cyrus Rashtchian,Valentyn Boreiko,Shichang Zhang,Himabindu Lakkaraju,Cynthia Rudin,Jennifer Wortman Vaughan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: XAI research suffers from a fundamental gap: explanations are rarely integrated into real-world workflows. This position paper argues the field must shift from ad-hoc methods to addressing foundational challenges like unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation, and missing feedback pipelines, supporting this via literature analysis and practitioner surveys, and concludes with an action-oriented checklist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the proliferation of XAI techniques, explanations are routinely generated and discarded without influencing real-world decision-making. This reflects deeper structural failures: no established methodologies exist for integrating explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems. The authors aim to diagnose why cumulative progress remains limited and to redirect the community toward foundational clarity.

Method: This is a position paper employing two empirical pillars: (1) an analysis of recent papers from ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR to identify recurring methodological shortcomings in XAI research, and (2) a survey of XAI practitioners to capture real-world perspectives on explanation utility and integration barriers. These are synthesized to support the central argument and inform a prescriptive checklist.

Result: The analysis of top-tier venue publications and practitioner survey responses reveals persistent, recurring issues: unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation objectives, and a systemic absence of pipelines that enable explanation-driven feedback loops. These structural deficiencies, rather than a lack of technical methods, are identified as the primary bottlenecks limiting XAI's real-world impact.

Conclusion: The ML community must pivot from developing ad-hoc XAI methods to tackling foundational and structural challenges. The authors propose a practical checklist to guide the field toward human-centered, action-oriented explanation systems, emphasizing problem formulation clarity and feedback integration as prerequisites for building actionable, explanation-driven AI.

Abstract: Despite the proliferation of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques -- from feature attributions to sparse autoencoders -- explanations rarely influence real-world workflows. In practice, they are often generated and discarded without guiding meaningful action. This gap reflects foundational shortcomings: research has not yet established methodologies for integrating explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems. This position paper argues that the machine learning community must pivot from ad-hoc XAI methods toward addressing foundational & structural challenges, including unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation objectives, and the absence of pipelines for explanation-driven feedback. We support this claim through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of XAI practitioners, revealing recurring issues that limit cumulative progress. We conclude by outlining a practical checklist designed to shift XAI toward a more human-centered, action-oriented paradigm. By emphasizing foundational clarity over the development of ad-hoc methods, we hope to provide a roadmap for integrating explanations into actionable, feedback-driven AI systems.

</details>


### [196] [CARPRT: Class-Aware Zero-Shot Prompt Reweighting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14125)
*Ruijiang Dong,Zesheng Ye,Jianzhong Qi,Lei Feng,Feng Liu,Gang Niu,Masashi Sugiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CARPRT introduces class-aware prompt reweighting for zero-shot VLM classification, assigning per-class weights to prompts instead of using a single global weighting vector. It estimates class-specific prompt relevance in a training-free manner by averaging image-text scores over predicted instances, then normalizes these to derive weights, outperforming class-independent methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt ensembling methods assign a single weighting vector shared across all classes, implicitly assuming prompts are conditionally independent of classes. This assumption fails in practice — e.g., "an aerial view of" suits "airport" but not "apple". The resulting mismatch limits zero-shot classification accuracy.

Method: CARPRT is a training-free, class-aware reweighting scheme. For each class label and each prompt, it computes class-specific relevance by averaging image-text similarity scores over images predicted to belong to that class under that prompt. These relevance estimates are then normalized to produce per-class weighting vectors, enabling class-conditional prompt aggregation.

Result: Evaluations on standard image classification benchmarks demonstrate that CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent prompt reweighting methods, validating the importance of modeling prompt-class dependencies.

Conclusion: Modeling prompt-class dependencies via class-aware reweighting is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and benefits broader VLM-based applications relying on prompt ensembling.

Abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot image classification by computing the similarity score between an image and textual descriptions, typically formed by inserting a class label (e.g., "cat") into a prompt (e.g., "a photo of a"). Since the score for a given image-class pair is sensitive to the choice of prompt, existing studies ensemble multiple prompts using a weighting vector to aggregate scores across different prompts. Yet, in current strategies, the weighting vector assigned to each prompt is shared across all classes, implicitly assuming that prompts are conditionally independent of classes, which often does not hold in practice, as a prompt like "an aerial view of" might be apt for "airport" but ill-suited for "apple". To address this, we propose class-aware zero-shot prompt reweighting (CARPRT). This scoring scheme adjusts the weighting vector for each class label by capturing the class-specific relevance of different prompts in a training-free manner. For each class label and every available prompt, we quantify their class-specific relevance by averaging image-text relevance scores over images predicted to that class under the given prompt. These estimates are then normalized to derive class-specific weights. Evaluations on standard image classification benchmarks show that CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent reweighting methods, confirming that modeling prompt-class dependencies is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and even broader VLM-based application settings that rely on prompt ensembling. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/CARPRT.

</details>


### [197] [Explainable Geospatial AI for Satellite Ground Station Siting Using LiDAR-Derived Terrain Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14127)
*Shohini Sarkar,Smithi Mahendran,Rishi Chudasama,Varun Mannam,Arav Luthra,Yuvraj Rekhi,Vivek Nadig,Arsh Goenka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning framework using LightGBM and open geospatial data predicts representative clutter height (RCH) with MAE of 1.79m and R²=0.765, reducing error by over 60% compared to the ITU-R P.452-18 baseline. SHAP analysis confirms physical plausibility, with tree canopy cover and land-cover semantics as top predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ITU-R P.452-18 practice assigns fixed clutter heights by land-use class, ignoring within-class variability. This leads to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for low Earth orbit (LEO) ground station siting and spectrum coordination. A globally deployable, data-driven alternative is needed.

Method: The authors define RCH as the robust 75th percentile clutter height statistic, use LiDAR-derived labels from the USGS 3D Elevation Program, and assemble inference-time features from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. Multiple regressors are evaluated; LightGBM is selected for accuracy, efficiency, and SHAP compatibility. Validation includes meter-scale error, tolerance bands, over/under-estimation tails, ITU regime agreement, and international land-cover-matched testing.

Result: The LightGBM model achieves MAE of 1.79m and R²=0.765, a >60% absolute error reduction versus ITU baseline. SHAP analysis identifies tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance as dominant predictors. Ablation studies (non-forest, segmentation-derived features) and international validation confirm robustness and global deployability.

Conclusion: Open geospatial data combined with interpretable ML can substantially improve clutter height modeling at global scale without sacrificing physical plausibility or deployability, offering a practical upgrade over static ITU land-use class assignments for RF planning and spectrum coordination.

Abstract: Representative clutter height (RCH) is a key parameter in radio propagation and interference analysis because it captures the dominant height of local obstructions that drive terminal clutter loss. Current practice often relies on fixed clutter heights assigned to land use classes in Recommendation ITU-R P.452-18, but this misses within class variation and can lead to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for low Earth orbit ground station siting and spectrum coordination. We present an interpretable, globally deployable machine learning framework for predicting RCH from open geospatial data. The model is trained using LiDAR derived labels from the U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program and inference time features from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. We define RCH using a robust 75th percentile clutter height statistic, evaluate multiple regressors, and select LightGBM for its accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility with feature attribution analysis. The final model achieves a mean absolute error of 1.79m and an R^2=0.765, reducing absolute error by more than 60% relative to the ITU baseline. Beyond aggregate fit, we evaluate domain facing criteria relevant to RF planning, including meter scale error, tolerance band accuracy, over and under estimation tails, agreement with ITU clutter height regimes, and SHAP-based physical plausibility. SHAP identifies tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance as the most influential predictors. Studies on segmentation derived features, non-forest ablations, and land-cover matched international validation show that open geospatial data can improve clutter modeling at scale without sacrificing interpretability or deployability.

</details>


### [198] [Certified Domain Consistency for Multi-Domain Retrieval: Label-Free Per-Domain Contamination Control with Conformal Risk Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14157)
*Jayakumar Manoharan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: C3R is a drop-in control layer that certifies per-domain contamination budgets in multi-domain retrieval by leveraging inferred domain posteriors and risk-controlling prediction sets, guaranteeing reduced contamination rather than merely bounding it, with validated stability across resampled calibrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-domain retrieval systems return relevant but wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics fail to detect. Conformal risk control provides only marginal bounds that under-cover the worst domains. There is a need for domain-aware contamination control with finite-sample guarantees that abstains when constraints are infeasible rather than silently violating them.

Method: C3R uses a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets. From an inferred domain posterior (no query-time labels), it certifies a per-domain contamination budget. The core transfer bound crosses from inferred to true domains with fully estimable slack, supports heterogeneous budgets, and inverts for deployment. Population validity is established via this bound plus controlled simulation.

Result: Across 1,000 resampled calibrations, the C3R certificate never violates (stability result), while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw. Soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds including public federal regulations. An LLM-judged probe shows wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control.

Conclusion: C3R provides a practical, frozen-stack, reranker-agnostic control layer that certifies domain-level contamination with finite-sample guarantees. It reliably abstains when constraints are infeasible and consistently outperforms marginal control methods, with strong replication across diverse testbeds.

Abstract: Retrieval over corpora that mix several domains often returns relevant but wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics miss and that conformal risk control bounds only marginally, under-covering the worst domains. This work introduces C3R, a drop-in control layer that, from an inferred domain posterior and no query-time label, certifies a per-domain contamination budget where feasible and otherwise abstains rather than silently violating; on the hardest domains it guarantees a reduction, not a tight bound. The core is a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets, whose finite-sample transfer bound crosses from the inferred to the true domain with fully estimable slack, supports heterogeneous budgets, and inverts for deployment. Population validity rests on this bound and a controlled simulation; across a thousand resampled calibrations the certificate never violates (a stability result) while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw, and soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds including an independent one from public federal regulations, and an LLM-judged downstream probe indicates wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control. The layer is frozen-stack and reranker-agnostic.

</details>


### [199] [QFireNet: A Quantum-Enhanced U-Net for Wildfire Segmentation from Sentinel-2 Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14160)
*Jaiman Munshi,Tanvi Tewary,Sawyer Bloom,Aidan Chu,Chetan Maviti,Kyon Winston-Bey,Harshit Badjatia,Farhan Kittur,Vardhan Madhavarapu,Varun Kota,Joshua Kwon,Nazia Rangwala-Vohra,Franz Klein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A quantum-hybrid U-Net using variational quantum circuits (QuFeX, QB-Net) in the bottleneck outperforms classical U-Net for wildfire satellite image segmentation; data mixing eliminates domain shift, significantly boosting performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is challenging due to class imbalance, high-dimensional spectral features, and atmospheric interference. The authors aim to leverage quantum machine learning to better model the complex spectral feature space than classical methods alone.

Method: The authors inject variational quantum circuits (QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes) into the bottleneck of a U-Net architecture for semantic segmentation of the Sen2Fire dataset. They compare against a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and explore classical enhancements: parameter compression, alternative loss functions, and uniform data mixing. Cross-dataset validation is performed on the CaBuAr dataset.

Result: Under matched conditions, QB-Net (F1=31.18) and QuFeX (F1=30.79) outperformed classical U-Net (F1=28.71). Classical FPN achieved 31.13. Data mixing removed domain shift between geographically-separated train/test sets, boosting FPN F1 to 39.76. Architecture generalizability was validated on CaBuAr.

Conclusion: Quantum machine learning shows potential advantage for wildfire image segmentation. Data mixing is critical for mitigating domain shift. Further experiments are needed to validate and extend these findings.

Abstract: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is a semantic image segmentation problem that has proven to be difficult due to challenges such as class imbalance, feature complexity, and atmospheric interference. In this paper, we build on the foundational U-Net image segmentation model to develop a quantum-hybrid solution in hopes of more effectively modeling the high-dimensional spectral feature space of the Sen2Fire dataset. We inject a variational quantum circuit in the bottleneck portion of U-Net, specifically the QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes. We test a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) for further comparative analysis of the model, and we also explore classical improvements to the U-Net model and its training process, including a compression of parameters, alternative loss functions, and uniform mixing of input data. Our primary finding is that under matched conditions, both QB-Net (with an $F_1$ score of 31.18) and QuFeX ($F_1 = 30.79$) outperformed the classical U-Net baseline results ($F_1 = 28.71$). Additionally, the classical FPN achieved a comparable score of 31.13. A crucial finding was that data mixing removed a significant domain shift between the geographically-separated train and test sets, which boosted the classical FPN $F_1$ score to 39.76. We validate the architecture's robustness and generalizability to the wildfire detection problem via cross-dataset transfer on the California Burned Areas (CaBuAr) dataset. Overall, we find that quantum machine learning has potential to provide an advantage in the problem of wildfire image segmentation, and further experiments will continue to validate and expand upon this finding.

</details>


### [200] [A Temporal Machine Learning-Based Time-to-Event Model for Predicting ALS Progression and Healthcare Utilization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14190)
*Zongliang Yue,Qi Li,Terry Heiman-Patterson,Frank Bearoff,Zhaohui Qin,Huanmei Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A digital-twin-inspired framework integrating ALSFRS-R trajectories with survival modeling enables individualized prediction of functional decline and wheelchair-free survival in ALS, with lower limb function emerging as the strongest predictor of earlier wheelchair use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ALS is a progressive, heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease where predicting clinically meaningful milestones like assistive device use remains challenging. There is a need for individualized, time-to-event prediction tools to support proactive care planning.

Method: The authors constructed a harmonized longitudinal dataset integrating diagnosis records, ALSFRS-R assessments, activities of daily living, and demographics. Correlation-based clustering identified coherent functional domains (bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, respiratory). Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) characterized nonlinear domain-specific decline. A temporal machine learning model predicted longitudinal functional decline and stage-dependent progression. Cox proportional hazards modeling identified key predictors of wheelchair access. Finally, a digital-twin-inspired temporal ML-based time-to-event (TTE) model generated individualized survival curves for dynamic wheelchair-free survival prediction.

Result: Lower limb function — particularly walking and stair climbing — emerged as the strongest predictor of earlier wheelchair access. The TTE framework successfully generates individualized survival curves and dynamically predicts wheelchair-free survival.

Conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, interpretable, and clinically actionable approach for linking ALS progression with personalized decision support, with applications in proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine.

Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease in which predicting clinically meaningful milestones, such as assistive device use, remains challenging. We developed a time-to-event, digital-twin-inspired framework that integrates longitudinal ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) trajectories with survival modeling to support individualized prediction of functional decline and assistive device utilization. We constructed a harmonized longitudinal dataset by integrating diagnosis records, ALSFRS-R assessments, activities of daily living, and demographic information, followed by preprocessing to ensure data quality, temporal alignment, and cohort consistency. Correlation-based clustering identified coherent functional domains spanning bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, and respiratory systems. Generalized additive mixed models characterized nonlinear, domain-specific functional decline across all domains. In addition, a temporal machine learning model was developed to predict longitudinal functional decline and capture stage-dependent disease progression. Cox proportional hazards modeling further identified lower limb function, particularly walking and stair climbing, as the strongest predictors of earlier wheelchair access. Building on these results, we implemented a digital twin-inspired temporal machine learning-based time-to-event (TTE) model that generates individualized survival curves and dynamically predicts wheelchair-free survival. This framework provides a scalable, interpretable, and clinically actionable approach for linking ALS progression with personalized decision support, with applications in proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine.

</details>


### [201] [Branching Policy Optimization: Sandbox-Native Language Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14171)
*Bowei He,Yankai Chen,Xiaokun Zhang,Xue Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BPO (Branching Policy Optimization) exploits deterministic, snapshottable sandboxes by constructing a single shared-prefix tree instead of independent trajectories, achieving an unbiased advantage estimator with strictly lower variance. This yields 3.6–6.1 absolute point gains over GRPO/RLOO, halves gradient-norm variance, and matches baselines with 38% fewer updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL algorithms (PPO, RLOO, GRPO) for LLM agents treat each rollout independently from scratch, ignoring that executable sandboxes are deterministic, snapshottable, and resumable. This wastes compute on redundant shared prefixes and inflates variance in advantage estimation by using unrelated trajectories as baselines.

Method: BPO builds a single tree of N leaves with shared prefixes. It (i) adaptively snapshots the sandbox at high-entropy decision points along a backbone trajectory, (ii) forks K alternative actions at each branch point and rolls them out to termination, and (iii) computes per-step advantages using sibling returns (same-prefix comparisons), rather than comparing across independent prompts. The authors prove this sibling-based estimator is unbiased with variance reduced by the prefix-explained portion of return variance.

Result: On WebShop, ALFWorld, and SWE-bench Verified using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, BPO outperforms GRPO and RLOO by 3.6–6.1 absolute success points at matched compute, reduces gradient-norm variance by 50%, and reaches the best baseline performance with 38% fewer policy updates.

Conclusion: Sandbox-native branching is a superior rollout topology for LLM agent RL, providing a simple, principled mechanism to reduce variance and improve sample efficiency without additional model components.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as the dominant paradigm for training large language model (LLM) agents that interact with executable sandboxes. State-of-the-art algorithms such as PPO, RLOO, and GRPO inherit their rollout topology from RLHF: for each prompt, N independent trajectories are sampled from the initial state, and an advantage is computed by subtracting a group baseline. This design ignores a defining property of agent sandboxes. They are deterministic, snapshottable, and resumable from any intermediate state. We argue that this property enables a fundamentally different rollout topology: rather than N independent trees of depth T, one can construct a single tree of N leaves whose siblings share prefixes, and therefore share variance. We instantiate this idea as Branching Policy Optimization (BPO), a sandbox-native RL algorithm that (i) adaptively snapshots the sandbox at high-entropy decision points along a backbone trajectory, (ii) forks K alternative actions per branch point and rolls out each to termination, and (iii) computes per-step advantages from sibling returns rather than from independent prompts. We prove this estimator is unbiased and has strictly lower variance than the trajectory-level baseline, with the reduction equal to the prefix-explained portion of return variance. On WebShop, ALFWorld, and SWE-bench Verified with Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B backbones, BPO improves success by 3.6--6.1 absolute points over GRPO and RLOO at matched compute, halves gradient-norm variance, and matches the best baseline using 38% fewer policy updates.

</details>


### [202] [Long-term User Engagement Optimization through Model-agnostic Downstream Rewards Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14192)
*Dingsu Wang,Filip Ryzner,Kelly He,Armando Ordorica,David Woo,Aditya Mantha,Liyao Lu,Usha Amrutha Nookala,Haoran Guo,Jiacong He,Olafur Gudmundsson,Matt Chun,Krystal Benitez,Dhruvil Deven Badani,Yijie Dylan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Presents a model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user retention in recommender systems at Pinterest. The approach uses offline screening to identify early, retention-predictive session behaviors and derives reward signals from observed user action patterns, achieving consistent engagement and retention gains across multiple surfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly optimizing long-term user retention in recommender systems is challenging because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Existing solutions using sequential modeling or reinforcement learning require task-specific reward engineering, substantial computational cost, and surface-specific implementations that are difficult to generalize.

Method: The authors formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session-level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. They propose several model-agnostic downstream reward signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources, and discuss the engineering effort to productionize these reward derivations within ranking models.

Result: Online A/B experiments show consistent improvements in both engagement and retention-related metrics. The framework has been successfully deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces: Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.

Conclusion: The proposed unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework effectively bridges the gap between short-term behavioral signals and long-term retention optimization in large-scale industrial recommender systems, demonstrating both generalizability across surfaces and practical production feasibility.

Abstract: As recommender systems mature in the past few years, their optimization objectives have evolved from a primary focusing on short-term behavioral signals to a broader emphasis on long-term user engagement and retention. However, directly optimizing retention is difficult because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Prior work has addressed this challenge with sequential modeling and reinforcement learning, but these approaches typically require task specific reward engineering, substantial computational overhead, and surface specific implementations that are difficult to generalize. In this paper, we present a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems. First, we formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. We then propose several model-agnostic downstream rewards signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. We further discuss the engineering effort to productionize the proposed rewards derivations and challenges we faced when adding them to our ranking models. Online A/B experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics, and the framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.

</details>


### [203] [How Much of a 10-K Matters? Aggregation-Dependent Value of Full-Text versus Risk-Factor Sentiment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14174)
*Sanggyu Sean Choi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates financial sentiment extraction from 10-K filings (particularly Item 1A risk-factor sections) trained against both return and volatility labels at sector, portfolio, and firm levels. Key finding: full-filing text outperforms at aggregated levels, while Item 1A excels at the individual-firm level. A supervised approach consistently beats the Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline, which shows a counterintuitive negative correlation with price.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial sentiment analysis has historically focused on news text and return-based supervision, neglecting 10-K filings and volatility — the very target that risk disclosures are designed to inform. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically evaluating how sentiment extraction from regulatory filings performs across different aggregation levels, target labels (return vs. volatility), and document scopes (full 10-K vs. Item 1A).

Method: The authors extend a supervised lexicon-learning approach to 10-K filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 technology constituents (2006–2023, 1,383 filings). They train sentiment scores against both return and volatility labels at three aggregation levels: sector, portfolio, and individual firm. This yields twelve sentiment metrics, which are evaluated on classification accuracy, correlation with realised market outcomes, and qualitative lexical content. A Loughran-McDonald dictionary serves as the baseline.

Result: Full-filing text produces more accurate sentiment at sector and portfolio levels for both return and volatility targets. At the individual-firm level, the narrower Item 1A section outperforms — attributed to the interaction between document volume and available independent training signal. The Loughran-McDonald baseline is consistently and strongly negatively correlated with price at every aggregation level, highlighting the inadequacy of generic financial dictionaries for regulatory text and the value of supervised methods.

Conclusion: Design choices — aggregation level, target label, and document scope — critically affect sentiment extraction quality from regulatory filings. The findings establish the methodology for a subsequent, larger-scale, multi-source sentiment-generation system. The consistent failure of the Loughran-McDonald baseline reinforces that supervised approaches are necessary for domain-specific regulatory disclosure text.

Abstract: Financial sentiment extraction has largely relied on news text and supervised extraction against return labels alone, leaving 10-K filings -- and volatility, the target risk disclosure is arguably best suited to informing -- comparatively unexplored. We extend a supervised lexicon-learning approach to 10-K filings and their Item 1A risk-factor sections, training sentiment scores against both return and volatility labels at three levels of aggregation: sector, portfolio, and individual firm. Across 1,383 filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 technology constituents (2006--2023), we evaluate the resulting twelve sentiment metrics on classification accuracy, correlation with realised market outcomes, and qualitative lexical content. Full-filing text produces more accurate sentiment at the sector and portfolio level for both targets, but this reverses at the individual-firm level, where the narrower Item 1A section performs better -- an effect we attribute to the interaction between document volume and the amount of independent training signal available at each level of aggregation. A Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline is consistently, strongly negatively correlated with price at every level tested, underscoring the value of a supervised approach for regulatory disclosure text. These findings, and the design choices they motivate, establish the sentiment-generation methodology underlying a subsequent, larger-scale, multi-source system.

</details>


### [204] [Low-Latency Relay Selection in NR-V2X Vehicular Communications via Graph Isomorphism Networks with Edge Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14176)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Emiliano Pallotti,Simone Angelini,Pierpaolo Salvo,Paola Vocca*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an edge-aware Learning-to-Optimise framework using Graph Isomorphism Networks with Edge Features (GINE) for real-time relay selection in C-V2X networks. A hybrid GINE-Pruned MILP strategy bridges learned and exact optimisation, achieving near-MILP accuracy with inference under 5ms and solver runtimes below 30ms for >98% of instances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable low-latency uplink in dense urban C-V2X networks is challenged by fast channel variations and blockages. Multi-hop relaying can restore coverage, but optimal relay-link activation under radio, capacity, and routing constraints is NP-hard, and MILP solvers scale poorly with graph size, making them unsuitable for stringent NR-V2X latency budgets.

Method: Each V2X snapshot is modelled as a directed graph with node features (vehicle state, traffic demand) and edge features (radio-link capacity). An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay configurations to supervise a GINE model, enabling edge-level relay activation via a single forward pass. A hybrid GP-MILP strategy uses GINE predictions to prune the MILP search space, combining learned efficiency with exact optimisation guarantees.

Result: On a large-scale OSM-SUMO-GEMV² dataset, GINE achieves link-level accuracy of 0.9589 and F1-score of 0.9544. It delivers end-to-end connectivity gains over a 1-hop MILP baseline (up to 9.2% with four RSUs, 12% with two RSUs). Inference latency is bounded within 5ms. GP-MILP preserves MILP-equivalent objective values with solver runtimes below 30ms for >98% of instances.

Conclusion: The GINE-based Learning-to-Optimise framework enables real-time, near-optimal relay selection for C-V2X networks, with tightly bounded latency suitable for NR-V2X. The GP-MILP hybrid offers MILP-grade optimality at drastically reduced runtime, making exact optimisation feasible within vehicular communication latency constraints.

Abstract: Reliable, low-latency uplink connectivity is a key requirement for C-V2X networks in dense urban environments, where fast channel variations and blockages often degrade direct vehicle-to-infrastructure links. Multi-hop relaying can restore coverage, but relay-link activation under radio, capacity, and routing constraints results in an NP-hard optimisation problem, typically solved via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), whose runtime scales poorly with graph size. This paper introduces an edge-aware Learning-to-Optimise framework for real-time relay selection. Each V2X snapshot is modelled as a directed graph: node features encode vehicle state and traffic demand, while edge features capture radio-link capacity. An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay configurations that supervise a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE), enabling edge-level relay activation through a single forward pass, with tightly bounded inference latency. To bridge learning and exact optimisation, we also propose a hybrid GINE-Pruned MILP (GP-MILP) strategy in which GINE predictions prune the MILP search space. Experiments on a large-scale dataset generated via an OSM-SUMO-GEMV$^2$ pipeline show that GINE closely matches MILP decisions at the link level (accuracy 0.9589), F1-score (0.9544) on validation) and yields consistent end-to-end connectivity gains over a 1-hop MILP baseline (up to 9.2% with four RSUs and 12% with two RSUs). Inference latency remains tightly bounded, with all evaluated instances completing within 5~ms.
