Method: The study proceeds in two phases: (1) a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store exposing 5M+ users to 1–6 sponsored slots, measuring causal effects on revenue, conversions, and engagement at both aggregate and query-segment levels; (2) design and deployment of e-LAAL (exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load), which combines a model-free, query-level decision rule (LAAL) that updates recommendations based on recent outcomes with static exploration arms that maintain support for counterfactual benchmarking. A finite-time dynamic-regret bound is proved for the architecture. e-LAAL is deployed at platform scale (22.3M users, 77.6M searches).

Result: The experiment reveals that increasing ad load from 1 to 6 slots raises revenue up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These averages mask significant heterogeneity: high-ad-conversion queries yield large marginal revenue gains from extra slots, while low-conversion queries show little or negative marginal revenue. The trade-off also shifts within-query based on advertiser composition (e.g., brand-advertiser presence). In production deployment, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue-conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms both uniform and historical query-dependent static policies.

Conclusion: Ad-load optimization cannot be treated as a uniform, static problem. Query-level heterogeneity and temporal dynamics are first-order concerns. e-LAAL provides a theoretically grounded, practically deployable adaptive framework that demonstrably improves platform outcomes by tailoring ad load to query-specific conditions while maintaining rigorous counterfactual evaluation capability.

Abstract: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

</details>


### [227] [HyperShadow: A Benchmark for Detecting 3D Projections of Higher-Dimensional Spatial Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14419)
*Akshay Sasi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyperShadow is a benchmark dataset testing whether a 3D point cloud is a native 3D shape or the lower-dimensional "shadow" (projection) of a higher-dimensional (4D–6D) rigid object. Unlike intrinsic-dimension estimation, which fails (71–73% accuracy), a learned point network achieves 96.6% accuracy by detecting projection signatures like density folds and topology changes. A temporal track introduces a zero-parameter rigidity witness (Kabsch alignment residual) that separates classes at AUROC 0.982.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ML datasets label "4D" as 3D+time, but higher spatial dimensions remain unexplored. The authors aim to create a controlled instrument to study what observable statistics in 3D data can certify incompatibility with a purely 3D explanation — distinguishing native 3D objects from projections of higher-dimensional rigid bodies, a task that intrinsic-dimension estimators fundamentally cannot solve.

Method: The authors procedurally generate shadows by projecting rigid objects from R^N (N=4–6) into 3D, creating a benchmark with four corruption tiers. They compare standard intrinsic-dimension estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) against a lightweight 190k-parameter point-cloud network. For the temporal track, they introduce a zero-parameter rigidity witness: computing the residual of optimal rigid 3D alignment (Kabsch algorithm) between consecutive frames of rotating objects, which is zero for true 3D rigid motion but non-zero for shadows of higher-dimensional rotations.

Result: Intrinsic-dimension estimators achieve only 71–73% accuracy, confirming the task's distinctness. The 190k-parameter point network reaches 96.6% accuracy across all corruption tiers and generalizes at 79–91% to unseen object families. The Kabsch-based rigidity witness achieves AUROC 0.982 on the temporal track, providing a fully interpretable, zero-parameter classifier.

Conclusion: HyperShadow demonstrates that detecting higher-dimensional provenance in 3D data requires learning projection-specific signatures — density folds, filled volumes with characteristic radial profiles, and topology changes — rather than dimensionality estimation. The benchmark serves as a controlled, reproducible instrument for probing the observable limits of 3D explanations, with no claims about physical reality.

Abstract: Machine-learning datasets labelled "4D" universally denote three spatial dimensions plus time. We introduce HyperShadow, the first public benchmark in which the fourth, fifth, and sixth dimensions are spatial: the task is to decide whether a 3D point cloud is a native three-dimensional shape or the projection, the "shadow", of a rigid object living in R^N (N = 4-6). We show this task is fundamentally distinct from intrinsic-dimension estimation: a shadow is still at-most-3-dimensional data, and standard estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) reach only 71-73% accuracy. Detection instead requires projection signatures, density folds, filled volumes with characteristic radial profiles, and topology changes, which a 190k-parameter point network recovers at 96.6% accuracy across four corruption tiers, generalizing at 79-91% to object families never seen in training. On a temporal track of rigidly rotating objects we introduce a zero-parameter rigidity witness: the residual of the optimal rigid 3D alignment (Kabsch) between consecutive frames, which must vanish for any rigid 3D motion but cannot vanish for the shadow of a rigid rotation in R^N. This single interpretable statistic separates the classes at AUROC 0.982. All data are generated reproducibly from seeds; the dataset, models, and code are released publicly. HyperShadow makes no claim about physical reality; it is a controlled instrument for studying which observable statistics can certify incompatibility with a purely three-dimensional explanation.

</details>


### [228] [Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14439)
*Andrew Liao,Hanchen Cui,Karthik Desingh,Aryan Deshwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An active evaluation framework is proposed that treats robot policy evaluation as sequential experimental design, using a probabilistic surrogate model to adaptively select test configurations for maximum information gain. Across 2331 real-world evaluations spanning 3 tasks, the method saves 20-40% of trials compared to random testing while systematically identifying failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalist robot manipulation policies face a fundamental evaluation bottleneck: real-world performance depends on a combinatorial explosion of task factors (object poses, camera viewpoints, etc.), making exhaustive evaluation intractable. Current narrow test suites miss critical failure modes and misrepresent deployment readiness. Real hardware evaluation is also slow and resource-intensive, creating a need for sample-efficient, information-rich evaluation strategies.

Method: The framework formalizes policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. A probabilistic surrogate model (likely a Gaussian Process) is fitted over a structured space of task factors. At each step, the next evaluation configuration is adaptively selected to maximize information gain about the policy's performance distribution. This enables sample-efficient characterization across unseen conditions and systematic identification of failure-prone regions.

Result: The approach was validated with 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations each. The active evaluation framework consistently saved the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to random testing baselines while providing richer characterization of policy behavior and failure modes.

Conclusion: Active evaluation via sequential experimental design offers a principled, sample-efficient alternative to ad-hoc test suites for robot manipulation policies. The substantial trial savings (20-40%) on real hardware demonstrate practical value for accelerating policy assessment and improving deployment confidence.

Abstract: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness. We propose an active evaluation framework that addresses this challenge by treating policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. Our approach fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain over the policy's performance distribution, allowing for sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and a systematic identification of failure-prone regions. We conduct 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations and find that our approach typically saves the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.

</details>


### [229] [Depth-Dependent Hidden-State Collapse in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14463)
*Patricia Medina,Hy P. G. Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSAE for LiDAR classification suffers from hidden-state collapse at encoder depth K=5, where representations become nearly constant (std ~10⁻⁵) and all classifiers converge to the same macro F1 of 0.224688. Product Coefficient augmentations neither improve pre-collapse performance nor prevent collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the effectiveness of Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) at varying encoder depths for LiDAR point-cloud classification, and to determine whether Product Coefficient feature augmentations can enhance representation quality or mitigate depth-related degradation.

Method: DSAE architectures with encoder depths K=1 through 5 are trained separately on LiDAR point-cloud data using both raw spatial coordinates (xyz) and xyz augmented with Product Coefficient features. The learned hidden representations are then evaluated using Random Forest, k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN), and a majority-class Dummy classifier. A theoretical bound is also proved, linking between-class hidden scatter to total hidden scatter, which is governed by hidden-state variance.

Result: At K=5, hidden-state standard deviation collapses to ~10⁻⁵ for both input types. All three classifiers yield identical macro F1 scores of 0.224688 — equivalent to the Dummy baseline. Product Coefficients fail to improve pre-collapse macro F1 or prevent the K=5 collapse. The theoretical analysis confirms that near-constant hidden representations cannot preserve class-separating structure.

Conclusion: Large-depth representation collapse (K=5) constitutes a concrete failure mode for DSAE applied to LiDAR point-cloud classification. Product Coefficient augmentations offer no mitigation under the tested DSAE configuration.

Abstract: We study Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification using spatial coordinates and Product Coefficient feature augmentations. The experiments compare separately trained DSAE architectures at encoder depths $K=1,\ldots,5$ and evaluate the resulting hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline. The main finding is a hidden-state collapse at $K=5$. For both xyz and xyz plus Product Coefficient inputs, the hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of $10^{-5}$, while all three classifiers attain the same macro F1 score of $0.224688$. We prove that between-class hidden scatter is bounded by total hidden scatter, which in turn is controlled by the reported hidden-state variance. Thus a nearly constant hidden representation cannot retain substantial class-separating structure. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the $K=5$ collapse in the present DSAE setting. These results identify large-depth representation collapse as a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification.

</details>


### [230] [Interleaved Noise Injection Improves Clean, Corrupted, and OOD Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14466)
*Matt L. Wiemann,Peter Melchior,Andrew K. Saydjari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Interleaved (on-off) noise injection outperforms standard monotonic decay schedules in stochastic optimization. The authors show impulse noise approximates Jacobian regularization (benefiting CNNs) while Gaussian noise acts as curvature penalty (benefiting ViTs), and propose gradient-norm stabilization to handle loss fluctuations when switching between clean/noisy phases. The method improves corruption robustness and OOD generalization across CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R at zero additional computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Noise injection is traditionally applied with a monotonic decay schedule, yet this approach limits exploration and can cause models to overfit to clean data late in training. The authors hypothesize that interleaving phases of noisy and clean data can help optimizers escape local minima and improve robustness without catastrophic forgetting, while also addressing architecture-specific failure modes (locality bias in CNNs, spurious large-scale features in ViTs).

Method: The core method is interleaved noise injection: alternating between training on clean data and noise-corrupted data (impulse or Gaussian). To handle the rapid loss fluctuations when switching phases, they introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates by the ratio of clean to noisy gradient magnitudes. They provide a theoretical analysis showing impulse noise approximates Jacobian regularization and Gaussian noise approximates a curvature penalty. The method is evaluated by stacking on top of other augmentations (e.g., AugMix, Mixup).

Result: Interleaved noise injection yields substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for both ResNet and ViT architectures. Impulse noise specifically counters CNN locality bias; Gaussian noise reduces ViT tendency toward large-scale spurious features. Best results are achieved when stacking interleaved noise injection with existing augmentation methods. Improvements come at essentially zero computational cost.

Conclusion: Interleaved noise injection is a simple, cost-free, and effective regularization tool that improves test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data. Its efficacy stems from architecture-specific regularization effects: Jacobian regularization for CNNs via impulse noise and curvature penalty for ViTs via Gaussian noise. The gradient-norm stabilization technique ensures stable training across phase switches.

Abstract: Noise injection is a well-known technique in stochastic optimization. We report its surprising effectiveness with an interleaved (on-off-on-off...) rather than the usual monotonic decay schedule. We present a theoretical analysis of noise injection, which confirms that corruption by impulse noise approximates a Jacobian regularization, whereas Gaussian noise acts as a curvature penalty. This regularization behavior has been invoked to explain why noise injection increases model robustness. But the interleaved nature of our proposed schedule produces superior results even for the optimization objective: mixing phases of noisy data permits the optimizer to escape local minima and increase exploration without the risk of catastrophically forgetting the important features from the clean data. To stabilize this training scheme against the rapid changes of the loss when switching between clean and noisy data, we introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes. We compare this method with other common augmentation methods and find substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures, with the best results being achieved by stacking our method on top of other augmentations. Through saliency and attention maps we show that the effect of interleaved noise injection stems from penalizing the failure modes encouraged by the inductive bias of the models: impulse noise works against the locality bias of convolutional (ResNet) architectures, and Gaussian noise reduces the tendency of attention-based models to pick up large-scale spurious features. Interleaved noise injection is therefore an effective tool to improve the test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data at essentially zero computational cost.

</details>


### [231] [Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14506)
*Yuxuan Zhu,Rohan Alur,Daniel Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs using PAC-Bayes compression bounds with a Gumbel-max reparameterization trick, and proposes Progressive RLVR — combining on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and quantization — which yields models 14,796x more compressible while retaining 84-97% of standard LoRA performance, with bounds exceeding base model accuracy by 9-51%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RLVR is widely used to improve LLM reasoning, the generalizability of RLVR-fine-tuned models is poorly understood, and no non-vacuous generalization bounds exist for this setting at scale. The authors aim to provide theoretical guarantees and practical methods to achieve strong generalization with high compressibility.

Method: The authors adapt PAC-Bayes compression bounds to RLVR fine-tuning and handle token-generation stochasticity via the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. They then propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA (low-rank adaptation with extremely small rank), and model quantization to operationalize these bounds empirically.

Result: Progressive RLVR retains 84-97% of standard LoRA fine-tuning performance while producing models 14,796x more compressible. Non-vacuous generalization bounds are achieved across four domains (math problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, Text-to-SQL). The bounds exceed base model accuracy by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of fine-tuned model accuracy.

Conclusion: PAC-Bayes compression bounds can yield non-vacuous generalization guarantees for billion-parameter LLMs under RLVR fine-tuning. Progressive RLVR offers a practical approach that balances strong performance with extreme compressibility, enabling theoretically grounded and empirically effective deployment.

Abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the generalizability of the resulting models remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale. Our approach adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds to this setting, and addresses the inherent stochasticity of token generation by applying the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. To operationalize these bounds, we propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization. Progressive RLVR empirically retains 84-97% performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning while producing models that are 14,796x more compressible. We show that this framework yields non-vacuous generalization bounds in four domains: mathematical problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL. Our bounds exceed the accuracy of the base model by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of the accuracy of the fine-tuned models.

</details>


### [232] [Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14516)
*Akhilesh Gogikar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether higher-order Runge-Kutta adaptive integrators (specifically a Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) pair with step control) improve neural network training under compute-matched budgets. Under fair comparison, the RK variant loses to plain Adam; its claimed adaptivity is illusory (step size pins at maximum, tolerances have no effect). A repaired version with true error control yields lower training loss but no test accuracy gain. The only real benefit — a small implicit regularization from gradient averaging — is matched or exceeded by cheaper first-order methods like RMSprop and NAdam.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work interprets optimizers as discretizations of gradient flows and claims that higher-order Runge-Kutta integrators with adaptive step control improve neural network training. However, these claims have rarely been tested under rigorous compute-matched protocols (equal gradient-evaluation budgets). The paper investigates whether the reported gains stem from genuine adaptivity or merely from using more gradient evaluations per step.

Method: The authors build a representative Adam variant using a Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) embedded Runge-Kutta pair with FSAL (First Same As Last) reuse and local-error-based step control. They evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol: every method receives the identical gradient-evaluation budget. They instrument the method to measure normalized error, step sizes, and sensitivity to tolerance parameters (rtol, hmax, h0). They then construct a repaired version with a true reject branch and error computed on the applied map, and conduct a pre-registered follow-up study with n=10 seeds to isolate mechanisms.

Result: Under compute-matched budgets, the adaptive RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch settings. Instrumentation reveals the adaptivity is fake: normalized error stays far below tolerance, step size pins at hmax from step one (98–100% of steps), and tolerance sweeps over 100× produce bit-identical trajectories. The method is effectively fixed-step Adam with averaged gradients at 3–4× cost. The repaired version (true adaptivity) achieves ~40× lower training loss than tuned Adam in full-batch, with an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule as the mechanism, but this does not translate to better test accuracy. The follow-up shows gradient averaging acts as a genuine implicit regularizer (beating lr-matched Adam/AdamW on 10/10 seeds), but RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at one-third the per-step cost.

Conclusion: Higher-order adaptive integration can achieve deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect from gradient averaging, but neither benefit exceeds what cheaper, well-tuned first-order baselines provide. The apparent adaptivity reported in prior work is an artifact of unequal compute budgets and parameter settings that disable the controller entirely.

Abstract: Interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations has motivated applying higher-order Runge-Kutta (RK) integrators to neural networks. We build a representative Adam variant (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair, FSAL reuse, local-error step control) and evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol giving every method the same gradient-evaluation budget - an accounting this literature rarely enforces. Under it the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch (RK's best-case) training. Instrumenting it shows the "adaptivity" is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, the step size pins at its growth cap from step one (98-100 percent of steps), and no rtol x hmax x h0 setting makes it act; tolerances spanning 100x give bit-identical trajectories. The method is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost. Repairing it (true reject branch; error on the applied map) reverses the full-batch result - about 40x lower training loss than tuned Adam - and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity (an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule) as the mechanism. But the gain is fragile to the initial step size and does not reach test accuracy. A pre-registered follow-up rules out the obvious explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob only hurts - leaving a trajectory effect, the controller selecting a minimum generalizing 1.3-3.4 points below first-order descent at equal depth. An n=10 study confirms one secondary effect: gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds - yet RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline does not already provide.

</details>


### [233] [A Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning Framework for Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14522)
*Zikun Zhang,Jiayuan Sheng,David D. Yao,Wenpin Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formulates continuous-time reinforcement learning (RL) for discrete state spaces using controlled continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs), derives policy gradient methods (continuous-time PPO and GRPO), and applies the framework to fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models—notably masked diffusion language models (dLLMs)—with techniques for efficient trajectory likelihood estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GRPO-based fine-tuning of diffusion models relies solely on terminal rewards, lacking the ability to incorporate intermediate reward or advantage signals throughout the denoising trajectory. Moreover, there is no unified continuous-time RL framework for discrete diffusion models that supports flexible reward structures and efficient policy optimization without requiring reward differentiability.

Method: The authors formulate RL in continuous time with discrete state spaces as a stochastic control problem over controlled CTMCs. They derive continuous-time policy gradient methods yielding continuous-time PPO and GRPO variants. This framework is applied to score-based discrete diffusion models, enabling intermediate reward integration throughout the denoising process. For masked diffusion models, they exploit analytically tractable probability ratios over the vocabulary simplex. For dLLMs, they introduce trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate trajectory likelihoods and reduce the cost of computing per-position probability ratios.

Result: The proposed methods are demonstrated on low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and on RL post-training of masked diffusion large language models for mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, showing effectiveness in both settings.

Conclusion: The continuous-time CTMC-based RL framework provides a principled and unified approach for reward-driven fine-tuning of discrete diffusion models, supporting intermediate rewards, flexible policy parameterizations, and computationally efficient estimation, with broad applicability to diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: We formulate reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time with discrete state spaces and possibly arbitrary action spaces via a stochastic control approach, where the state dynamics are modeled as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). We consider policy optimization problems and derive the corresponding policy gradient methods, leading to continuous-time variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). As a primary application, we develop a complete continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models. The proposed framework enables reward-driven optimization without requiring differentiability on the reward signals. In contrast to the existing GRPO-based approaches that only rely on terminal rewards, our formulation allows intermediate reward or advantage signals to be incorporated throughout the denoising trajectory. Importantly, when specialized to masked diffusion models (MDMs), our framework encompasses a rich class of policy parameterizations over the vocabulary simplex with analytically tractable probability ratios, providing a unified perspective on exploration and policy optimization in MDMs. For masked diffusion large language models (dLLMs), we further propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate computationally prohibitive trajectory likelihoods, reducing the computational cost of computing per-position probability ratios. We showcase the effectiveness of our methods on both low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of dLLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

</details>


### [234] [xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14530)
*Xiangdong Zhang,Xiaohan Qin,Sunan Zou,Tuo Dai,Xiaoming Shi,Huaijin Wu,Yebin Yang,Zhuo Xia,Shaofeng Zhang,Lin Yao,Yuliang Liu,Yu Cheng,Junchi Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: xHC extends Hyper-Connections beyond N=4 by solving two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back (via temporal feature augmentation) and cubic-cost residual mixing (via sparse updates to k=4 of N=16 streams). xHC-Flash further reduces memory traffic, making large-N residual-stream expansion practical for LLM pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HC-family methods plateau at N=4 due to (1) insufficient write-back information as stream count grows, and (2) residual-mixing generation cost scaling cubically with N. The authors aim to unlock meaningful expansion beyond N=4 to realize the promising scaling benefits of residual-stream expansion.

Method: xHC introduces two innovations: (1) temporal feature augmentation that enriches write-back information by incorporating historical stream features, and (2) a sparse residual-stream architecture that maintains N=16 streams but updates only k=4 per step while retaining dense read access. xHC-Flash is a memory-optimized implementation that reduces per-sublayer memory traffic from 73.5C to 40C.

Result: On 18B MoE models, xHC achieves +4.0 average downstream score improvement over mHC with modest training FLOPs overhead. Scaling-law experiments show vanilla and mHC require 1.50× and 1.19× the compute of xHC to reach the same loss. xHC-Flash reduces memory traffic to 40C (vs. 34C for mHC at N=4) while preserving full xHC gains.

Conclusion: xHC successfully scales HC-family methods to N=16, delivering consistent downstream improvements and superior compute efficiency. Combined with xHC-Flash, large-N residual-stream expansion becomes both effective and practical for large-scale LLM pretraining.

Abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of Transformers into $N$ parallel streams, providing a form of memory scaling beyond model width and depth. Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from $N{=}1$ to $N{=}4$ suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at $N{=}4$. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with $N$. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond $N{=}4$. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only $k=4$ of the $N=16$ streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require $1.50\times$ and $1.19\times$ the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-$N$ training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. We therefore introduce xHC-Flash, which reduces the per-sublayer memory traffic from $73.5C$ to $40C$, comparable to the $34C$ required by mHC at $N{=}4$, while retaining the gains of full xHC. Together, xHC and xHC-Flash make large-$N$ residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training.

</details>


### [235] [Muse: Representation Geometry of Muon Beyond Normalized Momentum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14536)
*Da Chang,Qiankun Shi,Lvgang Zhang,Di He,Yaoshuai Ma,Ganzhao Yuan,Yongxiang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a family of Muon-style optimizers that unifies different parameter-block representations (native, nearest-square, skinny, vector) under a shared momentum rule and Newton-Schulz backend. It shows that the shorter matrix dimension in each Frobenius-isometric representation governs singular-channel support, pullback scaling, and convergence bounds, with theoretical and empirical evidence that balanced non-native representations match native performance while dimensionally reduced ones degrade toward normalized momentum.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon optimizers polar-map matrix momentum but their behavior critically depends on how parameter blocks are represented before orthogonalization — a design choice whose geometry and consequences have not been systematically studied. Understanding this representation geometry is essential for principled optimizer design and for explaining when and why Muon-style updates succeed or fail.

Method: The authors formalize representation choice as inducing a polar steepest-descent geometry via Frobenius-isometric mappings. They analyze how the shorter matrix dimension determines: (1) the number of supported singular channels, (2) pullback scaling, and (3) constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. A teacher-student model is used to link early-stage dissipation to the nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio via curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko-Pastur spectral profile. Empirical validation uses LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M pretraining runs plus fixed-momentum diagnostics.

Result: Balanced non-native representations (e.g., nearest-square) match native representation performance in pretraining. Reducing the shorter dimension weakens scaling and singular-channel support, causing optimizer behavior to increasingly approximate normalized momentum. The Marchenko-Pastur analysis connects spectral structure to dissipation dynamics in the teacher-student setting.

Conclusion: Representation geometry is a first-class design dimension in Muon-style optimizers. The shorter matrix dimension acts as a capacity knob controlling singular-channel support and convergence properties. Balanced reshaping preserves performance, while aggressive dimensional reduction collapses the optimizer toward simpler momentum regimes.

Abstract: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, but their updates also depend on the representation of each parameter block before orthogonalization. We study this representation choice as a form of optimizer geometry and introduce {\method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers that shares the same momentum rule and Newton--Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry, in which the shorter matrix dimension determines the number of supported singular channels, the pullback scaling, and the constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. In a teacher--student model, curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko--Pastur spectral profile connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M, together with fixed-momentum diagnostics, show that balanced non-native representations can match the performance of the native representation, whereas reducing the shorter dimension weakens the scaling and singular-channel support, leading to behavior that increasingly resembles normalized momentum.

</details>


### [236] [CASP: Learning-Augmented Offline Approximation with Verifiable Certificates and Bounded-Loss PAC Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14545)
*Haifeng Li,Mo Hai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CASP proposes a framework where machine-learned predictions are used to prune search spaces for NP-hard optimization, but each pruning decision is verified in polynomial time before acceptance, preserving worst-case guarantees. The paper develops the learning theory for this certificate-augmented approach, showing it admits distribution-free learnability with sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$, unlike unverified commitment. Experiments across five problems confirm that verified deployment loses no optimality under distribution shift, while unverified pruning loses up to 26%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Using ML predictions to accelerate NP-hard optimization is appealing but risky: naively committing to a predictor's suggestion forfeits worst-case guarantees, and the prediction task itself is as hard as the original problem. The authors seek a middle ground where predictions guide search-space pruning but a sound polynomial-time verifier checks each pruning certificate, ensuring correctness is never compromised by poor predictions.

Method: The CASP framework pairs a predictor that outputs verifiable pruning certificates with a polynomial-time soundness verifier. The authors develop the PAC learning theory of this setup, proving that the verifier bounds the induced loss class uniformly, yielding sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ independent of cost spread. They analyze filtering noisy predictions via verifiable confidence, derive closed-form dominance margins over the standard min-combiner, and show symmetric LP policies stall on degenerate optimal faces while CASP predictions break ties effectively.

Result: The certificate class is distribution-free learnable at rate $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$, whereas unverified commitment admits no distribution-free rate and suffers a lower bound of $\Omega(R/\varepsilon^2)$ under cost spread $R$. Filtering by verifiable confidence dominates the min-combiner with a derived closed-form margin. On five NP-hard problems, unverified pruning loses up to 26% of the optimum under distribution shift, while CASP's verified deployment loses nothing.

Conclusion: CASP provides a principled way to safely integrate ML predictions into exact optimization without sacrificing worst-case guarantees. The learning theory shows certificate-based pruning is efficiently learnable where unverified approaches are not, and the experimental results validate that verification eliminates optimality loss under distribution shift.

Abstract: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

</details>


### [237] [Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14563)
*Tatthapong Srikitrungruang,Jaesung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PIE-PINN proposes a probabilistic physics-informed neural network framework for robustly estimating spatially heterogeneous Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data, using Laplace distributions, B-spline-guided networks, and hierarchical half-Cauchy scale models with alternating maximum-likelihood training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inverse elasticity problems are severely ill-posed when using low-resolution displacement measurements, as spatial details are obscured and measurement perturbations are amplified. Existing inverse methods require high-fidelity data and manually tuned loss weights, making them brittle to noise and resolution degradation. There is a need for a robust, adaptive framework that can handle these challenges without manual hyperparameter tuning.

Method: PIE-PINN models three residuals — displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium — using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic framework. A B-spline-guided displacement network provides a smooth global representation, with a neural network correction capturing local variations. A hierarchical half-Cauchy model adaptively scales displacement residual weights to downweight severe fitting errors. Training uses alternating maximum-likelihood: updating the mean displacement via weighted residual minimization, then updating the scale parameters to automatically adjust loss weights.

Result: Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate that PIE-PINN robustly recovers heterogeneous elastic properties, showing improved resilience to both measurement noise and low spatial resolution compared to existing deterministic inverse methods.

Conclusion: The probabilistic formulation with adaptive weighting via hierarchical scale modeling effectively addresses the ill-posedness of low-resolution inverse elasticity, enabling robust material property identification without manual loss tuning, even under significant noise and resolution constraints.

Abstract: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse elasticity problem because low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneous property variations, and small measurement perturbations or fitting errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing inverse methods often rely on high-fidelity observations and manually prespecified loss weights, limiting their adaptability and making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. We propose a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework for robust estimation of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data. PIE-PINN models displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. To improve robustness, the framework combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global representation of the displacement field, while the neural network correction captures local variations. The hierarchical scale model adaptively downweights severe displacement fitting errors, enabling more robust recovery of the latent mean displacement field. An alternating maximum-likelihood training strategy updates the mean through weighted residual minimization and updates the scales to adjust the loss weights. Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate the robustness of PIE-PINN.

</details>


### [238] [Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14571)
*Dante Lok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "gate-zero growth," a function-preserving operator for continual learning that adds residual blocks via zero-initialized gates. Under a transversality condition, this induces rank separation in the functional Jacobian, ensuring old directions remain unchanged while new gate directions provide the sole first-order source of new functional variation. This yields controlled function drift and Jacobian leakage. Experiments on a 300M→857M Transformer show near-zero forgetting, significantly outperforming non-FP baselines. The analysis also unifies LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters under a shared local geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting when model capacity is expanded. Existing function-preserving operators allow safe architecture growth but lack a rigorous geometric understanding of how functional variation emerges during subsequent training. The authors aim to provide a principled geometric framework that characterizes the local Jacobian structure at the growth point and guarantees controlled departure from function preservation.

Method: The authors propose gate-zero growth: adding new residual blocks gated by a scalar α initialized to zero. Under a transversality condition (new block output not contained in the span of existing Jacobian columns), they prove rank separation: the functional Jacobian decomposes into unchanged old directions, exactly flat new-weight directions, and new gate directions as the sole first-order source of functional change. This yields O(||α||²) function drift and O(||α||∞) Jacobian leakage bounds. The framework subsumes LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters as instances of the same local geometry.

Result: On a 300M→857M Transformer adapting from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth achieves near-zero old-domain forgetting (Δ_A < 0.1) under both Isolation (exact preservation) and Freeze-Nothing (joint-frontier) regimes. A non-FP stacked control (G_stack) exhibits an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under identical conditions.

Conclusion: Gate-zero growth provides a theoretically grounded, canonical FP operator for continual learning, with precise geometric guarantees on rank separation, drift, and leakage. It establishes a unifying local geometry for safe capacity activation that encompasses several existing adapter methods, and demonstrates strong empirical performance in large-scale Transformer continual learning.

Abstract: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

</details>


### [239] [Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14576)
*Hyemin Gu,Michael Tyrrell,Tuhin Sahai,Markos A. Katsoulakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the sublinear-growth principle: a stability condition requiring that the velocity field of each residual block in a deep network grow at most linearly with input magnitude (exponent q ≤ 1). This threshold is both necessary and sufficient for stable training, derived from ODE theory and optimal control. It provides a systematic framework for certifying architectural stability without relying on normalization layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep residual architectures can exhibit training instability, and practitioners rely on ad hoc fixes like layer normalization without a principled understanding of when and why stability breaks. The authors seek a rigorous, architecture-level criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for stable forward/backward dynamics, replacing trial-and-error design with a certifiable condition.

Method: The authors formulate residual networks as ODEs and analyze the velocity field v(x,t). Two parallel arguments establish q ≤ 1 as the stability threshold: (1) classical ODE theory proves global forward flow exists iff q ≤ 1, with blow-up at q > 1; (2) optimal-control analysis via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation shows the training optimum is bang-bang on the admissible boundary, so q > 1 yields divergent optima while q ≤ 1 is inherently safe. They develop an arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under five primitive operations (addition, scalar multiplication, linear transformation, element-wise nonlinearity, and composition) to certify q ≤ 1 compositionally. A parameter-free modification of the Mamba block (reducing q from 5 to 1) and experiments on Mamba and PatchTST validate the criterion.

Result: The q ≤ 1 criterion is established as both necessary and sufficient for stable training. The exponent arithmetic enables efficient certification at the architectural primitive level. The modified Mamba block achieves q = 1 without layer normalization and trains stably. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that stability is governed by the input-magnitude exponent, not by the presence or absence of normalization layers.

Conclusion: The sublinear-growth principle (q ≤ 1) defines the correct function space for residual architectures, where forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. This provides a principled replacement for ad hoc stability measures like layer normalization, enabling certified-stable architecture design from primitives. The framework unifies ODE stability theory with practical neural architecture design.

Abstract: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

</details>


### [240] [Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14607)
*Umid Suleymanov,Ilhama Novruzova,Khalid Mammadov,Natavan Hasanova,Murat Kantarcioglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first comprehensive study of how fairness-enhancing algorithms affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. Using an adapted Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, the authors uncover privacy disparities across subgroups, analyze how Differential Privacy interacts with fairness methods, and introduce a unified empirical framework for jointly evaluating fairness, privacy, and utility at the subpopulation level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has extensively studied how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question — how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage — has been underexplored. Additionally, existing privacy and fairness evaluations typically operate at the aggregate level, potentially obscuring important subpopulation-level disparities. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating the interplay between fairness interventions and membership inference risks across different subgroups.

Method: The authors adapt the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup-level auditing to measure membership inference privacy risks across different subpopulations. They systematically evaluate how various fairness-enhancing methods interact with Differential Privacy (DP), analyzing the distribution of privacy benefits and utility costs across subgroups under different model architectures, subgroup sizes, and mitigation strategies.

Result: Fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact varies depending on model architecture, subgroup size, and the specific mitigation strategy employed. DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Aggregate-level evaluations obscure significant privacy disparities that become visible only through subgroup auditing.

Conclusion: Fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level rather than solely in aggregate. The authors introduce the first unified empirical framework for conducting such joint subgroup auditing in practice, enabling practitioners to identify and address privacy disparities that would otherwise remain hidden.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

</details>


### [241] [Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14613)
*Jin Dai,Qiuzhen Zhang,Chenyun Dai,Danmei Lan,Can Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AG-SCL is a contrastive learning framework for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis that combines angular Gaussian full-covariance embeddings, adaptive logit adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation to improve rare arrhythmia detection while maintaining specificity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-tailed learning methods for ECG diagnosis focus on class frequency rebalancing but ignore direction-dependent morphological variability across classes. Rare but clinically important arrhythmias suffer from poor sensitivity due to this oversight.

Method: AG-SCL integrates: (1) Angular Gaussian contrastive learning modeling full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings; (2) Adaptive Logit Adjustment learning bounded label-state-specific priors instead of fixed frequency-based margins; (3) tail-aware augmentation generating morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band.

Result: On PTB-XL: balanced accuracy 0.838, sensitivity 0.709, specificity 0.968, mAP 0.495, TPR@5%FPR 0.778. On Noc-ECG: 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, 0.900. Largest gains in rare/morphologically unstable rhythms. Ablations confirmed all three components' contributions.

Conclusion: AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by unifying prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while preserving clinically relevant specificity.

Abstract: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets. On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

</details>


### [242] [Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14614)
*Weiwen Xu,Jia Liu,Hou Pong Chan,Long Li,Deng Cai,Min Chen,Hao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CPO replaces entropy-based advantage shaping in RLVR with token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions, providing a correctness-aware signal that outperforms entropy methods while maintaining generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Entropy, commonly used for advantage shaping in RLVR, cannot distinguish between useful uncertainty (exploration) and detrimental confusion (errors). This limits its effectiveness as a correctness signal for policy optimization.

Method: CPO computes token-level contrastive disagreement between two distributions: a reference-guided generation distribution and a vanilla generation distribution. This disagreement serves as a correctness-aware advantage shaping signal. The method also subsumes On-policy Distillation as a special case where an external teacher provides the posterior distribution, and it resolves the zero-advantage problem inherent in some RLVR setups.

Result: CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks while maintaining strong generalization. Correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively; balancing both yields optimal performance.

Conclusion: Contrastive disagreement is a more effective correctness signal than entropy for RLVR. CPO offers a unified framework that improves performance, resolves the zero-advantage problem, and naturally balances exploration and exploitation through correct and incorrect responses.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

</details>


### [243] [PolyQ: Codesigning End-to-End Quantization Framework for Scalable Edge CPU LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14618)
*Hyunwoo Oh,Suyeon Jang,Hanning Chen,KyungIn Nam,Sanggeon Yun,Ryozo Masukawa,Mohsen Imani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PolyQ is a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design that enables activation-aware per-channel bit allocation (from {2,3,4,8,16}) under a user-specified average-bit budget, converting fine-grained mixed-precision quantization into practical fractional-bit deployment with minimal runtime overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods either offer only coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that cannot be efficiently executed on CPUs due to irregular memory access patterns and layout overhead.

Method: PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from {2,3,4,8,16} via activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under an average-bit budget. A compile-time compiler then permutes and clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generates SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merges compatible permutations across operators to regularize layouts offline, keeping runtime free of reorder overhead.

Result: On Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B with WikiText-2, PolyQ achieves stable quality scaling from 3–6 bits and improves perplexity by 2.4–32.1% over prior methods at 3-bit target. On workstation, laptop, and mobile CPUs, layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with bit budget, and energy/token overhead remains below 2% relative to an optimized LUT backend.

Conclusion: Fractional-bit CPU deployment via PolyQ is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets, demonstrating that compiler/quantization co-design can bridge the gap between fine-grained quantization and efficient CPU execution.

Abstract: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods offer either coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs. We present PolyQ, a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design for activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under a user-specified average-bit budget. PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from $\{2,3,4,8,16\}$, then uses a compile-time model compiler to permute and cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This turns fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment method for CPU-only inference. Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ provides stable quality scaling from 3--6\,b and improves perplexity by 2.4--32.1\% over prior methods at a 3\,b target. End-to-end measurements on three representative CPUs -- workstation, laptop, and mobile -- show that compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8\%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2\% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end. These results show that fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

</details>


### [244] [TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14640)
*Wen Yang Tan,Jiawei Li,Fang Liu,Wei Zhang,Sumei Sun,Peng Cheng Wang,Elisa Y. M. Ang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIDE is a battery degradation estimator that integrates a knowledge-guided degradation prior, a monotone residual component, and contextual learning to achieve accurate, trustworthy, and interpretable battery health estimation. The trained model is distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate for model-level interpretability. Experiments show a 19.7% improvement in estimation fidelity over baselines, with reduced aging-consistency violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Battery health estimation is critical for management, control, and maintenance in battery-powered systems. In intelligent connected systems, estimation errors can propagate across devices and downstream decisions. Existing methods lack a joint treatment of accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability — all essential for practical deployment.

Method: TIDE employs a three-component backbone: (1) a knowledge-guided degradation prior that enforces trustworthy estimation by incorporating battery-domain knowledge; (2) a monotone residual component ensuring aging-consistent refinement; and (3) a contextual learning component capturing battery-specific operational effects for accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate to provide model-level interpretation of the learned estimation logic.

Result: TIDE achieves a 19.7% average improvement in overall estimation fidelity over representative baselines. The knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modeling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, enhancing trustworthiness. The backbone enables component-level interpretation, and symbolic distillation yields a compact model-level representation of the estimation logic.

Conclusion: TIDE successfully integrates accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability for battery health estimation, making it suitable for practical deployment in battery health monitoring and decision support within intelligent connected systems.

Abstract: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

</details>


### [245] [Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14652)
*Shusheng Xiao,Jinshuai Bai,Hyogu Jeong,Yunfei Xi,Yilin Gui,YuanTong Gu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for rapid conditional topology generation. It introduces a trajectory-aware formulation that uses volume-fraction-indexed BESO states to construct physically meaningful probability paths, enabling physics-guided generative learning without inference-time optimisation. The method outperforms diffusion-based baselines in compliance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and sampling speed, especially under limited data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional topology optimisation requires costly repeated FEA and sensitivity updates for each new design condition. Existing generative TO methods suffer from reliance on adversarial training, slow reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance for structural feasibility. The authors aim to develop a faster, physics-informed generative framework that eliminates inference-time optimisation while maintaining structural validity.

Method: Two FMTO formulations are proposed: (1) Linear FMTO, an endpoint-based baseline interpolating between Gaussian noise and BESO reference topology; (2) Trajectory-aware FMTO, which uses volume-fraction-indexed BESO intermediate states to construct the probability path and target velocity field, embedding optimisation history into flow learning. A path-velocity mismatch analysis is conducted to explain the trade-off between trajectory weighting and generation stability.

Result: FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with superior compliance performance, volume-fraction accuracy, and topology fidelity compared to a diffusion baseline, while requiring substantially fewer sampling steps. Trajectory-aware FMTO with moderate trajectory weighting achieves the best overall performance under limited training data. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and 3D generation validate path design influence and framework generalisability.

Conclusion: The trajectory-aware FMTO framework effectively integrates physics-guided BESO optimisation history into flow matching, enabling fast, diverse, and structurally feasible topology generation without inference-time optimisation. Moderate trajectory weighting balances guidance and generative flexibility, and the approach scales to 3D problems.

Abstract: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

</details>


### [246] [Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14672)
*Yusuke Sakemi,Tomoya Takeuchi,Takeo Hosomi,Kazuyuki Aihara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSTD proposes a memory-efficient training method for deep continuous-time SNNs by discretizing irregular spike times onto fixed grids, reducing memory from O(N_out·N_in) to O(N_out·M), and introduces temporal regularization for stable deep training, enabling up to 100× memory and 20× speed improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep continuous-time SNNs is bottlenecked by the prohibitive memory cost of exact spike-time computation, which requires storing candidate firing times across all presynaptic-postsynaptic neuron pairs. This O(N_out·N_in) memory scaling makes training deep networks on single GPUs infeasible.

Method: (1) Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization (DSTD): Maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at M fixed time intervals, approximating continuous membrane dynamics while decoupling memory from N_in. (2) Synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization: Organizes layer-wise firing windows to prevent dead neurons and enable pipelined processing across layers.

Result: DSTD reduced peak memory by up to ~100× and training time by up to ~20× compared to exact spike-time computation. Enabled training of 9-layer ConvSNN on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer ConvSNN on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

Conclusion: The proposed DSTD framework makes training deep continuous-time SNNs practically feasible on commodity hardware by fundamentally reducing the memory complexity of spike-time computation, while temporal regularization ensures stable deep training dynamics.

Abstract: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware.
