However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

</details>


### [247] [Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14705)
*Yuchang Zhu,Zezhong Xie,Huizhe Zhang,Huazhen Zhong,Jintang Li,Liang Chen,Zibin Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grad2Fair is a gradient-guided fairness method for GNNs that operates without demographic information — it detects bias via gradient distribution modes (GradDist metric) and directly debiases using gradients, avoiding inaccurate demographic proxies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN fairness methods assume full demographic availability. Attempts to use predicted demographics as proxies fail when predictions are inaccurate. The authors observe that gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, motivating a demographic-free approach.

Method: (1) GradDist: a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring distances between local modes in gradient distributions of misclassified nodes. (2) Grad2Fair: a gradient-guided debiasing framework that directly leverages gradient signals to enforce group fairness without any demographic prediction, enabling stable fairness performance.

Result: Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show Grad2Fair achieves superior fairness performance over baselines in most cases.

Conclusion: Gradients of misclassified nodes carry implicit demographic signals, and directly leveraging them for debiasing eliminates the need for noisy demographic proxies, yielding stable and effective fairness improvements in GNNs.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

</details>


### [248] [MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14706)
*Xin Li,Zixin Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MESHA is a strategic linear bandits algorithm for Best Arm Identification that combines uniform sampling with an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition to counter arms' strategic misreporting of features. It provably bounds failure probability and outperforms G-optimal design-based baselines that can starve the optimal arm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard linear BAI algorithms using G-optimal design sampling are vulnerable to strategic manipulation: arms may misreport their feature vectors to increase selection probability, and optimal design based on reported features can starve the truly optimal arm of sampling budget, causing algorithm failure.

Method: MESHA employs two key components: (1) naïve uniform sampling to reduce the impact of strategic feature reporting, and (2) an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC) that eliminates arms whose reported features deviate significantly from ground truth. The analysis considers arbitrary Nash Equilibrium and derives an upper bound on the failure probability within fixed budget T.

Result: The authors prove that arms attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize identification probability, derive an upper bound on MESHA's failure probability under budget T, and demonstrate that G-optimal design-based BAI algorithms fail in strategic settings due to budget starvation of the optimal arm. Numerical experiments show MESHA outperforms both OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines.

Conclusion: MESHA provides a robust solution for BAI in strategic linear bandits, demonstrating that uniform sampling combined with a Grim Trigger mechanism effectively mitigates strategic manipulation, unlike G-optimal design approaches that are fundamentally vulnerable in adversarial reporting environments.

Abstract: We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

</details>


### [249] [Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14719)
*Richard J. Fawley,Renato Cordeiro de Amorim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VoICE is a counterfactual explanation framework for feature-weighted k-means clustering that generates least-cost, parsimonious counterfactuals by projecting inputs onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights, data bounds, and homothetic contraction to ensure valid cluster membership.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactual explanations are well established in supervised learning but poorly adapted to clustering, where assignments lack labels and depend on partition geometry. Existing pairwise boundary-crossing approaches fail to reliably produce valid target-cluster membership. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a geometrically principled method.

Method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as a projection onto the complete weighted Voronoi region of a desired target cluster, integrating feature weights into both the distance metric and the optimization objective. The framework enforces actionability constraints, intersects target regions with data-derived bounds to prevent extrapolation, and applies homothetic contraction toward centroids to reduce boundary sensitivity. The result is a constrained optimization that yields minimal-cost, sparse feature changes guaranteeing target-cluster assignment.

Result: Across several benchmark datasets, VoICE consistently achieved valid target-cluster membership, whereas the leading pairwise baseline method failed to do so reliably.

Conclusion: Leveraging the full Voronoi geometry of the weighted partition, rather than a single pairwise boundary, is essential for generating valid and cost-effective counterfactual explanations in feature-weighted k-means clustering.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

</details>


### [250] [What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14731)
*Kumar Kshitij Patel,Rustem Islamov,Sebastian U Stich,Aurelien Lucchi,Eduard Gorbunov,Lingxiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proves that bounded second-order heterogeneity explains Local SGD efficiency for general convex objectives, establishes nearly tight upper and lower bounds, and extends the analysis to serial SGD with replacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Patel et al. (2025) showed second-order heterogeneity captures Local SGD efficiency for strongly convex objectives and conjectured it extends to general convex settings. This paper aims to prove that conjecture.

Method: Establishes improved convergence upper bounds for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity, complemented by improved lower bounds demonstrating near-tightness. Also applies the technique to derive a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement.

Result: Proves the conjecture that bounded second-order heterogeneity governs Local SGD efficiency for general convex objectives. Upper and lower bounds are nearly tight, providing a sharper convergence theory. Additionally shows second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients in serial SGD with replacement.

Conclusion: Second-order heterogeneity is the key structural condition that explains the practical success of Local SGD across both strongly convex and general convex settings, yielding a fine-grained and nearly complete theoretical picture.

Abstract: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

</details>


### [251] [GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14733)
*Xiangni Tian,Kaixian Yu,Runpeng Dai,Niansheng Tang,Hongtu Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAttNHP combines a self-attention encoder, soft semantic grouping with Hawkes priors, and non-crossing quantile regression to tackle long-range dependencies, mutual excitation/inhibition among event chains, and heavy-tailed inter-arrival times in Temporal Knowledge Graph forecasting, achieving SOTA on six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TKG forecasting methods suffer from three interrelated shortcomings: (1) difficulty encoding long-range temporal dependencies, (2) inability to model mutual excitation and inhibition between different event chains at the snapshot level, and (3) unreliable deterministic time predictors due to heavy-tailed, statistically sparse inter-arrival times.

Method: The proposed GAttNHP framework consists of three matched components: (1) a self-attention encoder that models each subject-relation chain as a continuous-time point process, capturing lingering excitation from distant history; (2) a semantic soft-grouping module that converts globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, enabling chains to share excitation patterns via latent group memberships rather than exhaustive pairwise computation; and (3) a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head that replaces mean-based time prediction with calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates robust to heavy-tailed distributions.

Result: GAttNHP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on six benchmark TKG datasets for both entity prediction and time prediction. Ablation studies show that the largest improvements occur on long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

Conclusion: The three-component design of GAttNHP — self-attention over continuous-time point processes, soft semantic grouping for efficient cross-chain excitation sharing, and NCQ regression for robust time prediction — jointly addresses the core failure modes of prior TKG forecasting models, with particularly pronounced gains on sparse, long-tail event chains.

Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

</details>


### [252] [ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14770)
*Xuemeng Liu,Zhengpin Li,Wanpeng Tang,Haotong Xie,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ChronoQG is the first benchmark framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), producing 16,011 verified questions across four datasets. It reveals that existing KGQG methods struggle significantly with preserving temporal constraints, establishing a new challenging testbed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KGQG benchmarks are built on static knowledge graphs that lack temporal scoping. They cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, or answer-determining temporal constraints, creating a critical evaluation gap.

Method: ChronoQG integrates three components: (1) a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, (2) topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and (3) trace-grounded question generation. This produces temporally faithful, hop-bounded questions from heterogeneous TKGs. The framework generates four benchmark datasets evaluated across temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and constraint types.

Result: Evaluation of representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines shows existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, particularly under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types, revealing a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG.

Conclusion: There is a significant performance gap between static and temporal KGQG. ChronoQG establishes a challenging and necessary benchmark for advancing temporally faithful question generation, highlighting that current methods are insufficient for temporal reasoning in question generation.

Abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

</details>


### [253] [Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14817)
*Jakub Paplhám,Willem Waegeman,Eyke Hüllermeier,Vojtěch Franc*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that standard proxy tasks for evaluating epistemic uncertainty (OOD detection, active learning) are misaligned with Bayes-optimal decision strategies. Using the epistemic reject-option framework, it proves the optimal selective prediction rule thresholds a convex combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. It then shows correlation-based disentanglement metrics fail to predict operational utility, proposing instead evaluation via the risk-regret-coverage surface, which yields rankings that can invert relative to proxy-task rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of epistemic uncertainty rely on proxy tasks (OOD detection, active learning) whose Bayes-optimal decision rules do not align with the uncertainty scores being evaluated. This misalignment raises doubts about whether these evaluations truly measure the utility of epistemic uncertainty estimates for downstream decision-making.

Method: The authors adopt the epistemic reject-option framework and formalize selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret. They derive the optimal selector theoretically as a threshold on a convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. They then propose evaluating disentangled uncertainty components by measuring the achievable risk-regret-coverage surface, which jointly assesses disentanglement quality and decision-theoretic utility, contrasting this with standard correlation-based disentanglement metrics.

Result: On datasets with dense human annotations, decision-theoretic rankings based on the proposed risk-regret-coverage surface disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions where methods top-ranked on one criterion are bottom-ranked on another. Standard correlation metrics between learned aleatoric and epistemic components also fail to predict operational utility.

Conclusion: Evaluation of epistemic uncertainty should be grounded in decision-theoretic criteria rather than proxy tasks or correlation-based disentanglement metrics. The risk-regret-coverage surface provides a principled diagnostic that reveals and resolves the shortcomings of current evaluation practices.

Abstract: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

</details>


### [254] [Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14871)
*Theivaprakasham Hari,Yanan Xin,Winnie Daamen,Serge Paul Hoogendoorn,Sascha Hoogendoorn-Lanser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APAL introduces an asymmetric, peak-aware loss function for time-series forecasting that penalizes under-prediction more heavily and upweights peak regions, complemented by a peak-critical evaluation protocol. It improves tail accuracy and peak-timing prediction across multiple backbones and datasets, particularly in pedestrian demand forecasting, while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard time-series forecasters use symmetric loss functions (MSE, MAE) and aggregate error metrics, which mask failures on rare demand spikes and extreme values. In operational settings (e.g., crowd demand forecasting), under-prediction carries substantially higher risk than over-prediction. There is a need for training objectives and evaluation protocols that explicitly address peak-prediction quality.

Method: The authors propose APAL (Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss), a model-agnostic loss function with two key mechanisms: (1) asymmetric penalization that weights under-predictions more heavily than over-predictions, and (2) peak-aware weighting that increases the importance of peak regions within each forecast window. They also introduce a peak-critical evaluation protocol using channel-wise tail error (Top-10%, Top-1%), peak precision/recall/F1 with timing tolerance, and peak timing error, complementing standard MAE/MSE.

Result: APAL was evaluated on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with primary focus on pedestrian demand (Melbourne pedestrian counts, beach visitor counts) and additional benchmark datasets. Results show improved tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical settings, with a controllable trade-off between peak metrics and aggregate error.

Conclusion: APAL offers a practical, model-agnostic solution for time-series forecasting applications where peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern, enabling practitioners to balance aggregate error against peak-critical performance.

Abstract: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

</details>


### [255] [PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14877)
*Ali Asadi,Krishnendu Chatterjee,Pavol Kebis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first positive result for decentralized, private-information PAC learning of turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives, establishing polynomial sample complexity bounds using a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reachability is a fundamental objective but notoriously hard to learn in reinforcement learning, with PAC learning proven impossible without extra assumptions in both MDPs and TBSGs. Prior work on TBSGs required two strong assumptions: (a) public information shared between players, and (b) centralized learning with a shared algorithm. The authors aim to relax both assumptions, enabling learning with private information and decentralized algorithms.

Method: The authors introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set in the adversarial TBSG setting. They then develop learning algorithms that operate under decentralized conditions with private information, and derive polynomial-sample complexity bounds with respect to the number of states, actions, the ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

Result: The paper establishes that decentralized and private-information PAC learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives is possible, providing the first positive result in this setting. A polynomial-sample complexity bound is proven, scaling with states, actions, the ECD parameter, and standard PAC parameters.

Conclusion: The strong assumptions of public information and centralized learning in prior TBSG reachability literature can be successfully relaxed. The game-theoretic ECD parameter provides a tractable measure for establishing sample complexity guarantees in the decentralized, private-information setting, opening the door for more realistic multi-agent RL scenarios.

Abstract: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

</details>


### [256] [Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14888)
*Robert Graham,Edward Stevinson,Yariv Barsheshat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on narrow, ideologically-aligned datasets causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains — a phenomenon called "ideological generalisation" — with amplification beyond few-shot prompting, including extreme out-of-distribution outputs, while preserving general capabilities like GSM8K accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether the standard practice of fine-tuning LMs on small, curated, moderation-compliant datasets inadvertently causes unintended ideological drift across unrelated domains, and to quantify the breadth and amplification of such effects.

Method: Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 and Gemma-3 on narrow, factually-defensible datasets (right/left-leaning economics Q&A, workplace HR policy, practical finance, food-safety) and measured resulting ideological shifts on unrelated topics (criminal justice, environment, cultural taste, pseudoscience beliefs). Compared fine-tuning effects against few-shot prompting baselines. Evaluated using judge-free evaluations, external benchmarks, and mixing with generic data. Proposed metrics: breadth (topic reach) and amplification (extremity relative to prompting).

Result: Fine-tuning produced matched ideological shifts across distant topics; food-safety fine-tuning increased sycophantic agreement with false health beliefs; few-shot prompting predicted generalisation direction but fine-tuning amplified shifts to extremes, including endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence; effects replicated on Gemma-3, survived mixing with generic data, and left GSM8K accuracy within ±1pp of baseline.

Conclusion: Fine-tuning on narrow, benign-appearing datasets poses a risk of "ideological generalisation" — broad, amplified ideological drift into unrelated and potentially harmful domains — even while preserving core model capabilities. This warrants careful auditing of fine-tuning data for unintended downstream effects.

Abstract: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

</details>


### [257] [Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14889)
*Jean-Marc Brossier,Olivier Lafitte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies optimal linear combinations of binary classifiers using truth tables to partition data into equivalence classes. It establishes conditions for existence/uniqueness of the global minimum of convexified empirical risk and derives explicit analytical formulas for optimal weights under Exponential and Logistic losses, bypassing iterative optimization. It also introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard approaches to combining classifiers (e.g., boosting) rely on iterative optimization, which obscures the underlying combinatorial structure of the problem. When the number of classifiers is large, the convexified empirical risk may fail to attain a minimum. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, geometrically grounded framework that yields analytical solutions and clarifies existence/uniqueness conditions.

Method: The method leverages truth tables to represent binary classifiers, partitioning the data into equivalence classes. This structuration enables a multidimensional generalization of classification-calibrated functions. The authors analyze the convexified empirical risk landscape by studying the geometry of the resulting polytopes, establishing sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of global minima. For the three-classifier case, they exhaustively enumerate all possible configurations. Analytical closed-form weight formulas are derived for Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions. The notion of φ-frontiers is introduced to assess classifier stability and data quality.

Result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of the global minimum of convexified empirical risk are established. In the three-classifier case, all configurations leading to unique solutions, infima, or non-unique minima are fully characterized. Explicit analytical formulas for optimal weights are obtained for Exponential and Logistic losses. The φ-frontier concept provides a tool for evaluating stability and data quality.

Conclusion: The truth-table structuration approach provides a powerful framework for understanding linear classifier combination. By replacing iterative optimization with analytical solutions, the method offers both computational advantages and deeper theoretical insight. The φ-frontier concept further enables practical assessment of classifier reliability and dataset quality.

Abstract: This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

</details>


### [258] [Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14895)
*Yu-Du Feng,Niels Mündler-Sasahara,Mark Vero,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a cost-effective method to improve reasoning language models (RLMs) by leveraging unused supervised fine-tuning data. The approach involves instruction tuning (without reasoning traces) on the RLM, then merging the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model. This boosts performance in both verifiable (e.g., coding) and hard-to-verify (e.g., text summarization) domains for under $3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLMs excel in verifiable domains like math and coding, where reinforcement learning relies on reliable output verification. However, training RLMs in domains lacking reliable verifiers remains challenging. Additionally, large amounts of supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions currently go unused. The authors aim to efficiently exploit these unused data to further improve RLM performance across both verifiable and unverifiable domains.

Method: The method consists of two stages: (1) Classic instruction tuning — applying supervised fine-tuning *without* reasoning traces on the RLM using existing human-written solution data. (2) Model merging — fusing the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover the original model's reasoning behavior on the target domain, thereby combining the benefits of both.

Result: Extensive evaluation shows the technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable domains (coding) and hard-to-verify domains (text summarization), while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. The method is highly cost-effective, requiring less than $3 to achieve these gains.

Conclusion: Unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions can be efficiently leveraged to improve RLM performance across diverse domains. The proposed instruction-tuning-then-merging pipeline is a low-cost, effective strategy that broadens RLM applicability beyond verifiable domains without sacrificing general reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

</details>


### [259] [A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14937)
*Christoph Jürgen Hemmer,Florian Plaswig,Daniel Durstewitz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DynaBase is a stripped-down, two-parameter version of the DynaMix foundation model that achieves competitive zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction by linearly blending the current latent state with the nearest in-context neighbor and its successor, revealing minimal mechanisms for in-context learning in this domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current foundation models for zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction achieve strong generalization but remain opaque "black boxes." The authors aim to strip down complex architectures to identify the minimal essential mechanisms underlying in-context learning for DS forecasting, thereby improving interpretability and theoretical understanding.

Method: The authors iteratively reduced the SOTA DynaMix model to a minimal two-parameter form called DynaBase. This model forecasts via a linear interpolation between the current latent state and the nearest neighbor (and its temporal successor) from the in-context set. The extreme simplicity enables direct optimization on DS reconstruction metrics and yields closed-form one-step analytical solutions for prediction MSE. Theoretical analysis reveals a one-parameter family of maps, with known algorithms (e.g., context-parroting) at one extreme and chaotic divergent behavior at the other.

Result: DynaBase achieves highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstruction across chaotic and cyclic systems despite using orders of magnitude fewer parameters than other foundation models. The one-parameter family analysis reconciles divergent observations in the literature, and different training strategies yield models optimized either for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction.

Conclusion: Minimal mechanisms — specifically nearest-neighbor lookup with linear blending — suffice for effective zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction. DynaBase provides an interpretable, mathematically tractable framework that unifies disparate findings in the literature and clarifies the trade-off between short-term prediction and long-term reconstruction fidelity.

Abstract: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

</details>


### [260] [Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14940)
*Phevos Paschalidis,Constantinos Daskalakis,Devavrat Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a method for causal inference in sequential, observational settings with outcome interference, using Ising models for binary outcomes across time and Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning. The approach accounts for latent confounders via low-rank factor structure and is validated on synthetic data and a COVID-19 vaccine case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal inference methods struggle with outcome interference (where one unit's outcome affects another's) in sequential observational settings with latent confounding. The authors aim to provide a computationally efficient method that can handle high-dimensional, time-series data with binary outcomes, where the number of units N and time steps T are both large.

Method: The authors model binary outcomes across N units and T time steps using a Markovian Ising model, where dependencies between units are captured by the Ising model's pairwise interactions, and external fields incorporate treatment effects and latent confounders. Latent confounders follow a low-rank factor structure akin to panel data models. Given a single high-dimensional sample, they employ Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for computationally efficient parameter learning. Causal quantities are then estimated by sampling from the learned model.

Result: Under mild assumptions, the authors establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation via MPLE and show that this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest. The method demonstrates strong empirical performance on synthetic experiments and provides meaningful insights in a real-world case study examining the causal effects of vaccination rates on COVID-19 death rates across US counties.

Conclusion: The proposed MPLE-based framework offers a principled and computationally tractable approach to causal inference under outcome interference in sequential observational studies, bridging Ising models, latent factor confounding, and causal estimands. The method scales to high-dimensional real-world applications, as evidenced by the COVID-19 analysis.

Abstract: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

</details>


### [261] [LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14952)
*Changhai Zhou,Kieran Liu,Yuhua Zhou,Qian Qiao,Jun Gao,Harry Zhang,Irvine Lu,Nolan Ho,Lucian Li,Andrew Lei,Cleon Cheng,Steven Chiang,Yihang Zeng,Di Zhang,Rio Yang,Kaijie Chen,Andrew Chen,Pony Ma,Weizhong Zhang,Cheng Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LongStraw is an execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training (via GRPO) under fixed GPU budgets by decoupling prompt scoring (no autograd) from lightweight response replay, demonstrated on Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2 at up to 4.46M tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A growing gap exists between inference context lengths (approaching millions of tokens) and RL post-training context lengths (often ≤256K tokens). This gap particularly affects AI agents whose long-horizon trajectories accumulate observations, tool outputs, and prior decisions. Existing post-training infrastructure cannot handle million-token contexts within fixed GPU budgets.

Method: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for GRPO-based RL post-training. It (1) evaluates the shared prompt without autograd to avoid storing the full forward graph, (2) retains only model-specific state (e.g., recurrent hidden states or compressed attention key-value caches) needed by later tokens, and (3) replays short response branches one at a time for gradient computation. This trades additional replay time for drastically reduced peak memory. Implementations target hybrid recurrent/full-attention (Qwen3.6-27B) and compressed-attention MoE (GLM-5.2) architectures.

Result: On 8 H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8, with only 0.21 GB additional peak memory when scaling group size. A stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, the full end-to-end execution path is validated at 2.1M tokens across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These results demonstrate execution capacity; full training correctness is not yet established due to detached prompt state and incomplete distributed forward/gradient paths.

Conclusion: LongStraw demonstrates the feasibility of million-token-scale RL post-training under constrained GPU budgets through architecture-aware execution strategies. However, the work establishes execution capacity rather than end-to-end training correctness, with several composition paths remaining incomplete.

Abstract: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

</details>


### [262] [Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14962)
*Ku Onoda,Paavo Parmas,Hiroki Furuta,Soichiro Nishimori,Yuta Oshima,Shohei Taniguchi,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Text-to-image models often lack diversity, generating images that cover only a subset of possible visual modes for a given prompt, which can amplify demographic bias. The authors formalize this as "target-mode coverage" and propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective that rewards samples for improving coverage across predefined semantic categories. Validated on synthetic data and SD3.5-M, the method improves fairness scores by 0.23–0.36 while preserving image quality and text alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: T2I models produce realistic images but exhibit limited mode coverage — samples from the same prompt often cluster around a narrow set of visual modes, and for person-centric prompts, this manifests as demographic skew (e.g., overrepresentation of certain races, genders, or ages). Existing approaches lack a principled mechanism to explicitly optimize for coverage across semantically specified target categories.

Method: The paper formalizes the problem as target-mode coverage — covering a predefined set of semantically specified modes. The core contribution is multi-axis max@K, a group-based RL objective: given a batch of K samples and per-category scores, it computes the maximum score per category across samples and sums these maxima. The credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, enabling different samples to specialize in covering different categories. The objective is applied to diffusion-based T2I models, validated first on a synthetic mixture and SD3.5-M with deterministic color rewards, then evaluated on perceived-appearance fairness.

Result: The credit-assignment mechanism was validated on synthetic data and SD3.5-M using pixel-based color rewards. For fairness evaluation across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improved the Fairness Score by 0.23–0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

Conclusion: Multi-axis max@K provides an effective group-level RL objective for improving target-mode coverage in T2I models, demonstrably reducing demographic skew without sacrificing generation quality or prompt alignment.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

</details>


### [263] [Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14995)
*Sara Ketabi,Matthias W. Wagner,Cynthia Hawkins,Uri Tabori,Birgit Betina Ertl-Wagner,Farzad Khalvati*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MseaCL proposes a multimodal contrastive learning framework that uses semantic similarity between radiology reports to mitigate false negatives in medical imaging, achieving significant improvements in downstream tasks like pediatric brain tumor classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional contrastive learning assumes instance-based correspondence, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. In medical settings, this fails because samples often share high-level semantic attributes, creating false negatives that degrade representation quality.

Method: The authors propose MseaCL, which incorporates semantic similarity between radiology reports as a guiding signal during contrastive learning. The framework is trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain MRI scans paired with radiology reports, using semantic-aware weighting to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples.

Result: The framework used as a pretraining stage achieved at least a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating notable improvements in downstream task performance.

Conclusion: MseaCL shows strong potential for producing more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications by addressing the false negative problem inherent in medical contrastive learning.

Abstract: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

</details>


### [264] [Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15067)
*Joshua Spear,Matthieu Komorowski,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire,Erica E. M. Moodie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kernel-WIS is a novel off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that combines the boundedness of Weighted Importance Sampling with the unbiasedness of standard Importance Sampling, achieving asymptotic consistency and superior empirical performance, especially under behavior policy misspecification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Off-policy evaluation using only offline data is challenging, particularly when the behavior policy is misspecified. Existing estimators like vanilla Importance Sampling (IS) suffer from high variance, while Weighted Importance Sampling (WIS) is bounded but biased. The authors aim to bridge this gap by designing an estimator that inherits the strengths of both approaches.

Method: The proposed Kernel-WIS estimator integrates the linear, unbiased property of vanilla IS with the bounded, variance-controlled property of vanilla WIS. It employs kernel-based weighting to smoothly interpolate between the two estimators, yielding an asymptotically consistent estimator suitable for contextual bandit settings with offline data.

Result: Kernel-WIS is proven to be asymptotically consistent and empirically outperforms strong baselines, including vanilla WIS. Its advantages are most pronounced under complex conditions such as behavior policy misspecification.

Conclusion: Kernel-WIS provides a principled and practical solution for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits, effectively combining the complementary strengths of IS and WIS. It is both theoretically grounded and empirically robust, making it well-suited for challenging real-world scenarios with imperfect behavior policies.

Abstract: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

</details>


### [265] [An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15077)
*Yao Cheng Li,Ana Larrañaga,Steven L. Brunton,Urban Fasel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This tutorial paper introduces the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method for discovering interpretable governing equations from limited data, progressively building from the standard algorithm to advanced extensions, with practical engineering case studies on UAV system identification and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineering problems often lack well-characterized governing equations, and while surrogate models like neural networks can approximate system behavior, they require large datasets and produce models with poor physical interpretability. SINDy addresses both limitations by enabling interpretable equation discovery from small datasets, yet its practical engineering adoption remains limited and under-documented.

Method: The paper presents SINDy as a sparse regression framework over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, organized in three parts: (1) the standard algorithm with progressive extensions including noise-robust weak-form variants, ensembling-based approaches, and constrained/parametrizable formulations; (2) a case study on UAV system identification; and (3) a case study on a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. An accompanying GitHub repository provides hands-on tutorial materials.

Result: The paper demonstrates through case studies that SINDy is simple to implement and flexible enough for advanced engineering applications, successfully identifying dynamics for both an unmanned aerial vehicle and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger using comparatively small datasets, while yielding physically interpretable governing equations.

Conclusion: SINDy offers a practical, interpretable alternative to black-box surrogate models for engineering system identification, bridging the gap between data-driven modeling and physical understanding. Its extensions make it robust to noise and applicable to constrained, parametrized real-world problems.

Abstract: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

</details>


### [266] [Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15080)
*Joshua Spear,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether covariate balance diagnostics can detect hidden confounding or model misspecification in offline RL for treatment recommendations, finds that existing studies are not statistically robust, and proposes future methodological directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline reinforcement learning is increasingly applied to derive optimal treatment recommendations from observational data. However, such data is susceptible to hidden confounding and model misspecification. The authors are motivated by the need to determine whether existing diagnostic tools—specifically covariate balance metrics—are adequate for detecting these threats to validity in offline RL studies.

Method: The authors apply covariate balance diagnostics to existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations, systematically evaluating whether these diagnostics can reliably detect hidden confounding or model misspecification. The approach involves assessing the relationship between balance metrics and potential sources of bias in the RL pipeline.

Result: The analysis reveals a dilemma: either (1) existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations carry a high risk of hidden bias, or (2) current covariate balance metrics are insufficient for evaluating such studies. In either case, existing offline RL studies cannot be considered statistically robust.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the current state of offline RL for treatment recommendations lacks demonstrated statistical robustness and calls for future research to develop more methodologically sound approaches, including better diagnostics for confounding and misspecification in this context.

Abstract: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

</details>


### [267] [Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15107)
*Sridhar Mahadevan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LINCS is a categorical framework that recasts machine learning as the repair of non-compositionality — failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches — extended to the tangent category setting. Learning problems are represented as sketches (graphs with commutativity, limit, and colimit conditions), and learning is formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point in an iterated tangent lift tower.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a unified categorical foundation for machine learning that shifts the notion of error from arithmetic loss to structural non-compositionality — the failure of universal factorization. This reframes learning as repairing diagrammatic consistency rather than minimizing scalar loss functions, offering a more general and compositional perspective applicable across diverse ML paradigms.

Method: The framework defines learning sketches S = (S, D, L, K) as graphs with commutativity conditions, limit cones, and colimit cocones. Non-compositionality is the obstruction Obs(Fact_S(D)) to a factorization problem. The tangent functor T lifts a model D to TD, and LINCS is the obstruction Obs(Fact_S(TD)), checking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve compositionality. The INC endofunctor iterates this tangent lift, producing a tower D, TD, T²D, ... . Using the Aczel–Mendler theorem, a final INC coalgebra (νT_INC) is proven to exist when T_INC admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier.

Result: The paper proves existence of a final INC coalgebra (a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize) under the condition that the INC endofunctor admits a set-based class realization creating its final carrier. This establishes a terminal object in the category of learning dynamics, formalizing ML as convergence to compositional consistency. Experimental validation is deferred to companion papers.

Conclusion: LINCS provides a rigorous categorical reformulation of machine learning as the iterative repair of non-compositionality through tangent lifts, culminating in a coalgebraic fixed point. This shifts the conceptual foundation of ML from numeric optimization to structural factorization, with potential applications across deep learning, LLMs, and reinforcement learning, though empirical validation remains forthcoming.

Abstract: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

</details>


### [268] [On-Policy Delta Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15161)
*Byeongho Heo,Jaehui Hwang,Sangdoo Yun,Dongyoon Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), a new reinforcement learning post-training method that uses a "delta signal" — the difference between a teacher model and its pre-instruction-tuning base model — as a distillation reward, rather than directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. This approach substantially improves on-policy distillation performance across math, science, and code reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods in RL directly imitate the teacher model's output distribution, but the fundamental design of distillation rewards remains underexplored. The authors argue that a more effective signal for transferring reasoning capabilities can be derived by capturing the changes induced specifically by reasoning instruction tuning.

Method: The authors propose the "delta signal" as a new distillation reward, computed as the difference between a teacher model and its base model (prior to instruction tuning for reasoning). This isolates reasoning-specific improvements. The resulting method, On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), uses this delta signal for token-level supervision during on-policy RL post-training.

Result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks show OPD² consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period.

Conclusion: The delta signal provides a more direct and effective mechanism for transferring reasoning capabilities in on-policy distillation, offering a simple yet powerful improvement over standard imitation-based approaches.

Abstract: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

</details>


### [269] [RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15180)
*Ahmet Demirkaya,Georgios Stratis,Tales Imbiriba,Zachary D. Danziger,Deniz Erdogmus*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid neural–physics framework that alternates between RTS smoothing for latent state inference and backpropagation for neural network parameter estimation to learn missing ODE components from partial state observations, retaining mechanistic interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many dynamical systems modeled by ODEs have partially unknown dynamics and only a subset of state variables are measured. Purely black-box neural approaches sacrifice interpretable structure, while purely mechanistic models cannot capture unknown components.

Method: A two-stage iterative framework: (1) With model parameters fixed, infer latent states from partial measurements via a Rauch–Tung–Striebel (RTS) smoother.
